I. Coal as a source of energy plays the paramount role in the development and growth of 
economy, therefore, Coal is metaphorically known as Black Diamond. Coal is the source of 
electricity generation in the Thermal Power Station. Moreover , o ther Industries of the economy 
like steel, cement, fertilizers, chemicals, papers and thousand of medium and Small Scale 
Industries are dependent of Coal for their process and energy requirements. 
1.1 The main subjects allocated to the Department of Coal under the Government of India 
(Allocation of Business) Rules , 1961, as amended from time to time , are development and 
exploitation of coal and lignite reserves in India; all matters relating to production, supply 
distribution and pricing of coal, development and operati on of coal washeries, administration of 
Coal Bearing Areas (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1957, administration of Public Sector 
Enterprises dealing with coal and lignite and all business incidental to the administration of 
above activities including matters concerning the State Government etc . 
1.2 '!'he Department of Coal has under its direct administration control the following two 
public sector undertakings. 
(i) Coal India Ltd.; and 
(ii) Neyveli Lign ite Corporation Ltd . 
1.2.1 Coal India Ltd . having headquarters at Calcutta , is the holding company with seven 
producing subsidiaries and one planning and design subsidiary , viz. 
(i) Eastern Coalfields Limited (ECL), Sanctoria (West Bengal ; 
(ii) Bharat Cocking Coal Ltd. (BCCL), Dhanabad (Biha r) 
(iii) Central Coalfields Ltd. (CCL), Ranchi (Bihar) 
(iv) Northern Coalfields Ltd. (N_~L) , Singrauli (Madhya Pradesh); 
(v) Western Coalfield Ltd. (WCL) , Nagpur (Maharash tra); 
(vi) South Eastern Coalfield Ltd. (SECL) , Bilaspur !madhya Pradesh); 
(vii)' Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd. (MCL), Sambalpur (Orissa ); and 
(viii) Central Mine Planning & Design Institute Ltd. (CMPDIL ), Ranchi (Bihar). 
1.2.2 The Department of Coal has also under its administrative control the Neyveli Lignite 
Corp oration Ltd., with headquarters at Neyveli in Tamil Nadu. The compan y is primar ily 
engaged in the exploitation of lignite deposits in Tamil nadu and generation of power from 
lignite based power projects . 
1.2.3 The Singareni Collieries Company Ltd. incorporated as public limited company in 1920 
became a Government company in 1956 with headquarters at Kothagudam in Andhra Pradesh. 
2 . The Secretary, during the course of oral evidence highlighted the performance of the 
coal sector . He submitted to the Committee that 
"The coal sector, after having witnessed recession in the recent past started showing 
positive growth in this year. Coal production and offtake have staged a recovery in the current 
year , when compared to the negative growth in 1998-99. Coal production from April to 
February in the current year is approximately 266 million tonne from April to February last 

year, the actual performance for the same period in the current year is more than 272 million 
tonne. We are confident that the current year's target of298.90 million tonne of coal production 
and offtake of about 300 mill1on tonne will be fully met. This will be a record-breaking 
achievement." 
2.1 However, the Secretary also elaborated the concern of Coal sector as under:-
" Indian coal is getting out-priced by the imported coal at certain destinations, 
particularly coastal regions in the country. Low rates of import duty, high railway 
freights, and additional burdens of royalty/taxes are the main factors contributing to the 
rise of more imports over the years. The basic import duty on non-coking coal which 
was 85 per cent in 1992-93 was reduced to 15 per cent in 1999-2000. The railway 
freight on coal has been continuously going up over the years. It has gone up by 68 per 
cent smce I 992. further, it is estimated that coal freight is also loaded by about 30 per 
cent for subsidizing the passenger traffic by the Rail"ays . For example, the coal going 
from South Eastern Coalfields or the Mahanandi Coalfields to the coastal areas in 
Gujarat and Maharashtra, has to bear a freight as high as 200 per cent to 300 per cent of 
the coal price. It is ironical that coal traffic, whit.h con ~tltutes between 45 per cent of the 
Indian Railway's total revenue is being subjected to most unreasonable hikes and 
additional burdens. We have been addressing the Ministry of Railways and the Ministry 
of Finance also to rationalize the freight structure and provide a level playing field to 
indigenous coal vis-a-vis imported coal. Unfortunateiy, without any succ~ss."

1 5. COMPENSATION FOR LAND ACQUISITION 
15.1 The Committee wanted to know the basic policy behind fixing of rate of compensation 
for land acquisition for exploration and Detailed Drilling. The Department of Coal informed that 
under Section 4 (1) of the Coal Bearing Areas Acquisition and Development Act, a notification 
is issued whenever it appears to the Central Government that coal is likely to be obtained from 
the land. Land is acquired only when it is established through the prospecting undertake'n in 
terms of notification u/s 4 ( 1) of the Act that coal is obtainable from the land and the coal 
companies find it commercially viable to exploit the coal deposits found therein. Section 13 of 
the Act lays down the principles and procedures for determination of compensation for 
acquisition of prospecting licenses, rights under mining leases , land, standing crops, trees etc. 
Section 13 (5) provides that compensation for land shall be determined after taking into 
consideration the market value of the land on the date of publication of the notification under 
Section 4 ( 1) of the Act. Fair market value · is assessed on the basis of the land transactions 
recorded in the office of local Registrar of the concerned area during the preceding three years. 

On the market value so assessed, solatium @ 30% and additional compensation @ 12% (for a 
maximum period of three years) is also payable. In case of delay in payment of compensation 
interest @ 9% for the first year and 15% for the subsequent years is paid the land losers to 
compensate for the delay. 
15.2 The Committee observes that regulatory provision for compensation for land acquisition 
for regional exploration and detailed drilling. Section 13(5) of th.e Coal Bearing Areas 
Acquisition and Development Act lapse down the principles and procedure for determination 
of compensation. The Committee is of the view that while making assessment of fair market 
value the Department of coal should take care the interest of persons whose land is being 
acquired and efforts should be taken for timely disposal of cases of compensation as this 
measures if implemented would give timely solve to the land owner as welt as save considerable 
about of money of Department of coal, its be given to land owner in case of delay of 
compensation cases.

17. PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN COAL MINING INDUSTRY 
17:·1 During the course of oral-evidence the Committee wanted to know the policy framework 
for inducing private investment in Coal Mining Industry and the programme undertaken in this 
regard. The Department of Coal informed the Committee that suitable amendment has been 
effected in the coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 to allow coal mining for captive 
consumption in power generation and such other end uses to be notified by the Central 
Government from time to time in addition to the existing provision for coal mining for captive 
consumption in iron and steel production. In exercise of the powers conferred on the Central 
Government under the June I 993 amendment, coal mining for captive consumption for cement 
production was allowed by a Gazette Notification issued on 15.3.96. These provision in the Coal 
Mines (Nationali sation) Act, 1973 as well as in the Gazette Notification apply to the public sector 
as well as private sector. Section 3 (3) (a) (iii) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, !973 as 
amended in June, 1993 provides that no company other than a company engaged in power 
generation, etc. can do coal mining. As such, the literal meaning of this provision conveys that the 
coal mining company and the end-user company has to be the same entity. 
17.2 However, in September, 1995 the then Ministry of Coal obtained the advice of the then 
Attorney General of India that coal mining by associated coal companies can be allowed provided 
the end-user company (e.g: power generating company. iron and steel producing company, etc.) 
holds at least 25% of voting equity in the coal mining company, the same principle was also made 
applicable in a situation when a holding company was formed that two subsidiaries viz. (i) the 
end-user company and (ii) the associated coal company. In the later situation, it was stipulated 
that the holding company should have at least 25% equity share at all times in both the end user 
company and the associated coal company. 

17.3 The Committee was given to understand that a Screening Committee has been 
constituted in Department of Coal to consider the proposals by various parties for allocation of 
captive coal mining blocks. 24 coal blocks have so far been offered to various parties in the 
private and public sector. Out of these 24 blocks, previous approval of the Central Government 
has been accorded in respect of 6 blocks under the proviso to Section 5 (I) of the Mines & 
Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1957, for grant of mining lease by the respective 
State Governments. The communications to the State Governments to convey the previous 
approval has been issued after the mining plans in respect of these blocks were approved by the 
Department of Coal. Two captive mining companies in the private secto r viz. (i) Bengal Emta 
coal Mining Limited and (ii) Jindal Steel and Power Limited have already started coal mining 
from their respective captive blocks. 
17.4 The Department of Coal informed the Committee that ratio of government and private 
participation in coal mining in the country is therefore 97.59% and 2.41% respectively as on 
31.3.99.

notification in the official Gazette with effect from such date as may be specified in the 
notification .

FOURTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry having been authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, 
present this Fourth Report of the Committee on the status of Mini Steel Plants. 
2. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling within the jurisdiction of 
the Ministries of Industry, Steel and Mines. 
3. The Committee at its meeting held on 15th June, 1993 identified 'Mini Steel Plants -
their status' as one of the subjects relating to the Ministry of Steel for its indepth study and 
report. The Committee directed the Secretariat to obtain a note on the subject for its 
consideration. 
4. The Committee held a general discussion on the existing status of Mini Steel Plants in 
the country on Monday, the 28th June, 1993 in the light of the note furnished by the 
Ministry. The Committee finalised a questionnaire for further clarifications by the Ministry 
on the subject. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretary of the Ministry on the 
subject on the 29th September, 1993. 
6. The Committee considered the subject in three sittings and considered and adopted 
the Report at its sitting held on 20th December, 1993.

refined to produce steel ingots/billets. During the seventies in view of the indigenous 
availability of steel melting scrap , units were allowed to produce mild steel ignots to meet 
the demand of structural steel for construction purposes. At present, there are 177 Mini

Besides there are also a large number of small induction furnaces which were estabiished 
as small-scale units to manufacture castings but now are also producing mild steel ingots. 
The Government are, however, not encouraging manufacture of steel in induction furnaces 
as these units are of small size wherein it is not possible to adequately refine steel in such 
furnaces. These furnaces , however , need less power than electric arc furnaces. The n•Jmber 
of induction furnaces is not known but it is estimated between 400 to 700. Their estimated 
production during 1992-93 was estimated around 1.01 million tonnes. The working group on 
Iron and Steel Industry fo.- the 8th Five Year Plan has estimated that the production of 
crude steel by Mini Steel Plants will increase from about 4.00 million tonnes in 1991-92 to 
7.5 million tonnes in 1996-97 and 11 million tonnes in 1999-2000 AD. 
7.2 In the new industrial policy announced by the Government in July , 1991, the iron 
and steel industry has been removed from the list of industries reserved for the public sector 
and also exempted from compulsory licensing under the Industries (Development and 
Regulation) Act, 1951. 

3 
7.3 The broad characteristics of the electric arc furnaces in the country are: 
(a) majority of them are of small size and scattered all over the country. About 73 per 
cent have capacities upto 12 tonnes only, therefore, their modernisation and 
upgradation of technology is limited. 
(b) only about 27 per cent are of sizes 15 tonnes and above and only about 5 per cent 
are in the range between 20 to 40 tonnes and 20 percent have capacity above 40 
tonnes per year which can be upgraded by modem technologies for quality steel 
production at economic costs. The Secretary of the Ministry during the course of his 
oral evidence clarified that out of 177 units 73 units are lying closed; 
(c) As per the version of the Ministry most of the electric arc furnaces in industrialised 
countries like USA, Japan, Canada, Western Europe are of the capacity of 20 
tonnes or larger and as per the extraneous information available to the Committee 
the capacity of EAF in these countries is 50 tonnes and above and their 
performance is far better than our mini steel plants based on consumption of raw 
material, productivity technological parametres and energy consumption. A com­

7.4 There have been considerable technological innovations and improvements in 
electric arc furnace steel making during the last twenty years which have resulted in 
reduction in power consumption, improvement in quality and yield. As many as 104 mini 
steel plants have adopted facilities like ultra high power transformer, secondary refining 
system, continuous casting machines etc. 
7.5 The Ministry in their note has also identified that mini steel plants are facing major 
problems like high cost of imported scrap and supply of power . The steel melting scrap is 

the main raw material input for the mini steel plants and cost of scrap constitutes over 60 
per cent of the available cost of production. The availability and price of scrap are major 
factors affecting the operation of mini steel plants . The Govenment furnished the following 
data regarding indigenous availability of scrap and imports during the last five years as

Projected demand of melting Scrap/Sponge Iron for 1993-94 is 
estimated at 76 lakh tonnes. Indigenous availability of melting Scrap 
and Sponge Iron is expected to be around 30 lakh tonnes and 25 
lakh tonnes respectively. Balance requirement of 21 lakh tonnes is 
expected to be met through imports. 
The import of scrap has since been decanalised and freely allowed. The rate per tonne 
of imported scrap varie'S according to fluctuations in demand and supply in the international 
scrap market. The Ministry have stated that it' is, therefore, not possible to indicate a 
specific rate throughout the year. The scrap prices were around Us $ 135 per tonnes (C&F) 
from May/June, 1992 upto December, 1992. Thereafter the prices have increased sharply, 
rising upto US $ 180 per tonne in June, 1993. The prices have now slightly declined to 
around US $ 165 to 170 per tonne and it is expected that they will settle around US $ 160 per 
tonne. At this rate , landed cost is around Rs. 5935/- per tonne. Main sources of import, 
countries of origin-wise are USA, U . K., Belgium and Germany. 
7.6 In order to reduce dependence on imported scrap, Government has identifed the 
sponge iron industry as a thrust area for increased production. Indigenous capacity of 24.9 
lakh tonnes has already been created and a further capacity of about 33.5 lakh tonnes is 
under implementation. Clarifying the extent to which the scrap is made available from Ship 
Breaking and the projected availability of scrap from this source during the next five years, 
the Ministry have stated that the total capacity of the shipbreaking industry in the country is 
estimated to be 1.7 million LDT per year with about 1.5 million LDT capacity available at 
the Alang Shipbreaking Yard alone. The process of shipb,reaking generates oply about 
8-1()% of melting scrap for use in the electric arc furnace units. The bulk of the scrap 
generated (about 66-68%) is re-rollable scrap which is used by there-rolling mills to produce 
steel for the construction industry .• The current production is about 1 million LDT or 7 lakh 
tonnes of re-rollable scrap. This is expected to increase to about 1.5-2 million LDT in the 
next five year i.e. 1-1.4 million tonnes of re-rollable scrap. 
The mini steel plants are highly power intensive in their operations and heavily 
dependent on uninterrupted electricity supply to them. Shortage of electricity greatly affects 
the productivity and viability of the mini steel plants. The viability of operations of mini 
steel plants vary from State to State because their is no uniform electricity tariff policy. 
7.7 The Ministry while clarifying a specific point relating to the per unit cost of 
production of mini steel plant in the country and how does it compare with other countries 

and steps which are proposed to be taken to reduce it substantially during 8th plan informed 
that the average cost of production of 1 tonne of mild steel ingot is about Rs. 10,887/­
through EAF route, (assuming imported scrap at US$ 160 per tonne), though the exact cost 
varies from plant to plant. In the absence of any authentic information of the cost of 
production of steel in other countries, it is not possible to compare the cost of production of 
steel with that of other countries. However, cost of scrap and power which are the major 
inputs for Electric Arc Furnace units is generally lower in the developed countries. 
7.8 The Ministry informed the Committee that the steel industry has requested for 
various reliefs to improve their viability, since demand is sluggish and input costs have gone 
up. The budget proposals for 1993-94 contain measures aimed at reducing the capital and 
production costs of industrial projects including steel plants. These include lowering of 
customs duty on project imports and reduction of minimum mterest rate on commercial 
advances. Besides, reduction of customs duty on imported raw materials & consumable like 
pig iron, isrro-alloys, refractories, graphite electrodes etc. will also reduce the production 
costs of steel. More recently representations from the industry regarding reduction of import 
duty on scrap as well as reduction in excise duty on steel is under consideration. 
8.1 Taking into account the documents and other material made available to it, the 
Committee finds that the present installed capacity of mini steel plants is 73.12 lakh tonnes 
per annum whereas the actual production level is 34 lakh tonnes only. The Committee notes 
with regret that no concrete measures were taken by the Ministry for ensuring optimum use 
of the installed capacity. The country can not afford any alibi in the matter of production of 
steel during the last several years. The Committee is not convinced with the argument that 
the shortage of raw material and power are the only constraints in achieving the objectives. 
The Committee has been informed that out of 177 mini steel plants, 73 units are lying closed 
ranging from one year to ten years for various reasons and, therefore, going by the figures, 
it will be seen that 40 per cent installed capacity is not giving any production. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that as a long term measure a technical 
evaluation group of the experts in the field may be constituted immediately to examine the 
problems of the mini steel plants in general and of the closed mini steel plants in particular. 
The Committee also suggests that short term ..remedial measures may also be introduced so 
that at least the installed capacity is made use of and the vast resources blocked in the closed 
units are generated for the larger good of the country. 
8.2 The Committee intends to emphasise that the mini steel plants play a dominant role 
in our economy. The construction sector is dependent on the mini steel plants for the iron 
which is an essential input for construction of houses, buildings, over-bridges, bridges, etc. 
The mini steel plants have however been left to fend for themselves and this sector has been 
neglected and has not been properly developed. The Committee is informed that the mini 
steel plants were brought under the licensing regime way back in 1973 in order to regulate 
the setting up of new units or expansion of the existing ones. But knowing fully well that 
majority of such plants were having capacities upto 12 tonnes only limiting the capacity of 
the plants to modernise and adopt modem technologies, such plants were not persuaded 
properly to increase their capacities to at least to 20 tonnes so that they could be modernised 
in due course. For the establishment of new plants permission should have been granted for 
large furnaces only keeping in view their future utility and modernisation. 
In the new Industrial Policy of 1991, the mini steel plants have been taken out from 
compulsory licensing schedule. Prior to that the mini steel plants were regulated for their 
modernisation, expansion and establishment. The Committee has not been informed that 
there was any system which could have motivated them for expansion on required lines 
where modernisation could be feasible. They were just allowed to expand without any future 

6 
planning. Their capacities were not taken into account while granting permission for their 
establishment or expansion. The money was just pumped into the plant without any 
consideration for future expansion. This is the picture, the Committee gets. Having come to 
this stage of having a large number of plants with a low capacity of 12 tonnes or below, their 
future and economic viability is doomed. They can neither expand nor modernise. They 
cannot become self supporting. They are a drain on the national resources. Government has 
not applied its mind to this problem. And all of a sudden in the new industrial Policy, the 
licensing has been taken away leaving them on their fate to the wiped out of the economic 
scene of the country. The Commitee records that this is not a very happy situation for a 
developing economy. The concern of the Ministry now at this stage should be to direct its 
attention to the basic question of the survival of these mini steel plants so that economic 
assets which are blocked into them start giving some return to the nation. It can be done if 
some scheme of their amalgamation or cluster type of management and strict monitoring are 
resorted to. This could be done, if Government could talk to the entrepreneurs of these mini 
steel plants on the methods for their survival. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should give due priority to 
the survival of these mini steel plants and prepare a compre~ensive plan for their development 
which may include providing fmancial assistance to them for their expansion and modernisa­
tion, and also making raw material namely the scrap and power, available at reasonable rates 
to the mini steel plants. 
8.3 The mini steel plants are facing major problem in respect of steel melting scrap 
which is the main raw material input of these plants and the cost of scrap constitutes over 60 
per cent of the variable cost of production. The entire demand of scrap can not be met 
indigenously and about 3 million tonnes of scrap has to be imported every year which is too 
costly in view of steep rise in the prices of scrap ·in the international market. However during 
the course of his oral evidence the Secretary could not specify the concrete steps which are 
being taken or proposed to be taken by the Government to overcom~ this problem. 
The Commitee, therefore, recommends that concrete planning is needed to increase the 
indigenous availability of scrap to reduce dependence on imported scrap. Though the import 
of scrap has since been decanalised but it is causing hardships to those mini steel plants whose 
capacity is very low as they are unable to import the scrap due to paucity of funds and also 
due to less quantity required by them. The Committee recommends that efforts should be 
made by the Government to bring together these mini steel plants and import their requisite 
quota of scrap on their behalf and distribute the same among them at "no profit no loss" 
basis. 
In this connection the Committee would like to observe that in order to provide raw 
material to the mini steel plant sector, ship breaking industry could be exploited - though 
ship breaking industry is concentrated at Alang in Gujarat and some Japanese companies 
have shown keen interest in this industry. In view of the fact that single huiied ships in the 
country are now being phased out and having a long coastal line at our disposal, ship 
breaking industry could be developed. 
The Committee would, therefore, recommend that while encouraging ship breaking 
industry proper and adequate protection to the fiShing industry and environmental protection 
need to be taken care of fully to get raw material for the mini steel plants to the extent 
possible. The Committee is conscious of the fact that major portion of the scrap that comes 
out from the ship breaking industry goes directly to rolling mills but it will certainly help the 
mini steel sector also. 
8.4 The another problem being faced by the mini s"teel plants is power which is in short 
supply. Mini steel plants are highly power intensive and require uninterrupted power supply 

for their operations. Unfortunately projections indicate that most of the States will remain 
deficit in power even by the end of the 8th and 9th Five Year Plans. 
Since the shortage of power greatly affects the productivity and economic viability of mini 
steel plants the Committee recommends that Government should evolve a policy to assist the 
mini steel . plants to generate electricity for their consumption without depending upon 
Electricity Boards which can be done by way of providing low rate interest loans by fmancial 
institutions for installing mini power plants to be jointly shared by cluster of industries 
including mini steel plants. At the same time it is essential that States may also be advised to 
fix special rates of tariff for the mini steel sector. 
8.5 The Committee finds that there is no mini steel plant in the backward region of 
North Eastern States and only 33 units in the Eastern a.1d 30 units in the Southern region 
respectively. It clearly reflects that in the entire North Eastern region and most of the 
industrially backward States, the mini steel sector has not been properly developed inspite of 
various concessional packages. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should provide infrastructural 
development of all the backward States/areas so that mini steel plants are established in such 
States which may develop their economy as well as generate employment for the people, of the 
area. 
8.6 The Committee finds that infrastructure of closed mini steel plants is not being 
utilised in any manner. The machinery, raw material, buildings and land are lying unused. 
The machines are becoming junk and similar is the case of material lying therein. If there is 
no possibility of their revival, efforts should be made to utilise the infrastructure somewhere 
else in other units . 
The Committee recommends that Government should undertake a survey of those closed 
mini steel plants in the country which can not be revived, about their assets and report to 
both the Houses of Parliament with a clear cut picture and action proposed to be taken 
thereon at the earliest opportunity. 
8. 7 The Committee finds that in the case of 18 units which were closed recently, the 
major reason advanced has been the market condition and the high prices of scrap. It has 
already been pointed out that the estimated demand for scrap in the country is 7 million 
tonnes per annum and indigenous availability of scrap is about three million tonnes per 
annum thus leaving a gap of 4 million tonnes which has to be imported. The import is now 
freely allowed but the international prices of scrap have risen period from US $ 135 per 
tonne to US $ 180 per tonne. Apart from this high cost factor the Government is charging an 
import duty of 12.50 per cent on the scrap. The Committee is of the opinion that this has 
certainly escalated the production costs of the tbe mini steel plants resulting in the closure of 
mini steel plants. The mini steel plants despite of raising the prices of their produce very 
frequently are not economically viable. The Committee appreciates that the import duty on 
the scrap was brought down from 35 per cent to 12.50 per cent but for the survival of the 
mini steel plants this is not enough. The prices of scrap in the international market is really 
on the high side. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the import duty on scrap be brought down 
considerably so as to enable the mini steel plants or Electric Arc Furnaces to survive. 
8.8 The mini steel plants generally produce ingots/billets or long products such as bars 
and rounds which are mainly used for construction purposes. In the General Budget 1993-94 
the excise duties on the products of mini steel plants was raised from Rs. 29()1.. to Rs. 100()1.. 
per tonne. This has further deepened the crisis in the mini steel plants industry which has 
been hard hit by the high price of scrap abroad and import duty on scrap. The increase in 
the excise duty has certainly affected the viability of mini steel plants. 

The Committee; therefore, recommends that the excise duty on the products of mini steel 
plants be lowered considerably so that the industry could survive. The Committee feels tltat 
since the excise duty on sponge iron is quite higher than that of scrap the mini steel plants 
cannot make use of sponge iron as a raw material at reasonable prices. The Committee, 
therefore, recommends that the issue of excise duty on sponge iron and scrap be examined 
together with a view to maintain a rationale. 
8.9 The main raw material input for the mini steel plants is steel melting scrap. Present 
requirement of mini steel plants is 7 million tonnes of scrap whereas indigenous availability 
of scrap is about 3 million tonnes. Sponge iron is a partial substitute for scrap. The 
Committee appreciates that some efforts are being made by the Government to increase the 
availability of sponge iron. 
The Committee, however, recommends that much more thrust is required to be made to 
increase the production of sponge iron in the country for the benefit of mini steel plants. 
8.10 At the .:!nd, the Committee notes with concern that more than ten thousand 
workers have been rendered jobless due to the closure of mini steel plants in various States 
and Union Territories in the country particularly in the States of Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat, 
Kerala, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal and no definite proposals for their 
rehabilitation have been placed before the Committee by the Government. It appears that 
the hapless workers of the closed mini steel plants have been left to fend for themselves. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should immediately undertake 
rehabilitation measures for such workers of the closed mini steel plants by either providing 
alternative jobs to them or giving them adequate help to enable them to gain self employment 
at the earliest. According to the Committee, the rehabilitation measures should specifically 
provide for training to the workers suited to their skill and potential so that they could utilise 
such training while opting for a suitable job somewhere else. 
8.11 The Committee, in general, has noted that the steel sector as a whole is in 
doldrum with a number of plants either closed or at the brink of closure due to continuous 
decline in their viability. In such continuing trend, privatisation of certain plants by 
Government particularly that of liSCO , Burnpur is on anvil. 
The Committee expresses its deep concern over the situation and impresses upon 
Government to explore all possible ways to revive the liSCO and other sick steel plants. 
8.12 The Committee trusts that the observations and recommendation s as mentioned 
above will receive serious consideration for implementation.

REPORT 
The Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and Validation) Bill, 1995 was introduced in 
Rajya Sabha on the 14th February, 1995 and was referred to the Committee on Industry by the 
Hon 'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on 2nd February, 2000 under Rule 270(b) of the Rules of 
Procedure and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha for examination and report thereon. 
2. The Bill aims to empower the Central government to direct the transfer of the land, or of 
the rights, in or over land or of the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine, coking coal 
mine or coke oven plant, vested in the Coal India Limited or in a subsidiary company to any 
subsidiary company of Coal India Limited or any other subsidiary company and to validate 
certain transfers of such land or rights. 
3. According to the statement of objects and reasons of the Bill, the coal industry was 
nationalized in two phases, that is, in 1972 and 1973. After nationalization, the coking and non­
coking coal mines in the Jharia coal field in Bihar and a few mines in Barakar and Mugma 
regions were directed to be vested in the Bharat Coking Coal Limited, Dhanbad. Most of the 
other coal mines in the states of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and 
Maharashtra were directed to be vested in the Coal Mines Authority Limited. Subsequently, a 
holding company namely, the Coal India Limited was set up with effect from the I st November, 
1975 initially with five subsidiaries. Later three more subsidiaries were created by delinking 
certain collieries from other subsidiaries. 
4. Ever since the nationalisation of the coal industry, though the land or rights in or over 
such land acquired under various Acts and the right, title interest in relation to a coal mine or a 
coke oven plant were directed to be vested in the Coal India Limited or its predecessor in title, its 
subsidiary companies were defacto managing such land, coal mines or plants. 
5. The statement of objects and reasons of the Bill points out that the absence of a formal 
legal title to the land or rights in or over such land or the right, title and interest in relation to a 
coal mine or coke oven plant, in the subsidiary companies has exposed them to litigation and 
other legal infirmities. While the Companies Act, I 956 contains provisions for reconstruction 
and amalgamations, such reconstruction or amalgamation could be given effect to prospectively 
only under that Act. 
6. Under the circumstances, the Bill intends to empower the Central Government to direct 
the transfer of land or the rights in or over such land or the right, title or interest in relation to a 
coal mine or coke oven plant vested in the Coal India Limited to a subsidiary company, or where 
such land or mine are vested in a subsidiary company, to another subsidiary company. It has also 
been considered necessary to validate all purported transfers of the land or rights in or over such 
land or the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine or coke oven plant from the Coal 
India Limited to a subsidiary comp&ny and from one subsidiary company to another subsidiary 
company before the commencement ofthe proposed legislation. 
7. As a matter of fact all the transfers and distribution of the coal mines to various 
subsidiaries of CIL were made by administrative orders and therefore the subsidiaries have been 
enjoying only the defacto possession over them. The title over these mines/properties have not 
passed on to the subsidiary companies of CIL till now and in the eyes of law CIL is still holding 
title over these mines. 
8. The background note on the Bill furnished by the Ministry of Coal gives the details of 
circumstances under which the present Bill needs immediate legislation. In August, 1990, the 
Supreme Court decided a matter in which Bharat Coking Coal Ltd. was the appellant and the 
l 

Government of Bihar and others were the respondents. The subject matter ofthe appeal was the 
legality of grant of mining lease by the Government of Bihar to remove slurry discharged from 
the Sudamdih coal washery of BCCL and deposited on the land forming part of the land in 
Sudamdih which was earlier acquired under the provisions of the Coal Bearting Areas 
(Acquisition & Development) Act, 1957. After the Central Government acquired the land some 
time in 1961, it was subsequently transferred to National Coal Development Corporation Ltd. in 
1962. This land formed part of Sudamdih and Moonidih group of mines developed by the 
erstwhile NCDC. The Central Government subsequently directed the transfer of Sudamdih and 
Moonidih group of mines to BCCL and advised Coal India Ltd. to take necessary steps to 
implement the decision. While the Moonidih and Sudamdih group of mines were transferred and 
delivered to BCCL w.e.f. 1.4.1975, legal formalities of transfer could not be completed. In the 
appeal which was heard by Supreme Court, the major issues to be decided were( a) whether slurry 
is coal and (b) whether BCCL has got the right to challenge the lease granted to the private party 
by the Government of Bihar by virtue ()f its'O~rship of the land on which the slurry was being 
deposited. Shri Lal Narayan Sinha, former Attorney General who was defending the case in the 
Supreme Court on behalf of BCCL, anticipated that BCCL's case in the Supreme Court might 
suffer from a serious infirmity owing to the absence of formal transfer deeds of sudamdih and 
Moonidih group of mines from CIL. To cure this infirmity it was suggested that the best course 
would be to undertake appropriate legislation. The Supreme Court has since decided the matter 
and had held that (i) slurry is coal and (ii) the coal company is free to dispose it. However, the 
question of dejure possession of the properties by the coal companies and the rights and liabilities 
that go with it remained unresolved until it could be cured by legislation. To meet similar 
situation in other property litigations, it was considered essential that assets and liabilities vested 
in subsidiary companies were legally transferred to them with retrospective effect. The then 
Attorney General, Shri K. Parasaran, also endorsed the view of Shri Lal Narayan Sinha. 
9 The Bill was introduced in the Rajya Sabha on 14.2.95 and thereafter it was referred to 
the Standing Committee on Energy for consideration. The Standing Committee on Energy 
presented its report to the Lok Sabha on 7th March, 1996 with the recommendation as under:-
" .. the proposed Bill, apparently serves no other purpose than to safeguard against the 
possibility of being challenged on grounds of lack of title to the subsidiary companies of Coal 
India Limited. The Committee, therefore, hold that what is required presently it to have a fresh 
lool< at the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, and to eliminate such shortcomings, if any, 
as exist in its effective implementation. The Committee, therefore, are unable to recommend the 
Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and Validation Bill, 1995 to the Parliament for adoption." 
1 0. The above views of the standing Committee seem to suggest an amendment to the Coal 
Mines (Nationalisation ) Act, 1973 for the purposes intended to be served by the Bill. 
11. Under Section 3 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 the right, title and interest 
of the private owners of the nationalised mines were transferred to and vested absolutely in the 
Central Government. Under Section 5(1) ofthe same Act, the right, title, interest, etc. ofthe coal 
mines were vested with the CIL. Section 5 (1) of the Act provides for one transfer of vesting by 
the Central Government to a Government company. The power has been once exercised. The 
Act does not provide for any subsequent power of the Central Government to change the 
transfere~. This is what has been proposed in the Bill. The Nationalisation Act does not provide 
for subsequent transfer of properties vested in CIL to the subsidiaries. Further, if the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 is to be amended, it can only be done by an amending Act which once 
again would imply that a fresh Bill would have to be prepared. In order to enable retrospective 
validation of the transfers, such a fresh Bill would have substantially the same provisions as the 
2 

prov1s1ons in the current Bill. Therefore, it was administratively and legally necessary for 
Government to go ahead with the enactment of the proposal Bill. 
12. The Ministry of Coal informed the Committee that the Bill was referred to the Ministry 
of Law for their advice on the under mentioned two points:-
(i) A confirmation that the proposed Bill is in accordance with the Law of the Land; 
and 
(ii) The extent to which the proposed encroaches on the existing state Governments. 
13. The Department of Legal Affairs, Ministry of Law gave their advice on the above two 
points on 9.5.97. On the first point Ministry of Coal gave a clear opinion that the Bill is in 
accordance with the Law of the Land. On the second point, however, Ministry of Law pointed 
out that the transfer of properties (i.e. nationalised coal mine) from CIL, the holding company ,to 
the subsidiaries company of the CIL by the proposed enactment to deprive the State Government 
of their legitimate revenue by way of Stamp Duty, Registration Fee etc. The opinion of the 
Ministry of Law on the second point was not acceptable to the Ministry of Coal because the 
transfer of the coal mines from CIL to the subsidiary had already taken place by administrative 
order~. 
14. The Ministry of Coal opines that the Bill intends to give retrospective effect to such 
transfer and therefore, the question of depriving the State Government of their revenue does not 
arise. This Ministry of Coal is of the opinion that the transfer under the Transfer of Properties 
Act would only give the title from the date of such transfers. Had the transfer of coal mines from 
CIL to subsidiaries taken place under the Transfer of Properties Act the opinion of the Ministry of 
Law would have been valid. The nationalisation of the private mines was done under the Coal 
Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and not under the Transfer of Properties Act. Even at the time 
of the nationalisation of the private coking and non-coking coal mines iii 1971-73, it could have 
been argued that since the nationalisation transferred the right, title and interest of the private 
owners in respect of their mines to the Central Government deprived the State Government of 
their revenue )(Stamp Duty, Registration Fee etc.) but this was not done. This Bill flows from the 
Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and the need for this Bill is to plug a gap retrospectively. 
15. When the Committee wanted to know as to what would be the status of Coal India Ltd., 
when once the rights are divested in the subsidiary companies, the Ministry of Coal informed as 
under:-
"Under Section 4 and 5 of Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation Act) 1972 and under 
section 3 of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation Act) 1973 the right, title and interest of the private 
owners in respect of Coking Coal Mines and Non-Coking Coal Mines stood transferred to and 
vested absolutely in Central Government. Under section 7 of Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation 
Act) 1972 and under section S(I) of Coal Mines (Nationalisation Act) 1973 the right, title and 
interest etc. of coal mines were vested with the Government Company CMAL (renamed as CIL). 
Thereafter by an administrative order issued by the Central Government nationalized coal 
industry was reorganized and the concept of Holding and Subsidiary companies introduced. 
Accordingly the new companies were incorporated and they were made ~ubsidiary companies of 
CIL and CIL became the holding company. Consequent on such reorganization and incorporation 
of subsidiary companies the administrative control of the mines in accordance with the 
geographical location was taken over by the respective subsidiary companies. They have been 
managing those coal mines as defacto owner despite no legal transfer of the ownership having 
been effected. It is significant to note that entire paid up shares of all the subsidiary companies are 
held by CIL. The proposed Coal India (Regulation of Transfers & Validation) Bill is to regulate 
transfer of the coal mines from CIL to subsidiaries and from one subsidiary to another in 
3 

accordance with the reorganisation of the coal industry from time to time. The status of CIL as a 
holding company would not, in any way be affected on transfer of ownership of coal mines in 
terms of the above stated BiiVAct. The holding company status of CIL would not be affected 
even after creation of more subsidiary companies or after formation of subsidiary companies of 
existing subsidiary companies and legal transfer of coal mines to these subsidiary companies 
from existing subsidiary companies. 
16. Replying to the query of the Committee regarding the objections of the State 
Governments received by the Ministry in connection with the Coal India (Regulation of Transfers 
& Validation) B.ill, 1995, the Ministry of Coal furnished the points of objection raised by 
Government of Assam and Government of Bihar on the said Bill. The Ministry of Coal informed 
the Committee that the Government of Assam have opposed the Bill on the following grounds 
(i) The lessee shall execute a Mining Lease Deed with the State Government 
concerned in respect of the coal mine in accordance with the Mineral Concession 
Rules, 1960 and the State Government s_hall have the right to determine the 
mining lease in respect of such coal mine, if the lease deed is not executed within 
the specified period due to any default on the part of the lessee. 
(ii) On expiry of the term of a lease, if Coal India or its subsidiary company, as the 
case may be, is not interested in any further renewal of the mining lease, the 
lessee shall hapd over the land, right, title and interest of the mining lease to the 
State Government. 
(iii) Coal India or its subsidiary company, as the case may be, shall handover all the 
isolated small pocket deposits of coal to the State Government, if the former has 
no plans for operating such deposits in near future. 
17. Regarding point no. 1, the Ministry of Coal contends that the lands, titles, etc., are vested 
in Coal Mines Authority Ltd./Coal India Ltd. following nationalization of Coal Mines in 1973 
which provided for deemed lease requiring no formal execution of mining lease under Mines and 
Minerals (Regulation & DCvel~p~ent~ Act, 1957 and Mineral Concessions Rules, 1960. This has 
been (RVided in Section 5(2) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 stipulating that 
where 'the land,. 'Xc. vest in a subs~diary company under Sub-Secti?n ( 1} ~f Section 5 of the same 
Act, such substdtary company shall on and from the date of such vestmg, be deemed to have 
become the Jessee in relation to such coal mine or coking coal mine as if a fresh mining lease 
related to such a eoal mine or coking coal mine have been granted to it under the Mineral 
Concessions Rule, 1960. In view of this, the view of the State Government is not sustainable. 
18. As regards point no. 2, the Ministry of Coal pleads that the question of handing over the 
land, right, title or interest of a mining lease to the State Government does not arise. The lands, 
titles, etc., are vested in Coal India Limited following the nationalization of coal mines in 1973 
and deemed lease is created by law (commonly called as statutory lease) unlike a contractual 
lease granted under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act, 1975 by execution 
of regular deed. 
19. The Ministry of Coal overrides point no. 3 by pointing out the proviso under Section 
3(3)(c) of Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 which provides for sub-leasing of isolated 
small pockets to the State Government undertakings or any person subject to fulfillment of the 
following conditions :-
(a) the reserves of coal in the area are in isolated small pockets or are not sufficient 
for scientific and economical development in a coordinated and integrated 
manner, and 
4 

(b) the coal produced by the sub-lease will not be required to be transported by rail. 
In view of the above provisions already incorporated in the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 it is not considered necessary to incorporate handing 
over of isolated small pockets to the State Government or the State Government 
Undertaking, in the Bill. 
20. The six points of objections raised by Government of Bihar in connection with the Bill is 
as under ;-
(i) The very preamble stating that "the transfer of the land or of the rights in or over 
land" without the permission of the State Government or without getting it 
transferred under the Transfer of Properties Act harms the interest of the State 
Government. 
(ii) Similarly in Section 3(1) of the proposed bill the words ''the transfer of the land 
or rights in or over such land or the right, title and interest in relation to a Coal 
Mine, Coking Coal Mine" is violative of the provisions of the India Registration 
Act, Bihar Tenancy Act, Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act, Santhal Parganas Tenancy 
Act, Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act and Mineral 
Concession Rules, 1960. 
(iii) Sub-Section 2 of Section 3 of the said bill usurps the rights of the State 
Government to grant the Transfer of Mining leases under Mines and Minerals 
(Regulation and Development) Act and Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. The 
approval of the State Government as lessor of the Mineral rights must be 
obtained by the Coal India or any of its subsidiaries Company before transferring 
a mining lease to one of its subsidiary <:;ompany or anoth_er subsidiary company. 
(iv) The Coal India or its subsidiary company, who becomes the transferee under the 
proposed bill cannot be tel')lled as a new lessee. This will be a case of substitution 
by operation of law, and this deprives the State Government from exercising its 
rights to grant/renew the Coal Mining lease. 
(v) The State Government will have no objection if the right, title and interest in 
relation to a Coal Mine, Coking Coal Mine or Coke oven Plant is transferred 
from Coal India, or its subsidiary to any of its other subsidiary as envisaged 
under the Companies Act but it cannot agree to such provision which infringes its 
right under the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act and 
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. 
(vi) Besides the above noted facts, the promulgation of the proposed bill will deprive 
the State Government of it revenue by way of fee on transfer of mining lease and 
stamp duty for its registration. 
21. With regards to point no. 1 of Government of Bihar, the Ministry of Coal views that 
since the properties have already been vested with the Central Government by a special Act of 
Parliament, i.e., the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973. VIS 3 of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 the right, title and interest of the coal mines were transferred to and 
vested absolutely in the Central Government free from all encumbrances. U/S 5( 1) of the same 
Act, the right, title, interest, etc. of the coal mines have been vested with the CIL. Since these are 
nationalized properties, transfer of these properties from CIL to a subsidiary or from one 
subsidiary to another subsidiary of the CIL does not attract the provisions of the Transfer of 
Propert}LAct. 
5 

22. Regarding point No. 2 of Bihar Government, the Ministry of Coal points out that since 
the proposed enactment seeks to regularizes or validate the transfer of the properties already 
vested with the CIL u/s 5(1) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 therefore, the Bill 
flows from the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act. It is noteworthy that Sec.28 of the Act has an 
over-riding provision which stipulates that the Nationalisation Act shall have effect 
notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith in any other law for the time being in force. 
Therefore, the Ministry of Coal argues that the propose enactment overrides the Acts of State 
Legislature like Bihar Tenancy Act, Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act, Santhal Parganas Tenancy A~t. 
23. As regards the point of violation of the provisions of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation 
and Development) Act, 1957 (MMRD Act) and Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 (MCR-1960), 
the Ministry of Coal put forth the following arguments :-
"The acquisition of mines by the Central government under the Nationlisation Act is not 
as a result of the actual grant by the State Government as done under Mineral Concession Rules 
(MCR), 1960 framed under MMRD Act, 1957 but by a legal fiction. The legal fictions have their 
limitations. In the matter of grant of mining lease by the State, the MMRD Act and the MCR 
contemplated a particular area dimensions in respect of different minerals within which, in its 
discretion, the State is to grant lease. Quite clearly such provisions in the matter of an actual grant 
could not be applied in the case ofNationalisation by a legal fiction, as provided in the Act. The 
effect of deeming provision is of particular importance". 
24. The Ministry of Coal , further , clarifies that the provision of MCR , 1960 cannot be lifted 
and applied in toto to the Coal Mines Nationalised under the 1973 Act. Section 4 of the 
Nationalisation Act brings in the legal fiction of a grant under the Mineral Concession Rules 
(MCR). While Section 6 of the same Act provides that by the force of the very vesting, such 
acquired property will stand freed and discharged from any trust, ob~igations, mortgage, charge, 
lien and ~ other encumbrances affecting such property in any manner, shall be deemed to have 
been withdrawn. The provisions of Section 6 of the 1973 Act wipes out all encumbrances. The 
expression "encumbrances" has been judicially interpreted to include any burden on property, any 
right or interest created by the owner in limitation of his own. The Ministry pinpoints that by 
virtue of the provisions of the Coal Mines Nationalization Act , the concept of legal fiction of ... 
graQt under the Mineral Concession Rules (MCR) must yield to the provisions of the wiping out 
the encumbral'\ces. The main objective is stipulated in the preamble of the Nationalisation Act and 
that being the purpose and. the context, the provisions of the Mineral Concession Rules (MCR) 
cannot be applied in toto . The preamble attached to the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act 1973 
reads as under :-
"An Act to provide for the acquisition and transfer of the right, title and interest of the owner~ in 
respect of the coal mines specified in the schedule with a view to reorganizing and reconstructltig 
such coal mines so as to ensure the rational, coordinated and scientific development and 
utilisation of coal resources consistent with the growing requirements of the country, in order that 
the ownership and control of such resources are vested in the State and thereby so distributed as 
best to sub serve the common good, and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto". 
25. The Ministry of Coal pointed out that the word "State" in the above cited preamble of the 
Nationalisation Act is obviously the "Union of India". The Ministry concluded that Section 28 of 
(Nationalisation) Act 1973 carries an overriding effect in terms of which where there is conflict 
between the Coal mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and MMRD Act and MCR framed there 
under, then the provision of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act 1973 will override the 
provisions of MMRD Act, etc., protento. Therefore, the exclusive ownership and control and the 
distribution/transfer of the property by the Central Government in fulfillment of the objective of 
the Nationalisation Act will always prevail upon the provisions of the MMRD Act, 1957 and the 
6 

MCR, 1960 framed hereunder. Section 3(2) of the Bill provides that if the right, etc, is vested 
with a subsidiary uls 3(1) of the proposed enactment, that subsidiary will become a deemed lessee 
as if a fresh mining lease has been granted to it under MCR 1960 framed under Section 13 of 
MMRD Act, 1957. As such, the proposed enactment is not violative of the MMRD Act and 
Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. However, if there is any conflict between the Nationalisation 
Act and MMRD Act, the former will prevail by virtue of the overriding provision in Sec. 28 of 
the Nationalisation Act. 
26. As regards point no. 3, the Ministry of Coal argues that U/S 4 of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 , the Central Government became deemed lessee of the State 
Government. Similarly, after the nationalized mines were transferred to the CIL uls 5(1) of the 
Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, the CIL became the deemed lessee as per Sec. 5(2) of the 
same Act. The deemed leases are not contractual leases granted under MMRD Act, 1957 read 
with the Mineral Concession Rules (MCR), 1960. The deemed leases are created by a fiction of 
law, Sec. 3(2) of the Bill, intends to make the subsidiary the deemed lessee of the State 
Government after the rights, etc., are transferred to it by CIL or another subsidiary. 
27. Pertaining to the point no. 4, the Bill does not intend to make Coal India as the transferee 
since the nationalized mines have already been transferred to CIL uls 5( 1) of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act 1973, Sec. 3 (2) of the Bill is just an exlension of that provision in the 
Nationalisation Act. Since the deemed leases have already been created by a fiction of law uls 
5(2) of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973, there is no scope of discretion with the State 
Government to grant or renew the same coal mining leases. 
28. Regarding the point no. 5, the Ministry of Coal opines that the transfer of properties 
under the Companies Act does not make much material difference over the ownership of the 
transferred properties. It has already been clarified that the Bill does not infringe the rights of the 
State Government under MMRD Act and Mineral Concession Rules (MCR) by virtue of Sec. 28, 
of the Nationalisation Act, the provision ofthe Nationalisation Act will prevail over MMRD Act 
and Mineral Concession Rules (MCR). 
29. With regard to point no. 6, the Ministry of Coal views that the properties in question is 
the national properties so, in the national interest their transfer should be exempted from the 
payment of stamp duty. Transfer of funds from Central Government to State Government is not 
national income. Had the properties been under private ownership, payment of stamp duty would 
have been justified. Moreover, transfer of these properties under Transfer of Property Act and 
registration of the transfers on payment of stamp duties are not possible since the properties have 
already been transferred and registration of transfer with a retrospective effect is not possible. As 
regards future transfers, payment of stamp duty is not justified since these are nationalized 
properties. New transfers of properties acquired under Coal Bearing (CB) Act is also not justified

30. The Ministry of Coal held the view that CIL is the holding company and the proposed

"As far as the holding company control is concerned, that is in no way diluted, because the

transfer any substantial interest in its property, has to take the approval of Coal India. In any

question that the control of the Coal India would, in any way, get diluted after the property is 
transferred. It is only to take care of the legal anomaly that we want the property to be transferred 
so that they do not get into any legal problems in respect of management of these mines".

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION OF THE COMMITTEE 
The Committee observes that main object ofthe Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and 
Validation) Bill, 1995 is to empower the Central Government to direct the transfer of land, on the 
rights in or over or of the right, title and interest in relation to a Coal Mine, Coking Coal Mine or 
Coke Oven Plant, vested in Coal India Limited or in a subsidiary company to any subsidiary 
company and to validate certain transfers of such land or sights. Speaking on practical terms, the 
proposed legislation simply aims at legalisations of transfers of properties from Coal India 
Limited to its subsidiaries and that too without vitiating the managing and controlling mechanism 
of Coal India Limited over its subsidiaries. The Bill aims at turning the situation from de facto to 
de jure. De facto transfer of property has already taken place through administrative orders. 
2. The Committee feels that the necessity of the proposed enactment arose due to 
shortcomings in the Coal Nationalisation Act, under which provision was made for taking over 
all the mines by the Central Government, not by Coal India. Under that Act, Government was 
given the power to transfer it to the Government Company, which was done to erstwhile CMAL 
and now Coal India Limited. There was no provision in the Nationalisation Act for second 
transfer from Coal India to its subsidiaries which have already been done through administrative 
order. Therefore, the proposed legislation is a validation legislation for enabling the Government 
to provide -legal basis to a defacto transfer and convert the same into de-jure. 
3. The Committee understands the problem of giving validation to the transfer of properties 
through the Coal Nationalisation Validation Act, because, unfortunately, the properties of Coal 
India today, which are sought to be transferred to the subsidiaries, are not all covered by the 
nationalization scheme, that is so, because the Coal Mines Nationalisation Act had a very specific 
schedule attached to the Act which designated the mines that were to be taken over. It is 
noteworthy that there are other transfer of properties under the Coal-~earing, Act and the Land 
Acquisition Act, which would still not be covered. The same transfer couldn't be done through 
the Transfer of property Act because the said Act allows only prospective transfer. So, the 
Committee is of the view that the only way to clear up the mess of ownership is to bring forth a 
separate legislation. 
4. The Committee notes the Opinion/suggestion of Shri Lal Narayan Sinha, former 
Attorney General (who was defending the case in the Supreme Court on behalf of BCCL) and 
then Attorney General, Shri K. Parasnath, who endorsed the view of Shri Lal Narayan Sinha for 
undertaking the recourse for appropriate legislation so that, as on date, whatever is held by 
subsidiaries, could be transferred to them without involving any legal wrangle. 
5. The Committee understands that CIL have created a structure of subsidiaries but the 
subsidiaries had not been transferred the property in legal sense, therefore, existing structure of 
arrangement may lead to some kind of problem in future. The problem occurred in Bharat 
Coking Coal Ltd. VS Government of Bihar and others and the Supreme Court decided the 
matter. However, the question of de-jure possession of the properties by the Coal companies and 
the rights and liabilities that go with it remained unresolved which is intended to be cured by the 
proposed legislation. 
6. The Committee, while examining the points of objections raised by the Governments of 
Assam and Bihar on the present Bill and the comments of the Ministry of Coal, is ofthe view that 
the Ministry of Coal has successfully clarified the points of objections of both the state 
Governments. The Committee observes that the lands, titles etc. vested in Coal Mines Authority 
Ltd/Coal India Ltd. following nationalization of Coal Mines in 1973 which provided for deemed 
9 

lease require no formal execution of mining lease under Mines and Minerals (Regulation & 
Development) Act, 1957 and Mineral Concession Rules, 1960. 
7. The Committee is also of the opinion that since Section 3 of the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act, 1973 transfers and vests the right, title and interest of the Coal Mines in 
the Central Government free from all encumbrances and Section-S( I) of the said Act has vested 
the right, title, interest etc., of the Coal Mines with the CIL and because these are nationalized 
properties, the transfer of these properties from CIL to a subsidiary or from one subsidiary to 
another subsidiary of the CIL, does not harm the interest of the State(s). 
8. The Committee endorses the view that the proposed enactment overrides the Acts of 
State Legislature namely Bihar Tenancy Act, Chhotanagpur Tenancy Act, Santhal Parganas 
Tenancy Act because, it flows from the Coal Mines (Nationalisation ) Act and Section-28 of the 
Coal Nationalisation Act has an overriding provision stipulating that the Nationalisation Act shall 
have effect notwithstanding anything in consisting therewith in any other law for the time being 
in force. 
9. The Committee also notes and endorses the contention of the Ministry of Coal that since 
the acquisition of Mines by the Central Government under the Nationalisation Act is not as a 
,.result of the actual grant by the state as done under Minerals Concession Rules (MCR}, 1960 
framed under MMRD Act. 1957 but by a legal fiction and also because Section-28 of the 
Nationalisation Act, 1973 having an overriding effect in terms of which where there is conflict 
between the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 and MMRD Act and MCR framed there 
under, then the provision of the Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1973 wHI override the 
provisions of MMRD Act. etc., therefore, the question that the proposed enactment violates the 
provision of MMRD Act and MCR does not arise. 
10. During the course of oral-evidence of Secretaries to the Department of Legislation 
(Ministry of Law Justice and Company Affairs) and the Ministry of Coal, the Committee got an 
assurance that the Bill will not dilute the control of Coal India over the subsidiaries. The 
Secretary, Coal, assured that the Bill will do nothing to dilute the Government's ownership of 
either the Coal India or the subsidiaries i.e., the control of Government over the subsidiaries 
would be as complete as of Coal India. Under the Article, of Association of Subsidiary 
Companies, the Subsidiary Companies cannot do certain things without the approval from Coal 
India e.g., it cannot dispose of a substantial part of its assets without approval from Coal India 
neither the majo'r investment decision of the subsidiaries can be done without the approval of 
Coal·lndia. The Articles of Association also says that, if the subsidiary is going to a foreign 
company or going in for a joint venture, it has to go "in and through" the Coal lndia.The 
Committee is satisfied with the explanation of the Migistry of Coal and the Ministry of Law, 
Justice and Company Affairs (Legislative Depart!}lellt). 
11. Having heard the Secretaries.__ Ministry of Coal and Legislative Department, Ministry of 
Law Justice and Company Affairs and the clarifications given by them to the various queries and 
having considered the papers furnished by the Ministry, the Committee agrees* with the proposal 
of the Ministry to empower the Central Government to direct the transfer of the land or of the 
right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine, coking coal mine or coke oven plant, vested in 
the Coal India Limited or in subsidiary company to any subsidiary company of Coal India 
Limited or any other subsidiary company and to validate certain transfers of such land or rights. 
12. The Committee decided to adopt Clause 2, 3 & 4 in the original form. 
13. Clause 1 i.e., the Enacting Formula and the Title, were adopted, with changes of 
consequential nature, namely, "1995 and Forty-Sixth" to be substituted by "2000" and Fifty-first, 
respectively. 
10 

14. The Committee therefore, recommends the Coal India (Regulation of Transfers and 
Validation) Bill, 1995 as amended to the Parliament for adoption.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS 
The coal industry was nationalised in two phases, that is, in 1972 and· 1973. After 
nationalisation, the coking and non-coking coal mines in the Jharia CoalFields in Bihar and a few 
mines in Barakar and Mugma regions were directed to be vested in the Bharat Coking Coal 
Limited, Dhanbad. Most of the other coal mines in the States of Assam, Bihar, West Bengal, 
Orissa, Madhya Pradesh and Maharashtra were directed to be vested in the Coal Mines Authority 
Limited. Subsequently, a holding company, namely, the Coal1ndia Limited was set up with effect 
from the 1st November, 1975, initially with five subsidiaries. Later three more subsidiaries were 
created by del inking certain collieries from other subsidiaries. 
2. Ever since the nationalisation of the coal industry, though the land or rights in or over such land 
acquired under various Acts and the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine or a coke 
oven plant were directed to be \lested in the Coal India Limited or its predecessor in title, its 
subsidiary companies were de facto managing such land, coal mines or plants. 
3. The absence of a formal legal title to the land or rights in or over such land or the right, title and 
interest in relation to a coal mine or coke oven plant, in the subsidiary companies has exposed 
them to litigation and other legal infirmities. While the Companies Act, 1956 contains provisions 
for reconstruction and amalgamations, such reconstruction or amalgamation could be given effect 
to prospectively only under that Act. 
4. It has, therefore, been considered necessary to empower the Central Government to direct the 
transfer of land or the rights in or over such land or the right, title or interest in relation to a coal 
mine or coke oven plant vested in the Coal India Limited to a subsidiary company, or where such 
land or mine are vested in a subsidiary company, to another subsidiary company. It has also been 
considered necessary to validate all purported transfers of the land or rights in or over such land or 
the right, title and interest in relation to a coal mine or coke oven plant from the Coal India 
Limited to a subsidiary company and from one subsidiary company to another subsidiary company 
before the commencement of the proposed legislation. 
5. The Bill seeks to achieve the above objects.

L the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry. having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Forty-third Report on 
the Credit Flow to Small scale Industries. Taking into account the significance of Small Scale 
Sector it was decided in the Committee's meeting held on 25th September, 2000 that the 
Committee should assess the Credit Flow to the Sector in the aftermath of the policy announced 
by the Hon'ble Prime Minister in the First National Conference of SSI Sector on the 30th August, 
2000. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 25th September, 2000, inter-alia examined the 
background note on the Credit Flow to SSI sector furnished by the Ministry of SSI and A&RI 
and thereafter, decided to have interaction with officials of the Ministry of Small Scale 
Industries and Agro & Rural Industries, RBI!Banks/Financial Institutions/KVIC and 
representatives of SSI Association and NGOs to assess the impact of the policy/package on the 
SSI units. 
3. The Committee in its next meeting held on 4th October, 2000 decided to undertake a 
visit to Mumbai from gth to II th October, 2000 to take stock of the ground realities pertaining to 
credit facilities being extended to SSI sector by the Banks and Financial Institutions. 
4. The Report has been prepared on the basis of the background note furnished by the 
Ministry of SSI and A&RI and discussions held in three days meeting in Mumbai with the 
representatives of SSI and NGO and officials the Ministry of SSI and A&RI and RBI/Banks 
and Financial Institutions. On behalf of the Committee I wish to thank all the representatives and 
officials who appeared before the Committee and·· placed their considered views. The 
Committee, while appreciating the concern of the Government to SSI Sector, hopes that the 
Government will implement the recommendations made in the present report in order to ensure 
the continued credit flow to SSI sector. 
5. The Committee in its meeting held on 18th December, 2000 considered and adopted 
the Report.

REPORT 
Small Scale Industries Sector plays paramount role in the National economy and has 
vast potential in terms of employment, output, export promotion, expansion of base for 
indigenous entrepreneurship and decentralization of industries in rural areas. The number of 
persons employed in the SSI sector was 171.58 lakhs while the production of the sector at 
current prices was Rs.5,27,515 crore produced in more than 3 million units. The SSI sector 
export performance has been of the order of Rs.48,979 crores. In this respect the achievement 
of growth in SSI sector has been 7. 7. per cent in 1998-99 compared to 4 per cent growth in the 
industrial sector. The Employment growth between 1998-99 has been of the order of 2.62 
percent over previous year which has been better than the overall growth in the employment 
of around I per cent. The sector has exceeded the employment target in 81h Five Year Plan and 
the achievement in the Ninth Five Year Plan is satisfactory in this regard with a growth rate 
around 4 per cent per year. 
During the course of examination of Demand for Grants (2000-0 1) pertaining to the 
Ministry of Small Scale Industry and Agro & Rural Industries, the Department Related 
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry took up the issue of credit flow to SSI Sector in 
detail. It was informed to the Committee by the Secretary that the problematic area in the sector 
is about SSI credit, as percentage of net banking credit was about 16 per cent, in March, 1996 
which went up to 17.33 per cent in March, 1999. In absolute terms, the credit to the SSI sector 
has increased to Rs.42,674 crores in March, 1999 which is a significant improvement, compared 
with the figure of Rs.30,000 crores il'l March, 1996. However, the disturbing feature is that the 
amount of credit to the tiny sector is not adequate. But at the end of March, 1999, the tiny sector 
got a credit of Rs.8,837.47 crores which is about 20.7 per cent of the credit going to the SSI 
sector and as per the norms laid down by the RBI, 60 per cent of the SSI credit should have gone 
to the tiny sector. It is this reason which has prompted to launch the Credit Guarantee Scheme. 
Moreover the RBI had advised the banks to introduce special branches for the small scale sector 
and 3 89 branches have already been set lip. The banks have also been directed by Ministry of 
Finance to enhance the coverage of Small Scale Industries branches to individual districts. 
Apart from this, SIDBI has introduced Single Window Scheme for working capital and term 
loans. Since the Small Scale Industries sector is facing the problem because of absence of 
working capital loans in time and in case ifthe same institution will be responsible for both term 
loans and working capital, the situation will improve. 
The Committee was informed during examination of Demands for Grants (2000-200 1) 
that in order to improve the credit flow to Small Scale Industries the Credit Guarantee Scheme 
has been launched during the year 2000-2001. This' provides for contribution to a fund to 
generate loans without any collateral. The scheme will be implemented jointly by the Central 
Government and Small Industries Development Bank of India through a trust. The funds required 
for the scheme will be provided by Government of India and SIDBI in the ratio of 4: 1. SIDBI is 
also presently administrating the technology development and modernisation funds scheme for 
assisting technological development and modernisation of Small Scale Industries units. This 
scheme has certain concessional features including interest at prime lending rate for direct 
assistance for improving the credit flow. In past also RBI had issued instruction that out of funds 
normally available to Small Scale Industries sector, 40% would be given to the units with 
investment in Plan and machinery up to Rs.S lakhs, 20% to the unit with investment between Rs.S 
lakhs and 25 lakhs and remaining 40% for other units. The single window scheme of SIDBI has 
also been extended to all the districts.

not entertain new entrepreneurs and not even provided the application forms. New exporters with 
confirm orders do not get the opportunity to even open a bank account. 
The Committee in its 40

Ministry of SSI and A&RI recommended that in order to mitigate financial difficulties in the 
early stages of start up , venture capital companies should be established to provide financial and 
managerial assistance to the new enterprises.
