XII       BILL DISCOUNTING SYSTEM
 
12.1     When the Secretary was asked to comment on Bill Discounting System and  possibility of its introduction in SSI
sector, he had stated that the scheme is available through SIDBI to large manufacturers.   But for that the large
manufacturer has also to accept those  Bills because the small scale entrepreneurs are not so strong and the large
manufacturers take undue advantage of this in case of delayed payment; they will not agree to discounting and the bank
will not accept it.  He further stated they had in the last package got this  done with the RBI and RBI  had now 
instructed all the commercial banks that the working capital limits of large manufacturers shall have a percentage
against which payments will be made only to small scale entrepreneurs.   Secondly, there is a thing called the factoring
service.  The small entrepreneur goes to the bank and the bank gives him some money and the bank, in turn, receives it
from the large manufacturer.  He stated that they have requested that a legislation be introduced in India on the lines it is
available in some other countries.  Then, in the balance sheet they  will have to specify how much do they owe.  These
are the two measures that they have now thought of.  He ,however, agreed that if we had more and more banks having 
this kind of situation, then some payments would  flow to the small entrepreneurs as well.
 
12.2     The Committee recommends that the banks should set up subsidiaries for bill discounting and other services.
The  factoring system should be strengthened and made effective. This would foster growth of trade and industry in the
present liberalised competitive environment. The RBI and the government should also establish discount houses on the
pattern of discount houses in London and other cities to help small enterprises. In case,  it is essential,  a legislation may
be enacted  in this regard on the lines of other countries.

XIII      SMALL INDUSTRIES DEVELOPMENT BANK OF INDIA (SIDBI)
 
13.1     SIDBI is the principal financial institution for small scale industries which financies units having  investment in
plant and machinery upto Rs.100 lakh. While the world over , the concept of small and medium enterprises is more
prevalent, this statutory restriction  prevents SIDBI  from  operating widely which affects  the  competitiveness of
SIDBI vis-à-vis commercial bank and othe Development Financing Institutions (DFIs).
 
13.2     The Committee therefore recommends that SIDBI should enlarge the scope of  its assistance to small and
medium enterprises. Expansion by SIDBI  in the operational canvas will generate additional revenue for SIDBI thus
helping it to undertake more promotional and developmental activities for strengthening tiny/SSI Sector in the WTO
regime.
 
13.3     Due to continued sizable assistance at below the cost of funds under refinance, special schemes of assistance and
various promotional and developmental activities, there has been squeeze on the spirit available to SIDBI particularly in
the last few years. SIDBI has been requesting Government of India to allow access to concessional sources of funding to
enable the Bank to continue concessional lending to SSIs and take developmental activities in tandem with the policy
prescriptions of Government of India in the WTO regime.
 
13.4     The Committee recommends that Ministry should impress upon the Ministry of Finance/RBI to assist SIDBI  for
raising low cost resources so as to remain viable while taking up various developmental activities in the SSI sector.
 
13.5     The Union Budget 2001-02 has, interalia, withdrawn the tax-exempt status hitherto available to SIDBI under
Section 50 of SIDBI Act. This would have a negative impact on the profitability and viability of SIDBI particularly
when no other perceptible form of resource support is made available to the Bank. This may also have an adverse
impact on the rating of SIDBI  which is already under strain on account of proposed transfer of SFCs shareholding from
IDBI to SIDBI.
 
13.6     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tax - exempt status as provided in the Small Industries
Development Bank of India (Amendment) Act,  2000,  may be retained. Ministry of Finance may be approached to
restore the status of SIDBI as before.
 
13.7     While it is desirable that SIDBI should operate on a larger canvass, it would also be appropriate to rope in
private banks for financing purposes. In that case government would have to extend tax benefits to these  financial
institutions when they lend to tiny units. 
 
13.8     The Committee therefore recommends that tax relief may be provided to private banks in case they carve out
certain percentage of the funds to lend to the tiny sector.Ministry of Finance may be approached in this regard.
 
13.9     The Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 40
th Report had also
recommended that SIDBI should take initiative and act as a watchdog to monitor the activities of Indian and foreign
banks. However, this would require adequate provisions for SIDBI to monitor the activities of primary lending
institutions with regard to their assistance and policies towards SSI sector.
 
13.10   The Committee,  reiterating its earlier recommendation, further suggests that the necessary administrative
powers be bestowed  on SIDBI to enable it to discharge its co-ordination role effectively.  
 
13.11   The Committee has been informed that the attitude of the lower level bank officials is very negative towards the
SSI units. The non-cooperation on their part hampers the development of  Small sector.
 
13.12   The Committee feels that there should be regular meeting of banks and SSIs representatives  to monitor loan
requirement of SSI. The Committee recommends that attitudinal changes should be brought in the mindset of lower
level bank officials towards the SSI units and they may be given proper training, incentives etc. for the purpose.   The

XIV     PROVIDING INFRASTRUCTURE SUPPORT TO SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
14.1     The Committee has been informed that providing basic infrastructure to SSI clusters through industrial estates
has been the traditional strategy of most governments for promoting small scale industries. However, increasingly small
scale units, especially in hi-tech areas, are in need of specialized infrastructure and services of international standards.
Pure private initiative in infrastructure is not feasible because of low  returns and long gestation periods,  it was added.
 
14.2     The Committee recommends that  specialized facilities can be jointly funded by government and user industries
and thereafter handed over to specialist private agencies for maintenance. Joint ventures between the Government and
industry associations for the  purpose can also be considered.
 
XV       SUPPORT TO FIGHT ANTI DUMPING PRACTICES
 
15.1     The small scale sector finds itself constrained from meeting the threat posed by dumping on account of their
unorganized nature, ignorance, lack of necessary data and limited resource availability, the representatives of industrial
organisations informed.
 
15.2     Hence the Committee suggests  that financial and legal assistance be provided by the government to fight the
anti - dumping cases abroad and for filing antidumping petitions within the country.
 
15.3     The Committee observes that it takes 90 days to review economic fallout of imported goods in country and 
imposition of  anti-dumping duty thereon. By that time huge financial losses would  have already occurred   to the
country which are irretrievable. The Committee observes that in order to preclude the possibility of economic losses,
anti-dumping monitoring should be expedited. The Committee therefore recommends that the administrative ministry
should review the pros and cons in this regard and take timely action. The system that exists in other countries may be
examined. India can also emulate such a system.
 
15.4     The Committee was informed by the Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries  and Agro and Rural
Industries that in America there exists a law under which on a complaint, antidumping duty is imposed on the imported
goods in the first instance.  After considering all pros and cons only, a decision will be taken either to lift ban or
continue it.
 
15.5     The Committee understands that enacting law in this matter is not the concern of this ministry.  The Committee,
therefore,  recommends that the matter may be taken up with the concerned administrative ministry for making a law, if
necessary.  Otherwise necessary regulations may be prepared by the concerned Ministry and the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries   and Agro & Rural Industries  may pursue it.
 
15.6     One of the representatives of the industries stated that even if we were not able to hold the imported goods with
tariff barriers, but at least we can have non-tariff barriers.  We can ask them to comply with our regulations.  Printing of
MRP should be made compulsory on the imported goods.  Similarly, these goods should comply with ISI regulations. 
He was confident that by these steps, we can stop dumping of goods.
 
15.7     Secretary informed the Committee that the provisions related to MRP  as well as ISI mark should apply in the
same manner on the imported goods as they apply to the indigeniously manufactured items.  Any packed commodity
that is  sold in India shall have to have the year of manufacturing, expiry date and  maximum retail price.  Any importer
can sell his imported goods in India only when he meets these requirements.  The items should also indicate  the
contents  inside the pack.  Wherever it is written in the concerned country’s  language then it shall have the English
version also.  Similarly, he informed the Committee that  the imported items should meet the Indian standard just as in
the case of indigenously  manufactured products.   He  further stated that they had implemented these things four

The Secretary further informed the Committee that the Ministry  would like to propose to the Ministry of Commerce for
implementation of a scheme under which the imported products shall carry a  guarantee from the country of origin.”  In
other countries imported goods carry a guarantee from the country of its origin.  The Secretary stated that the same

15.8     The Committee feels that availability  of    imported commodities, relatively of cheap quality without  carrying 
MRP   and ISI labels, poses a serious threat to the domestic industries, particularly the small   scale sector. The
Government should look into this matter on priority basis and take all appropriate measures to protect the interests of
domestic industries from unfair competition from imported goods.
 
15.9     The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Ministry is contemplating to implement the guarantee system in
consultation with the Ministry of Commerce. The Committee recommends that an immediate action may be taken in
this regard and implemented expeditiously.
 
XVI     RATIONALIZATION OF TAXES AND TARIFFS FOR SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
 
16.1     There is an urgent need for rationalization and simplification of tax structure to enhance the competitiveness of
small scale industry. While the budget has   endeavored to rationalize the tax structure, some anomalies still remain.
Some of  the problems faced by SSIs with respect to distortions arising out of iniquitous tax structure, have been 
brought to the notice of the Committee.
 
16.2     For the cable industry, while cables are allowed to be imported at the basic customs duty of 15 percent or 25
percent, the raw material which goes into the manufacture of cables has a basic customs duty of 35 percent plus 16
percent CVD plus 4 percent Special Auxillary Duty (SAD). This increases the cost of production of the domestic
manufacturer as compared to the     imported product. There is an urgent need to take remedial measures to rationalize
the  customs duty on raw materials.       
 
16.3     The Committee  suggests that the SAD on raw material be made MODATABLE as this would reduce the raw
material cost.
 
16.4     The Committee was also informed that  granite and marble  industries  should be  treated at par . It was also
stated that  in the edible  oil Industry, the running mills  have to pay  75%  duty were as  the sick  units have to pay 55%
duty and   this differential duty  for sick. Mill and running mill should not be there.  It   was also pointed out during the
course of discussion  that the  limit of  one crore rupees on roller  bearings industry has been removed.  It was felt that 
there should be one crore rupees limit.   The Committee appreciates  that most of these  demands have been met  by the
Government  in the recent budget.
 
16.5     The Committee recognizes that special and friendly relations exist between India and Nepal in all spheres of
activities including bilateral trade. The manufacturers’ representatives of vanaspati, silk, woolen, copper wire, etc.
operating in the small scale sector explained their difficulties vis-à-vis the imports from Nepal. These representatives
mentioned that the manufacturers in Nepal have an edge over them in pricing of their products in as much as they are
allowed import of raw-material at zero customs duty. The Indian  manufacturers, however, have to pay customs duty on
imported raw-material.
 
16.6     The Committee would like the Ministry to look into this aspect of unfair competition being posed by the imports
from Nepal. The Committee understands that the Indo-Nepal Trade Treaty is due for review during the later part of
2001. It would, therefore, recommend that this matter may be looked into and corrective measures taken.
 
16.7     The  Committee also desires that the items like footwear, agricultural implements etc. used by the poorer
sections of the society should be available at cheaper prices. Government may consider reducing taxes on such items.
 
XVII    MARKETING

17.1     Marketing companies are assuming an increasingly important role in the emerging competitive environment.
The Committee has been informed that  marketing outfits in all the developing economies have the prime role in
marketing of products. Our banking sector does not recognize marketing as an essential activity for SMEs and,
therefore, adequate financing is not available for the sector.
 
17.2     The Committee, therefore, is of the view  that the marketing and distribution companies need to be considered
for being  given the status of industry for the purpose of getting financial assistance from banks and Fls as well as lead
institutions.
 
17.3     Marketing and developing brand image of the SSI products also has not been handled effectively. The role of
KVIC in marketing the products has been increased in Budget 2000-2001, but no new marketing techniques or
involvement of private institutions have been envisaged.
 
17.4     The Committee  recommends promotion of private sector participation in marketing of SSI products through
proper incentives like granting  tax relief in a manner similar to 80 HHC currently available on exports for companies
marketing SSI products.
 
XVIII   EXPORTS BY SSI SECTOR
 
18.1     The SSI sector in India covers a wide spectrum of industries categorized under small, tiny and cottage segments
ranging from small artisan/handicraft units to modern production units with significant investments and produces a vide
range of products exceeding 7500. The industrial policy 1990 laid emphasis on the steps to enhance the contribution of
SSI sector in  overall exports,  employment  generation and   dispersal  of
industries in rural areas. 800 items are currently reserved for exclusive manufacture in the SSI sector although there is
no regulation or restriction on marketing the reserved items by large industries.
 
18.2     But the Committee notes with dissatisfaction  that even as the industrial policy laid emphasis on the steps to
enhance  the contribution of the SSI Sector in over all exports, the performance of the SSI sector in this regard  has been
disparaging  and the contribution is negligible.  The Committee feels that perhaps serious marketing efforts were not
made by those concerned and it was left to its own fate. Though Government has been extending preferences in respect
of purchase of items manufactured by SSIs and  a number of steps taken in the recent post reform period by the Govt.
like FDI, establishment of growth centers, export promotion, marketing etc. exports of SSI products have not taken off 
at the expected level.
 
18.3     The Committee, therefore, observes that efforts made for export of SSI products are inadequate and  there is
need to improve the quality of products for this purpose.
 
18.4     The Committee also  recommends that exports should be increased by making SSI products qualitatively better
and cost effective.
 
XIX     PROBLEM OF DELAYED PAYMENTS TO SSI UNITS
 
19.1     The Committee has been given to  understand that at present Balance Sheet of the Companies indicate the
amount due to SSI units. But interest due to SSI units on account of delayed payment is not shown separately. As a
result, there is no authentic source on which the Income Tax authorities can rely to disallow the interest due, payable or
paid by any buyer in accordance with the Delayed Payment Act, 1993 for the purposes of computation of income under
Income Tax Act 1961 as deduction.
 
19.2     The Committee, recommends that the interest due or payable or paid to SSI units on account of delayed
payments as per the provisions of the Delayed Payments Act 1993 (as amended) may be shown separately in the
Balance Sheet of Companies.

FIFTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. 
having been authorised by the Committee to present on its behalf , do hereb y present this Fifth 
Report of the Committee on the Status of the Sponge Iron Industri es und er the Ministry of Steel. 
2. The Committee in its sitting held on 28th June , 1993 considered a note receiv ed from the 
Ministry of Steel on Sponge Iron and decjded to send a questionnaire to the Ministr y on the 
subject for their replies. In its sitting held on 29th September , 1993, the Committe e heard the 
views of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel by way of clarifications to the repl ies sent by the 
Ministry to the said questionnaire. 
3. The Committee considered in depth the problems prevailing in sponge iron industr y and 
Government's efforts to protect its interests. The Committee had deliberations on the overall 
present scenario with a view to project the possible ways in salvaging the sponge Iron Indust ries. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the report at its sitting held on the lOth February. 
1994. 
5. Based on the papers and other relevant material on the subject and also the evidence of 
the Secretary, the Committee had noted the following picture of the Sponge Iron indu stry in the 
country. 
5.1 Sponge iron is a partial substitute for steel melting Scrap. It is a met allic product 
produced by direct induction of high grade iron ore or pellets in the solid stat e i.e. without the 
material going into the liquid phase as in the blast furnace. It is also known as Direct Reduced 
Iron (DRI) or Hot Briquetted Iron (HBI). This reduction of iron ore can be achieved by using 
either carbon bearing material such as non-coking coal or a suitable redu cing gas produced by 
reforming of natural gas. On the other hand sponge iron can also be used in the integrated steel 
plants to replace steel melting scrap to some extent as a coolant in the LD convertors and as a 
part of the change mix in the basic oxygen furnace and open hearth furnace. 
5.2 Non-coking coal and natural gas are the two main ingredients in spong e iron technology. 
Earlier the technology was limited upto use. of non-coking coal but with the technological 
innovation gas based sponge iron plants have also been set up. While coal based technology 
involves reduction of iron ore in a rotary kiln using non-coking coal as a reduct ant, gas based one 
uses Hydrogen or Carbon Mono Oxide or a mixture of both as reductant s. Gas based sponge iron 
manufacturing process requires high-grade iron ore with around 65%. At present non-coking coal 
is imported for sponge iron industry. Less availability of high grade of iron ore and Jack of 
required allocation of natural gas have proved to be impediments in proper development of 
sponge iron industries. 
5.3 According to Government 's report , a number of steps have been taken to promote the 
sponge iron industry as a major thrust area. Broadly, the sponge iron industr y was delicensed in 
March, 1985. Then under the new industrial policy the requirement of obta ining registration for 
setting up new plants was dispensed with in 1991. Sponge iron is also includ ed in the list of "High 
Priority Industries" in the new policy. The production capacity of first coal based plant which was 
set up in 1981, has been doubled from 30,000 tpa to 60,000 tpa. Governm ent have also set up a 
Linkage Committee in the Ministry of Steel to assist the enterpreneures , inte rested in setting up 
sponge iron plants, by way of providing single window clearance for linkage in the production of 
coal and movement of coal and iron ore by the Railways. The Committee has been given to 
under stan d that the Ministry of Steel has been successful in pursuading the Ministry of Petroleum 

and Natural Gas with regard to allocation of natural gas for gas based sponge iron plants of a 
capacity of 4 million tonnes per annum. 
5.4 During the course of his evidence the Secretary, Ministry of Steel informed the Committee 
that at present Government have allocated natural gas to five sponge iron plants. These plants are 
namely (i) Essar Gujarat Ltd., Gujarat (ii) Grasim Industries Ltd., Maharashtra (iii) Nippon Demo 
!spat Ltd., Maharashtra (iv) Kalyani Steels Ltd ., Maharashtra and (v) Usha Rect ifire Ltd., U.P. He 
further informed that the Petroleum Ministry has got a priority list and gas is allocated mainly to 
the power and fertilizer sector. There is no surplus gas available for further allocat ion to any of 
steeVsponge iron plants. If an industrialist wants to set up a plant he approac hes the Ministry of 
Steel by way of filling up a memorandum opting for v~rious available linkages such as coal, gas, 
railways etc. and for such purpose a Linkage Committee has been set up in the Ministry to liaison 
on his behalf with the concerned authorities. 
5.5 The installed production capacity of sponge iron has increased. from 30,000 tones in 1980-81 
to about 18 lakh tonnes in 1992-93. The production during last 4 years has increased from 
1.9 lakh tonnes in 1988-89 to 12.8 lakh tonnes in 1991-92 as per the details given below:-

implementation. The total additional capacity under implementation is around 45 lakh tonnes.

According to Government's estimate the annual production of company in 1992-93 was 
expected to be around 49,000 tonnes against the fixed target of 51,000 tonnes due to 
deterioration in the quality of coal supplied by Singareni Collieries, lower ash carbon contents in 
coal and adverse conditions of transportation of iron ore. 
5.6 The Committee has been informed by the Secretary that an installed capacity of 6 million 
tonnes of sponge iron would be created by the end of the Ylllth Five Year Plan. as against the 
Present installed capacity of 2.49 million tonnes. Various units are coming into operation from 
time to time while some other units are at different stages of completion. A majority of them will 
come into operat ion in the year 1994-95. Some units are likely to come into operation in the year 
1995-96. One unit will come into operation in 1996-97. All these projects were given linkages 
during Seventh Five Year Plan. The target so fixed is not a restrictive target and the same can go 
beyond that depending on dynamics and demand of the situation in the years to come. However 
he added that no investment is proposed to be made by Government in achieving the projected 
production targets and the entire additional capacity is expected to be set up in the private sector. 
Government would welcome the proposals from private enterpreneurs in that regard. According 
to the Secretary, Government have no information about expansion of capacity utilisation being 
undertaken, if any, by a specific private unit. The Committee has been given to understand that 
one lndustrial Enterpreneur's Memorandum has been filled for a sponge iron plant of 15,000 
tonnes per annum capacity in Goa. Government presumes that this would be coal based project 
but no request for coal linkage has been received by it from the ente rpreneur. Accordin g to the 
Secretary in such cases it is presumed that those who do not follow up their proposals , it mea ns 
they are not serious about their proposals. 
5. 7 The high cost of production has severely affected the capacity utilisati o n of sponge iron 
plants for which the present duty structure in mainl y responsible. Sponge Iron Manuf acturers 
Association and some sponge iron producers have repres ented against present dut y structur e with 
following requests:-
(i) reduction of customs duty on iron ore, iron ore pellets and non-coking coal in order to 
reduce the cost of raw material; 
(ii) keeping customs duty on imported scrap at a level that would allow sponge iro n 
producers to get a remunerative prices. 
According to Government's reports customs duty on iron ore has been brought down from 
90% to 20% and on iron ore pellets from 35% to 15% in the current year's budget. 
During the course of oral evidence the Secretary informed the Committee that their 
recommendations about providing non-coking coal facility to the producers is under consideration 

of the Finance Ministry. Another recommendation regarding reduction of import duty on scrap 
from 12% to 5% is also pending for considerat ion of the Ministry of Finance. According to the 
Secretary any proposal which goes from any Ministry to the Ministry of Finance for giving reliefs to 
the various industries is looked into by the Finance Ministry from the point of view of their effect 
on the overall revenue and resource position. Government are supporting the sponge iron industry 
to come up and its policies are attuned to see that sponge iron industry in India grows and at the 
same time to ensure that mini steel plants do not suffer. To maintain such balance a set of packages 
has been taken up with Finance Ministry so that the cost of production also comes clown. 
The Committee has noted that the following average production cost of sponge iron worked out 
in 1992:-
Gas based (old plants) Rs. 5102 per tonne 
Gas based (new plants) Rs. 5402 per tonne 
Coal based (old plants) Rs. 4150 per tonne 
Coal based (new plants) Rs. 5150 per tonne 
While clarifying the reasons for difference in production of new and old plants, the Secretary 
informed the Committee that old plants generally get fully depreciated and their fixed cost goes 
clown as a result of which cost of production becomes cheaper. On thf' ::::i1er hand the newer plants 
have got a heavy investment and their servicing cost is much higher which raises the cost of 
production. However, performance-wise new plants are better. 
5.8 ln the note furnished to the Committee the Ministry has informed that no study has been 
conducted to compare our production costs with production costs in other countries. The Secretary 
informed the Committee that as per the information available to them, sponge iron in the 
developed countries is generally produced for captive consumption. Information or data on 
international price of sponge iron is not even available with Sponge Iron Manufacturers' Association 
a~ nobody is importing spong iron from abroad, However. Government would make an attempt to 
conduct a study about it. About the quality of sponge iron of new plants the Secretary informed the 
Committee that the same is comparable to international level because of availability of good quality 
iron ore in the country. 
6.0 On the basis of the documents and other material made available and also the oral evidence 
of the Secretary of the Ministry of Steel before it the Committee notes that rhe manufacturing 
process of the sponge iron has not been 'technologically sound and cost effective. The Committee 
has noted the requirement of high grade iron ore in sponge iron manufacturing process but good 
quality iron ore is not being extracted due to unscientific methods being used for this purpose. For 
example out of the total recoverable reserves of 76.1 million tonnes of iron ore in Goa only 13.5 
million tonnes is high grade and these deposits are rather scattered. The Committee feels that the 
available deposits of iron are in Goa are most valuable in terms of qual ity and if the same are 
extracted in a more scien tific way dependence in terms of import could be reduced to some extent. 
Though expensive but there is possibility of extracting iron ore of good qual ity in Goa by tak ing out 
the water out of the deposites which have otherwise remained unexplored clue to water level. 
The Committee observes that import of non-coking coal has been quite expensive. No serious 
efforts have been undertaken so far to ensure availability of good quality coal for sponge iron sector 
from the coal reserves available within the country and this had Jed to dependence on imports. The 
Commitree feels that the Ministry of Steel should urgently take up the matter with the Ministry of 
Coal so that good quality coal is made available to sponge iron industry at cheaper rates 
indigenously. 'Alternatively it would be cheaper if only coa l is imported and the non-coking process 
of the same is done in the country itself. The Committee expresses its concern over slackness and 
indifferent attitude of Government in not allotting gas to sponge iron industry despite the fact that 
sponge iron is included in the list of "High Priority Industries" in the new Ind ustrial Policy. The 

Committee is not convinced with Ministry's plea about non-availability of the same. The Committee 
feels that a lot of natural gas which is wasted everyday by way of flaring up could be utilised by 
allocating to sponge iron sector. Needful pursuasion with the Petroleum Ministry should be initiated 
in this direction. The Committee recommends that immediate steps be taken by the Ministry in 
getting the allocation of required natural gas to sponge iron industry for better productivity on the 
lines of power and fertilizer sectors. Implementation of certain units I projects would otherwise be 
jeopardisecl due to delay in supply of natural gas which will be a national Loss. 
6.1 The Committee is not satisfied with the growth of sponge iron production in the country. 
As per Government's own submission the production has been far below the installed capacity in 
most of the coal as well as gas based plants. The Committee feels that crucial areas like supply of 
better quality of coal and transportation of iron ore have been neglected to a large extent. Such lack 
of proper monitoring and feed back bas resulted into less capacity utilisation of the plants. The 
Committee is particularly not happy with the actual production figures in respect of Sponge Iron 
India Limited which is a PSU where the production has not reached the expected level despite of 
Government's efforts since the installation of the unit. The company has not only failed in achieving 
the production target but its performance in generating its internal resources has also been far from 
satisfactory during 1992-93 in comparison to 1991-92. The Company is thus in urgent need of 
protection in terms of supply of good quality of coal and favourable transportation conditions of 
iron for maintaining its viability. The Committee is not convinced with the Government's steps for 
achieving the proposed production targets of 6 million tonnes of sponge iron as projected at the end 
of Ylllth Five Year Plan. The Committee feels that the Ministry has no clear cut perception in 
achieving the target as no investment is proposed to be made by Government during the current 
plan and the entire additional capacity is expected to be set up in the private sector. The 
Government have downgraded its priorities towards the sponge iron industry by conceding the fact 
that it has no information about expansion of capacity utilisation being undertaken, if any, by 
private units. The Committee notes that Government have failed to intimate the Committee about 
the definite proposals which have come from the private sector which may enhance the production 
of sponge iron in future . The Committee observes that Government has by doing so left much to be 
desired by staking its claim for achieving the projected production target either in the absence of 
any Government investment or definite private proposals about setting new plants during VII Ith 
Plan period. The Committee therefore , recommends that Government should review its production 
targets and reschedule its priorities as per the available infrastructure vis-a-vis planning on ground 
realities. 
6.2 In the present conditions private enterpreneurs have a major role to play in contributing 
towards growth of sponge iron production in the country and a time has come when suitable 
package of incentives be given to them. The Committee has noted that as per present procedure an 
industrialist who wishes to set up a plant is required to fill up an Industrial Enterprenuer . 
Memorandum which is processed by a Linkage Committee in the Ministry. The Committee finds 
that follow up of the proposal is left to the enterpreneur. A system is required to be devised in the 
Ministry where the processing of private proposals could be expedited with constant and proper 
coordination with the concerned authorities and regular intraction with the enterpreneur should be 
maintained till a final decision is taken on his proposal. The Committee impresses upon the 
Government to immed iately process the proposals pending before it and devise an effective 
mechanism for their time bound implementation. 
6.3 The Committee is conscious about the factors responsible for increase in the production 
cost of sponge iron. It has been given to understand that the cost of production of sponge iron with 
present duty structure is very high. Suggestions of the manufacturers regarding reduction of customs 
duty on iron ore, iron ore pellets and non-coking coal are pending for clearance with Ministry of 
Finance. The Committee feels that the import duty of 35% on sponge iron is on the high side. This 
has increased a great burden on the sponge iron producers who have passed the same to the 

consumers by incre asing the prices five times since the last budger. This rising trend of prices would 
severely affect the industry as a whole . The Committee feels that budget relief annoui1ced this year 
have passed neither to the manufacturers nor the consumers. Consequently the steel industry in 
general and spon gl.! iron sector in particular is at the brink of disaster due to discriminatory 
approach of the Government. The Committee recommends that urgent remedial steps should be 
taken to revive the units I plants which have become sick and also those likely to be affected and 
appropriate duty reli"ef be given to the industry. 
6.4 The Committee finds that the no study has been conducted by Government to compare our 
production costs with production costs in other countries. The Committee is unhappy to note that 
such information is not available with any of the manufacturers. The Committee takes a serious 
note of such lack of foresightedness and initiative particularly in the present juncture when the 
country is to go global and accelerate the process of liberlisation and the required information could 
be more effect ive in the world scenerio. The Committee would like Government to conduct a 
comparative study of production cost of sponge iron in other countries so that the same could be a 
guiding factor while projecting <I balanced and well planned approach in arresting the rising cost of 
indigenous production on the basis of the experience of other wuntries in the matter. 
6.5 The Committee reitrates its concern for the urgent need for promotion of sponge iron 
industry , which has to play a vital role in secondary sector of steel production in the country. There 
is much scope for improvement in the planning so as to ensure capacity utilisation. The Committee 
is confident that practical and result oriented mechanism would be adopted by Government keeping 
in view the fact that the industry is exposed to favourable and positive options under the new 
Industrial Policy and it is included as ''High Priority Areas". If not given the requ ired protection at 
the juncture, the Committee foresees a bleak future for the industry which would be a tremendous 
national loss to economic regeneration and industrial growth. 
6.6 The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations as mentioned above will 
receive serious consideration for implementation. 
MOTURU HANUMANTHA RAO 
Chairman 
Department Related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry.

3.2 Replying to the Commi"ee's query regarding the extent of participation of private 
enterpr ise into Non-Ferrous Mrning and Metallu rgical Industries and steps being taken to 
promote foreign investment. the Ministry of Mines stated tltat the Indian Mining Sector was 
opened up in stages. to private. including foreign investment, as part of the structural adju'>lntcnt 
programme of the Indian economy. This has been done in tune with the gen~ral economic 
libcralisation and reforms introduced by the Government in various sectors. The Nauonal 
Mineral Policy, 1993, enunciated this policy of encouraging private. including foreign investment 
in the mineral sector. The Mines & Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957, the ba_sic 
3. 

statute, was amended in 1994, by which foreign direct investment (FDI) in the mineral sector was 
welcomed for the first time. Recently, in January, 2000, it has been further amended to grant 
greater security of tenure , and to simplify procedures, etc. so that the mining regime in India 
today is on par with global standards in this regard . 
3.3 The Central Government has const ituted the foreign Investment Promotion Board (FlPB) 
for clearance of applications for the foreign direct investment proposals. Since January 199\ the 
Government had been ,allowing FDI upto 50% in mining (except in respect of mining gold, silver 
and precious stones) and 74% in metallurb'Y and minera l processing through the automatic route. 
For FDI above these limits, the proposals had to come before the FIPB which used to consider 
them on a case to case basis. The FDI policy has been further liberalised w.e.f. ll 'h February , 
2000 to accelerate foreign investment in the mineral sector There will henceforth be no difference 
in tbe caps on foreign equity holdings to be allowed at ihe stages of exploration and that of 
mining:-
(a) For all minerals with which the Ministry of Mines is concerned other than diamonds 
& precious stones , foreign equ ity holding up to J 00% is allowed on the automatic 
route, for both explorat ion and mining. 
(b) In case of diamonds & precious stones, foreign equity up to 74% is allowed on the 
automatic route for both explora tion and mining operations. For proposals seeking 
higher than 74% foreign equity, the cases will have to come to FJPB for clearance. 
(c) Foreign equity upto 100% is allowed on the automatic route for processing of 
minerals and metallurgy . 
(d) There is no requirement of NOC from an exist ing joint venture partner for fresh 
investments . The prospective investo r will only have to give a declaration that he has 
no existingjoint venture for the same area and/or the partic~ar mineral.

project was worked out assuming that the project wou ld be financed by internal resources of

23. Tax proposal affecting Steel Industry 
23.1 Reacting on the existing tax-structure the Ministry of Steel stated that the existing tax 
structu re is quite progressive and reasonable for the growt h of the steel indu stry .Over the years 
the gove rnment has reduced the import duties on raw materials for stee l industry and have 
removed anomalies existing in the tax structure. The Ministry of Stee l viewed that there are 
certai n issues i.e. Reduction in import duty on non coking coal from 25% to 5% at par wit h 
coking coa l ;Reduc tion in import duty on metallurgical coke from 15% to 5%.; Reduction in 
import duty on some of the raw materials for refractory making; Reduction in import duty on low 
silica limestone. zinc and graphite electrodes which are inputs for steel making and Reduction in 
excise duty on l ong products like GP/GC sheets which are used for rural housing which need to 
be addressed. 
23 .. 2 The Committee is pleased to note that the existing tax struct ure is progressive and 
reasonable for the growth of steel industry . The Committee hopes that the Ministry of 
Steel wou ld take up the remaining anomalies in the existing tax-structure affect ing the 
general prospects of stee l industry . 
24. Problems in Exports and Imports 
24.1 The Secretary, during the course of his oral evidence, informed the Committee " unless and 
until, we have export market for ourselves, our industry will not be able to sustain for itself. We 
have been able to export 3 million tonnes in a year. But, in the recent past, countries like the U.S. 
and Europe have imposed anti-dump ing duties. On the one hand, the U.S. talks about WTO 
compatibi lity, and whenever India takes any act ion to safeguard its industry, they say that it 
should be done as per the provisions of the WTO; whereas, on the ot her hand, in their own 
country, they are placing all sorts of restrictions and imposing very high duties the Secretary 
s~ated. He further stated that recently, in the Clinton regime, they passed an Act which provides 
that the revenue collected by way of anti-dumping duties could be passed on to the steel units. 
S:>, it is essential for us to keep our foothold in the internati onal market , the Secretary felt. 
Another problem is imports in the form of inflow of seconds and defectives at a very cheap rate 
the Secretary informed. That is also harming the domestic steel industry. The Ministry of Steel 
have taken up the matter with the Ministry of Commerce, and after a great deal of persuasion , the 
Ministry of Comme rce have agreed to impose some sort of non-tariff barriers, at least, for 
stconds and defectives, the Secretary added. 
24.2 The Comm ittee understand that exports are essential ingredieht of the growth of industry. 
Similarly, imports should not ca use glaring damag e to the indigenous industry. The Committee 
therefore recommends that Ministry of Commerce may take necessary steps to find solution, to 
the problems of our steel industry faced in internati ona l market in respect of exports and from the 
imports. Ministry of Steel may pursue the matter with Ministry of Com merce. 
25. Railway Freight 
25.1 The Secretary informed the Comm ittee that because of the two percent increase in the freight 
in the Railway Budget of 2001-2002 they have been adversely affected. In fact, it is only the 
public sector companies like SAIL and RINL which are using rail for transporting their finished 
products. The new steel plants are using road traffic for transporting their finished products. 

Even this two per cent hike in freight is going to cost the SAIL about Rs. 28 crores more and to 
RINL about Rs. I 0 crores more, the Secretary added. 
25.2. The Secretary also informed that another problem with the Railways is relating to 
transport of iron-ore from Bailadila to Vizag. When that railway line was constructed, the 
Railways incurred a lot of expenditure on constructing that line. At that time, it was decided to 
levy some additional freight on transportation of iron-ore. The additional freight was charged for 
the entire sector. It was also decided at that time that when the traffic would reach the level of 60 
lakh tonnes per annum, that additional freight would be withdrawn . Today, the traffic has 
reached to 120 lakh tonnes per annum. But it is still continuing. The Secretary also stated that 
they have taken up this issue with the Ministry of Railways and there is a strong case for 
withdrawal on this surcharge. 
25.3 The Committee understands that the two percent hike in railway freight would have a 
severe impact on SAIL and RINL. Ministry of Steel may take up the matter with Railways. The 
Committee also feels that the additional freight charged on transportation of iron ore from 
Baladila to Vizag should have been stopped after it reached the level of 60 lakh tonnes per annum 
as per the decision taken at that time. Now, it has reached 120 lakh tonnes. The Committee 
recommends that the Ministry of Steel may pursue the matter with Railways and Railways also 
may consider removing this at the earliest. 
26. Anti Dumping 
26.1 The Secretary Ministry of Steel during the course of oral evidence stated ,"the USA has 
the largest market for our exports. The anti dumping duty is against a company specific and 
product specific . But, there is a legal battle. In some cases, we have won and in some cases we 
have lost. Suppose, some company is exporting against contract in USA. The moment anti­
dumping duty is imposed, that schedule is affected for next six months . What happens in USA is 
that they first impose preliminary determination in very large number of cases, and just on first 
hearing, they see what is the preliminary case and they impose a duty of 40-45% . Generally , 
after hearing both the parties 50% of case are disposed of in this way an early stage. 
Whether the duty is conformed or it is not confirmed , is decided later . When the Committee 
sought to know as to why this cannot be done in India, he informed the Committee they ," we 
have made a request before the Ministry of Commerce.... We want some amendment to the 
procedures. We have already requested the Ministry that provisional duties must be imposed ". 
26.2 The Committee observes with concern that the anti-dumping system that is prevailing in 
other countries is different from that of ours. In the anti-dumping system of our country, 
complaints are received and after examination of those complaints , the witnes ses are called . Then 
the whole thing is enquired upon and it takes a long time, may be one year or six months. Later 
on, the decision is taken. During this period of complaint and inquiry, the materials will 
automatically be coming into the country. Then after one year, if it is found that this import was 
not required, then imposition of certain restrictions is resorted to. But by that time, the damage 
would have taken place to the industry or to the trade . The Committee feels that the time has 
come for our country to think and act on it seriously. The Committee recommends that our anti­
dumping law also may be brought at par with that of other countries, particularly America.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 4-5
 
4.         The Sub-Committee feels that recovery of pending cases should be expedited by fixing accountability at district
administration level also.  In addition the record of pending cases be computerised and updated at regular intervals.  There
should be time bound specific targets to be monitored at District level by District magistrates.
 
5.         The Sub-Committee impresses upon the Government to explore ways and means for recovery of PMRY loans
under defaults, as delays occur in serving of notices and appearance in the Court.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The Office has been monitoring to improve/expedite the recovery of loan dues under the PMRY.  The State/UTs
have been requested to include in their existing Land Revenue Arrears Recovery Acts, recovery of loan arrears under
PMRY, so that these are recoverable as arrears of land revenue.  The State/UTs were requested to conduct joint recovery
drives.  A letter was written to State/UTs on 26.6.2000 reiterating the need to take necessary steps to improve recovery of
loan under the scheme.  A copy of the letter written to State/UTs on 26.6.2000 is enclosed for ready reference (Annexure
– III).
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION NO.  6             
 
The Sub-Committee observes that bankers generally raise their concern about the late communication of targets to
them from the Government.  For example, targets are being communicated in August/September wherein they are to be
achievable by March (end of financial year).  The Sub-Committee recommends that the targets for PMRY should be
communicated to Banks from the Government, well in time to avoid any kind of time constraint.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The basic target for the year 2000-2001 under the PMRY were communicated to State/UTs and to the RBI on
19.4.2000.  The additional targets under the scheme were communicated to the State/UTs and to the RBI on 16.6.2000. 
The RBI has been requested to convey the bank-wise target as early as possible in the light of the recommendation of the

Committee.  A copy of the letter written to the RBI in this regard is enclosed. (Annexure – II).
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION NO. 7 & 11
 
7.         The Sub-Committee impresses upon the Government that DICs should avoid disproportionate sponsoring of
applications under PMRY.  This act, in return, will minimise the pendency rate of applications.
 
11.       The Sub-Committee has noticed that DICs fail to complete the identification process well in advance.  As a matter
of fact, in place of transmission of applications to banks under PMRY, in a phased manner, they do the same in bunching.
 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that it has to be ensured that the flow of applications from DICs to
banks; take place in a phased manner and the practice of bunching of applications should be stopped.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The Office of the Dev. Commissioner(SSI), while communicating the annual target to the State/UTs prescribes a
quarterly schedule for sponsoring of applications by the District Task force Committees to banks.  A copy of the schedule
is enclosed for ready reference (Annexure – IV).  The State/UTs have been requested to issue necessary instructions to the
DICs to adhere to the schedule prescribed for sponsoring of applications to avoid disproportionate sponsoring of
applications to banks to avoid bunching of applications at the fag end of the year.  A copy of the letter issued to State/UTs
is enclosed. (Annexure – V)
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/ OBSERVATION NO. 8
 
The Sub-Committee observes that under PMRY, quality applications are not being sponsored to   banks.  As
regards this shortcoming, the Sub-Committee feels that Branch Managers should be involved actively in selecting the
beneficiaries and the activities.
           
ACTION TAKEN
 
The guidelines of the PMRY scheme provides for the inclusion of the lead bank and other participating banks as
the members of the district task force committees.  The subsequent guidelines also provide that all participating banks in a
district may participate in the district task force committee meetings on a rotational basis.  A copy of the letter is enclosed
(Annexure – VI).  The RBI vide Circular dated 19.11.96 has instructed to CMDs of all Indian Scheduled Commercial
Banks that banks can receive the applications directly and send them to the sponsoring agencies with their observations on
the viability and bankability of the project.  A copy of the letter is enclosed for ready reference. (Annexure – VII)
 
            The RBI has been requested to reiterate the necessary instructions in view of the recommendation of the
Committee.
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 9
 
As per the provisions made under PMRY, loans should be in the ratio of 50%, 30% and 20% in respect  of
industry, services and business sector.  During the course of the discussion, the Sub-Committee came to know that mostly
applications are received for business activities and applications regarding industry are few in numbers.  The Sub-
Committee feels that steps should be taken to ensure that the ratio of loans for all three activities are maintained according
to provisions contained in the Scheme.
 
 
 
ACTION TAKEN

            The State/UTs have been requested to sponsor more applications for industry sector in view of the fact that it has
more employment potential.  A copy of the letter issued to State/UTs is enclosed. (Annexure – V).
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION  NO. 12
 
The Sub-Committee notes that PMRY Club is a novel idea.  As a result of implementation of this, majority of the
problems such as creation of assets, marketing arrangement and repayment of bank’s dues etc. will be easily overcome. 
The Sub-Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be taken to ensure that PMRY Clubs should be
encouraged to start its operation in all the prominent centres.
 
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The State/UTs have been requested to explore the possibility for starting the PMRY club in their States/UTs.  A
copy of the letter written to State/UTs is enclosed for ready reference. (Annexure – V).
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION NO.13
 
The Sub-Committee notes with discontent that the reduction in disbursement as compared to loan amount applied
for has been dampening the spirit and enthusiasm of borrowers of PMRY.  So, the Sub-Committee impresses upon the
Government to take suitable corrective measures as regards the cases, the quantum of which is sizeable, where it is
presumed by bankers that borrowers are incapable to executing the projects or there is likelyhood of less demand in the
area due to saturation of activity and thus the loan applied for is reduced without following any yardstick.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The matter was discussed in the 10
th Meeting of High Powered Committee for the PMRY held on 22.3.2000 and it
was decided that banks may be advised by the RBI to adequately finance micro enterprises set up under the PMRY so that
they do not become unviable due to inadequate funds. The RBI has issued instructions to CMDs,  Indian Scheduled
Commercial Banks to assess properly the working capital need of the units to be set up under the scheme.  A copy of the
letter is enclosed for ready reference. (Annexure – IX)
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO.14
 
The Sub-Committee is unhappy to note that in several cases of PMRY loans, the disbursement is stopped or
delayed on unjustified/flimsy grounds.  Thus, the Sub-Committee recommends that suitable measures should be taken
concerning the stoppage/delay of disbursement of PMRY loans on such grounds.
 
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The RBI vide its letter dated 10.12.97 addressed to CMDs of all Indian Scheduled Commercial Banks has stated
that in several cases banks have delayed disbursement of loan on unjustified/flimsy grounds. A copy of the letter written
by the RBI is enclosed for ready reference (Annexure – X).  The RBI is requested to initiate action on the
recommendation of the committee. 
 
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION NO.18
 
The Sub-Committee notes with discontent that till now banks are not very enthusiastic about projects under
PMRY.

19.       The Sub-Committee feels that appropriate measures are still needed to generate awareness and educate the people

The Sub-Committee, through its discussion, came to know that Margin Money Scheme of REGP is in its nascent

level.

The Sub-Committee feels that model proposals on illustrative rural industries should be prepared and circulated to 
bank branches for their guidance.  Nonetheless, while preparing these model proposals concerning REGP, industries

ACTION TAKEN

The Sub-Committee came to know that the employment generated by coir industry is by and large considered as
part time. Thus the Sub-Committee recommends that Government should ensure the implementation of various measures

under Domestic Market Development and Export Promotion are aimed at developing the market of coir and coir products
in India and abroad. There has been an increasing trend in the domestic as well as international market for coir products,
as evidenced by the enhancement in domestic consumption and exports.

The marketing and sale of coir products in India still require the acceleration. The Sub-Committee feels that
Government should augment the marketing and sales of coir products in the domestic market.

The following actions have been initiated  to augment the marketing and sales of  coir products in the domestic
market:-
 
1.

2.
      Publicity on TV network and  in print media.
 
 
3.

under implementation since 1.4.1999. The modified parameters include enhancement in the project cost for self
employment ventures to be set up under industry and service sector from Rs.1 lakh to Rs.2 lakhs.  The project cost for self
employment ventures to be set up under business sector continues to Rs.1 lakh.  A copy of the modified guidelines is
enclosed for ready reference.  (Annexure – I)
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 20
 
            The Sub-Committee feels that necessary measures are required to check the instances where the loans/subsidy are
being utilized for the purpose other than the purposes for which these are granted.
 
ACTION TAKEN REPORT:
 
            The Office of the Dev. Commissioner(SSI) vide letter dated 11.5.99 addressed to all State/UTs and to the RBI has
forwarded the views of M/o Law & Justice that cases can be filed against those borrowers who mis-utilise the loan

52nd Report

sanctioned to them under the PMRY.  A copy of the letter dated 19.5.99 is enclosed for ready reference. (Annexure – XI)
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 26
 
The Sub-Committee recommends that monitoring cells should be set up at Regional/Zonal offices to monitor the
progress of REGP regularly.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
In order to monitor the implementation of the Margin Money Scheme and also guide the potential entrepreneurs,
State Level Task Forces on the MMS have been constituted under the Chairmanship of the Commissioner of Industries of
the respective State/UT.  This Task Force includes Chairman of State Level Bankers Committee (SLBC) and Managing
Director of State Apex Cooperative Bank, Chairman of RRBs etc.
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 28
 
The Sub-Committee notes with discontent that funds for Rural Employment Generation Programme including
District Special  Employment Programme and RPDS Block Development Programme are still to be disbursed and
apparently making the Scheme dysfunctional.  The Sub-Committee recommends that Government should take all
necessary steps to overcome such situation and ascertain the continuous flow of funds by the KVIC.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The District Special Employment Programme and RPDS Blocks Development Programme of the KVIC have been
merged in its normal programme of the REGP w.e.f. 1.4.1999 and as such no separate funds are allocated.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 32
 
The Sub-Committee feels that requisite amendments in  KVIC’s notification should be brought out, concerning the
population criteria in Margin Money Scheme, as there are some villages which are classified as Municipal Villages in
Kerala State.
 
ACTION  TAKEN 
 
Since there  are some States like Kerala, where density of population is high and characteristic of rural area is
slowly fading away, certain amendments to the KVIC’s Act, to accommodate larger population may be appropriate.  The
Government amended KVIC Act in this regard vide Notification dated  27.10.1994 and the definition of Village is as
under:-
 
“The area comprises any village and includes area comprised any town, the population of which does not exceed
20,000 or such other figures as the Central Government may specify from time to time”.
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 34
 
The Sub-Committee notes that programmes for the KVIC sector should be finalised in advance, so that the State
Boards can prepare their action plan in accordance with the guidelines of the KVIC.  The Sub-Committee also views that
there is necessity to ensure the confidence of entrepreneurs about the continuation of the programme and easy availability
of funds.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
Regarding Margin Money Scheme, the RBI has already provided necessary code Numbers to Village Industries

52nd Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/52ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:12:27]
and Margin Money Scheme which will enables the Banks to incorporate necessary provision for this scheme in the
District Credit Plans at appropriate stage.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 35
 
The Sub-Committee came to know that Khadi sector has been providing more employment opportunities
especially for the women folk in rural areas.  Some of the State Governments have been providing incentive wages for
spinners and weavers.  The Sub-Committee thus feels that Central Government should also provide such wage incentives
in order to retain and improve the employment opportunities in Khadi sector.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The wage rate/incentive of Khadi Sector is regulated by the provision made in the Khadi cost chart.
 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS NO. 45
 
The Sub-Committee came to know that usual annual average stock holding of coir products is of Rs. 15 Crore. The
Sub-Committee feels that adequate measures should be taken by Government to clear the stock holding of coir products.
 
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The measures taken for domestic market development and export promotion are expected to increase the demand
for coir and coir and coir products.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH REPLIES OF THE GOVERNMENT
HAVE NOT BEEN ACCPETED BY THE COMMITTEE
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 2
 
The Sub-Committee notes that under PMRY, there is subsidy ceiling of Rs.7,500/.  The Sub-Committee is of the
view that the practice of subsidy ceiling may be dispensed with and instead 15 per cent subsidy may be made, admissible
for all quantum of loan amount.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The rate of subsidy has since been revised for the NE States.  It is @ 15 per cent of the project cost subject to a
ceiling of Rs.15,000/- per beneficiary.  It has been decided in the 10
th Meeting of High powered Committee for PMRY
that the ceiling on subsidy may also be raised for weaker sections i.e. SC/STs, ex-servicemen, physically disabled persons
and women and also for the States/UTs of J&K, Sikkim, Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.  This could be
implemented only after approval from the Cabinet.
 
COMMENTS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee  hopes  that   approval of Cabinet  would  be obtained  at the earliest and it would be implemented
expeditiously.
 
RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION NO.3
 
The Sub-Committee observes that the recovery under PMRY is far from satisfaction.  The Sub-Committee,
accordingly, is of the view that the recovery process of PMRY loans at bank level can be strengthened by creating District

52nd Report

level Recovery cells with every bank.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The RBI has been requested to initiate necessary action on the recommendations of the Committee.  A copy of the
communication sent to RBI is enclosed.  (Annexure – II). 
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The Committee recommends that the Government may pursue the matter with RBI for an early implementation of
the recommendation.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO.  10
 
The general view is that viability aspects of proposals are ignored by DICs while sponsoring the  applications
under PMRY.  The Sub-Committee recommends that DICs should go thoroughly into the details of each and every
proposal including spot verification, technical feasibility and financial viability.
In this connection, the Sub-Committee further recommends that the plea of helplessness from DICs, for want of
staff should not be taken as an excuse.
 
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The issue was discussed in the 10
th Meeting of the High powered Committee for the PMRY held on 22.3.2000 
and it was decided that State/UTs may be requested to instruct to the DICs to identify viable projects in their respective
districts and prepare project profiles for the guidelines of the prospective entrepreneurs under the PMRY.  In addition
project profiles prepared by the SISIs used by various financial institutions (FIs) and similar agencies can also utilised.  A
copy of the letter written to all State/UTs is enclosed for ready reference. (Annexure – VIII).
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee feels that DICs will have to play a pro-active role. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its
recommendation that DICs should go thoroughly into every proposal. DICs  should invariably prepare project profiles for
assistance of  prospective entrepreneurs.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 15
 
The Sub-Committee strongly recommends that necessary steps should be taken by the bank management to do
away with the prevailing psychosis of bank branches that if they start sanctioning the cases of PMRY on regular basis then
pending cases of non-performing banks will be thrust upon them.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The finding of the committee has been communicated to the RBI.  A copy of the letter written to RBI is enclosed
for ready reference. (Annexure – II)
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee feels that RBI needs to do a thorough review of the system.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 16  &  17
 
16.       The Sub-Committee strongly recommends that RBI’s guidelines for disposing of applications under PMRY within
the time-period of thirty days must be adhered to by banks.  Concerning it, the responsibilities should be fixed to
undertake needful corrective measures.

17.       The Sub-Committee impresses upon the Government to take suitable steps to minimise the rejection ratio by banks
against number of applications received, as in some of areas/regions, alarmingly it has been reported to be even 40 to 50
per cent.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
            The findings of the committee have been communicated to the RBI.  The  RBI has been requested to view
seriously the high rejections of applications by banks as observed by the committee.  RBI has been requested to issue
necessary instructions in this regard.  A copy of the letter written to the RBI is enclosed. (Annexure – II).
 
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The matter  requires to be pursued   vigorously  with RBI and progress thereof monitored  regularly.  After the RBI
has issued instructions, implementation  should be regularly reviewed and monitored.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 29
 
The Sub-Committee notes that concerning Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate Scheme, in most of the cases,
banks differ on ISES issued by the KVIC.  The Sub-Committee recommends that government should take necessary
initiatives to curb this practice.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
In this context, the recommendation made by the Committee to review the flow of institutional credit to the Khadi
sector under the Chairmanship of Shri S. K. Kalia, the then Managing Director of NABARD in 1993, was taken into
consideration and a Circular was issued by the RBI on 28
th July, 1994 (copy enclosed).  Annexure XII.
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation in this regard and feels that RBI should regularly monitor this
so as to curb the practice.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 31
 
The Sub-Committee recommends that necessary initiatives should be taken, so that NABARD’S  participation in
KVIC’s Margin Money Scheme enhances particularly for NABARD’S refinance facility for the purpose.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The KVIC regularly inter-acts with the NABARD on various issues, where NABARD can give
suggestions/guidance.  As an example, before engaging Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Cooperative Banks under the
Margin Money Scheme, the KVIC sought guidance of the NABARD. The KVIC  ensures to invite NABARD and hear its
views/suggestions while conducting quarterly review meetings of the Nationalised Banks engaged in the implementation
of Margin Money Scheme.
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The  Committee  is   of the view that  enhancement of  NABARD’s  participation in KVIC’s Margin Money
Scheme in respect of refinance facility   should   be  ensured .  
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 33

Over a period of time, more than 25% of the Khadi units have become sick due to various reasons.  There is no
programme with the KVIC for rehabilitating the sick units.  The Sub-Committee thus recommends that revival of sick
units should become a continuous programme alongwith the establishment of new units.  Moreover, the continuous
monitoring of the functioning of the old units will ensure the recovery of dues and continuous employment in rural areas.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The KVIC has already formulated guidelines for revitalizing sick Khadi institutions (copy enclosed) Annexure
XIII.
 
COMMENTS/OBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
The guidelines may be implemented at the earliest. Implementation of  guidelines for  revitalizing  sick khadi
institutions  should be monitored   properly .   The Committee   reiterates  the recommendation that revival    of sick units 
should become a  continuous  process alongwith  the  establishment of   new units.
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 36
 
The Sub-Committee came to know that KVIBs have been implementing Margin Money Scheme of the KVIC,
wherein the scheme envisages loan portion of the project cost to be met from Consortium Bank  Credit (CBC) sources and
margin money from the KVIB budgetary sources.  The Sub-Committee recommends that KVIBs should be better
equipped and strengthened so that they can become the catalysts of rural industries in the country.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The KVIC impress upon the State Governments to strengthen the infrastructure facilities of State KVI Boards so
that they can implement the programme in a more effective manner.
 
In order to implement the REGP/Margin Money Scheme, the KVIC had also placed Margin Money Grant with
State/UT KVI Boards in advance, so that the programme can be implemented without any delay.  However, it is observed
that due to weak infrastructure facilities some of the State/UT KVI Boards are not in a position to utilise such grants made
available to them even after a lapse of considerable time.  As far as projects under Margin Money Scheme are concerned,
the State/UT KVI Boards are empowered to recommend projects by ensuring its techno-economic viability without
awaiting for the prior approval from the KVIC.
 
 
COMMENT/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            It is unfortunate that funds are not being utilized  due to  lack  of infrastructure facilities. Central Govt. should take
up the matter with all state/UT Govts. for improving infrastructure facilities.
 
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO. 37
 
The Sub-Committee impresses upon the Government that more importance should be given for marketing of the
goods produced by KVI sector.  This will facilitate the expansion of rural industries by providing linkages.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
The KVIC has already launched common brand names for selected village industries products.
 
COMMENTSOBSERVATION  OF THE COMMITTEE
 
            The Committee is  not satisfied   with the  steps taken so far  for  marketing  of goods  produced by KVI Sector

and it  lacks  competitive   edge.  The Committee  desires that     this should be taken vigorously on the lines of private and
other commercial  organizations  to promote  goods  in the market    and earn recognition.    The Committee reiterates  its
earlier recommendation in this regard. Better marketing strategies are required to be adopted.   
 
 
RECOMMENDATION NO.42
 
            The Sub-Committee came to know that existing Co-operativisation Scheme was approved in the Eight Plan period.
The quantum of assistance allotted for managerial subsidy is not enough to appoint managerial personnel in the societies.
In addition, the cost of machines proposed under equipment assistance is not updated. Some of the machines could not be

curled coir and rubberised coir products are not included in this Scheme.
            Hence, the Sub-Committee is of the opinion that the quantum of assistance should be revised according to the
prevailing marketing rate and 100 per cent cost should be provided under this scheme.

REPORT
NATIONAL ALUMINIUM COMPANY LTD. (NALCO)
 
1.         Brief   Background
1.1       The  National Aluminium Company Ltd. (NALCO)  was incorporated on 7
th January, 1981 as the second public
sector company in the Aluminium Sector with a view to exploit a part of the large deposits of bauxite discovered in the
east coast. Nalco operates   bauxite mines  at panchpatmali in district Koraput (Orissa).  It runs a  0.8  million tonnes per
Annum  alumina refinery at   Damanjodi in Koraput  District, and  230000  tonnes per  Annum  Aluminium   Smelter  at
Angul  in Orissa.  The authorised capital of the company  has been reduced    from Rs. 1288.62  crores to  Rs.644.31
crores after the approval  of the  Cabinet.   The Government of India  holds  87.15% of equity  in Nalco, the balance
12.85%  being  held by financial institutions, employees, public etc.Nalco is a zero debt company  and  has been granted
Miniratna status by Government of India and it has also been  classified  as a    star  trading house. Nalco  exports 
Alumina  & Aluminium to  over thirty countries.  It has been  accorded ISO  9002 & ISO  14001 certification.

Modernisation Restructuring and Expansion programme  from 18th  to 25th January, 2001. The Committee visited

CMD and various other officials of NALCO during the visit at Bhubaneshwar on 24th January 2001. Further,  during the

th April, 2001  on the various issues pertaining to Nalco. The CMD of Nalco also
responded to the various queries raised by the members present during this meeting.
Expansion programme of  NALCO
Nalco  has undertaken   a  massive   expansion programme of   Rs.3700 crores  of  its       bauxite mines, alumina
refinery, smelter, captive power plant and port facilities.  The resources for the entire  expansion programme  are to be
internally generated.
This includes expansion    of  the capacity of  bauxite mines  from 2.4 millions tonnes  per year  to 4.8 million tonnes 
per year and that of  Alumina Refinery from 0.8  million tonnes  per year  to 1.575 million tonnes per year   at an 
investment  of Rs.1664.60 crores.    The project   was to be implemented within 51 months from the date of government
approval i.e. 18.12.1996.
The Government also approved   expansion of capacity of  Aluminium Smelter and Captive Power Plant of Nalco at 
Angul   so as to  increase the capacity of the Smelter from  230000 TPY  to 345000 TPY  and  that  of the  captive
power plant from the existing  720 MW   to  840 MW at an  investment of Rs.2062 crores .  The project  was also to be
implemented in  51 months from  the date of  Government approval i.e. 3
rd February 1998.
4.         Expansion of  NALCO’S port facilities
4.1       The Committee visited the Nalco’s port facilities at Visakhapatnam  on 20
th January, 2001.        The Committee
took a tour of the entire facility through sea .  This port facility is             located             on 9.14 hectares  and caters to
import of 1.2 lakh tonnes of Caustic Soda and   exports of 3.75 lakh tonnes of calcined alumina.  In addition it also
handles export of Aluminium    Metal by containers/barges and also imports  materials through Visakhapatnam Port.   
Nalco has  obtained on lease an additional 1.424 hectares of land   from Visakhapatnam     Port for expansion purpose.

6.    Financial restructuring
During  the course of discussions at Bhubhaneswar,    the Committee    asked  CMD, Nalco  about the    the     reasons 
for reducing the   paid up   share capital of Nalco to 50%  from Rs.1288.62           crore to 644.31 crore in  the year
1998.  The Committee also  asked  about the   impact of  such  capital restructuring   on the  physical and financial
performance of the company.  The CMD of Nalco  informed    that   relative to  (a) Sales turnover, (b) Profits after  tax
and (c) Financial ratios including  paid up capital of competitors like  Hindalco and Indal, the paid up share capital   of 
Rs.1288.62 crore of Nalco  was considered very much on the higher side and  hence the stock          performance ratios
like EPS, PE multiple and Share price etc. were   low  and  was not adequately  reflecting the  intrinsic   strength   of
Nalco. Hence, capital restructuring  was done with the prior permission of the government. Accordingly 50% of paid up
equity capital of 1288.62% was converted to redeemable secured debentures. The paid up equity capital after
restructuring was 644.31 crores out of which Govt of India holding is Rs.561.50 crores(87.15%).  The Committee was
also informed that the original project cost was partly financed by external commercial borrowings and partly by equity
subscribed by govt. of India. The entire foreign currency loan has been repaid by 30.09.98  and Nalco has become a zero
debt company except for debt created out of equity capital through a scheme of capital restructuring with the prior

Committee was further informed that there are    many plants  world wide working  with  their technology.  M/s
Engineers India Limited(EIL) were the prime Indian consultants for Mines, Alumina Refinery and Aluminium smelter.
They have also been engaged for the ongoing expansion projects of Bauxite mine, Alumina refinery and smelter plants.
M/s Development Consultants Ltd(DCL) were the consultants for the captive power plant and steam generation plant
and M/s Howe India (P) ltd for the Port facilities. M/s Dasturco have been appointed as consultant for expansion of
Captive Power Plant and M/s. MECON for expansion of Port facilities. The Committee was  apprised that the  quality
of   Alumina and  Aluminium produced  by Nalco meets all international  quality   standards  because of its technology. 
The  cost   of production of  Alumina  of  Nalco is lowest in the world because of appropriate technology and logistics.

It is good to obtain outside technology whenever required. The Committee recommends that Nalco should have a
