INTRODUCTION

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on

Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Sixty-sixth Report
of Sub-Committee-IV for Ministry of Mines ( of Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry) on performance review of Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research
Development and Design Centre which is under the administrative control of Department of
Mines ( Ministry of Mines and Coal )
2. The Committee on Industry at its meeting held on 120 February, .2001 inter-alia
constituted Sub-Committee-IV for Ministry of Mines. The Sub-Committee took up the issue of
performance review of Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development and Design Centre
(JNARDDC) . The Sub-Committee visited Nagpur from 11" to 14" September, 2001 and
interacted with the management and scientist of Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research
Development and Design Centre (JNARDDC).

3. The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 7" December, 2001 heard the Secretary,
Ministry of Mines and officials concerned. The Report has been prepared on the basis of on the
spot study and interaction with the Secretary , Ministry of Mines and officials of JNARDDC.

4 The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 26" December, 2001 considered and adopted
the Report.

5. The Committee at its meeting held on 26" December, 2001 considered and adopted the
Report.

NEW DELHL RAMDAS AGARWAL
December 26, 2001 Chairman,

JAWAHARLAL NEHRU ALUMINIUM RESEARCH DEVELOPMENT AND DESIGN
CENTRE (JNARDDC)

JNARDDC was registered as a society in 1987 to provide modern technological
inputs to primary and secondary aluminium Industries based on optimum utilisation of
existing facilities and further development of technical capabilities. The centre was set
up by the Ministry of Mines, Government of India as a project with assistance from the
United National Development Programme (UNDP) with a total cost of Rs.36.00 crore
consisting of a contribution of Rs.19.00 crores from Government of India and Rs.17.00
crores from UNDP. The Centre became fully operational since January, 1996 having the
capabilities for Geology and evaluation of bauxites; beneficiation and upgradation of
bauxites; total characterization of bauxites; technological testing of bauxites; energy
audit of alumina plant, foundry, system plant, chemical plant, etc.; process monitoring;
mathematical modeling; and downstream processing technology. The centre is equipped
with world class facilities for the study of bauxite, alumina and aluminium for the
benefit of the aluminium industry. It can also offer support to other non-ferrous
industries steel plants and the SSI in the areas of mining, chemical and mineralogical
analysis, energy auditing, failure analysis, microstructure studies and information
services. JNARDDC has six major divisions which includes  bauxite-alumina
technology; smelter-carbon technology; downstream technology; environment and waste
management; process control and modeling and process and product development.

1.2. JNARDDC _ is an autonomous body set up by the Ministry of Mines, Government of
India in April, 1989 to cater to the R&D needs of the Indian Aluminium Industries. The Sub-
Committee was apprised that JNARDDC isa "Centre of Excellence" with well established
facilities for the study of bauxite, alumina and aluminium. At the initial stage partial financial
and technological assistance was provided under United Nations Development Programme (
UNDP) of UNIDO. The Centre became fully functional since the beginning of 1996.
JNARDDC also offers analytical and testing facilities to other non-ferrous industries, to steel
plants and small-scale industries, mainly in the areas of mining, chemical and mineralogical
analysis, energy auditing failure analysis, micro structural studies and information services.

2.0 OBJECTIVES OF JNARDDC

2.1 The management of JNARDDC apprised the Sub-Committee of the objectives of
Centre which are as under:-

(i) To assimilate and adapt the technologies available in India for the production
of alumina and aluminium and to develop indigenous know-how and basic
engineering packages for future alumina and aluminium plants to be set up in
the country.

(ii) To undertake research programmes especially in the area of reduction in material
and energy consumption and to provide analytical services to the industries.

(iii) 10 set up and operate a data bank in the areas of bauxite, alumina and
aluminium production for the benefit of the industries.

(iv) 10 provide training to the personnel employed in the Indian aluminium industry
through organization of workshops, seminars and group training programmes.


2.2 The Sub-Committee was also apprised of the Mission Statement of JNARDDC which
stipulates "To provide modern technological inputs to primary and secondary aluminium
industries based on optimum utilisation of existing facilities | and further development of
technical capabilities". In order to achieve the mission statement JNARDDC has _ its
inherent capabilities which inter-alia include Geology and evaluation of bauxite deposits;
Computer based exploration and mine planning; Beneficiation and upgradation of laterites and
bauxites ; Total characterization of bauxites including trace elements and organic carbon ;
Techno-economic evaluation of bauxite’ deposit for bauxite production and non-metallurgical
application; Technological testing of bauxite including large scale laboratory tests for de-
silication, digestion, precipitation and settling, Pre-feasibility and basic engineering package
for bauxite mining and alumina plant; Energy audit of alumina plan, foundry, steam plant,
chemical plant etc., Mass and heat balances of Bayer’s process; Process monitoring of
aluminium _ electrolytic cell; Mathematical modeling of processes including simulation of
aluminium smelter process; and Defect characterisation and analysis in All alloy products.

2.3. The Committee , while appreciating the objectives for setting up the Research
Centre for Aluminium Industries has noticed during its visit that the Centre is well
equipped with modern analytical facilities and process development monitoring and control
facilities in order to carry out research work in the areas of bauxite, alumina and
aluminium smelting. The Committee recommends that the Centre should strive its
best to achieve its cherished goal and make all efforts towards removing the problems
being faced by the Indian aluminium industry .

4.0 ON-GOING PROJECTS OF JNARDDC

4.1 The Sub-Committee was informed that the Centre is presently working on the
technology oriented projects which inter-alia includes , De-ironing of East Coast bauxite; Low
pressure Digestion technology; removal and Control of Organics in Bayer process; recycling of
Aluminium scrap ; utilisation of aluminium industry wastes; and development of Can-stock
materials. The major ongoing projects are as under:-

1. De-ironing Eastern Ghat bauxite

2. Improvement of Digestion Efficiency of East Coast Bauxite and Enhancement of
Alumina Productivity

process :

4.2. The Committee notes the projects undertaken by JNARDDC and. hopes that the
efforts made by the Centre would be utilised as the store house of all aluminium related
“experiments and observations " and the knowledge and experience skimmed of the
efforts would be helpful in removing the problems of aluminium industry. The
Committee also hope that each project under study by JNARDDC must involve the
highest degree of intellectual honesty as far as the relevance and the purpose of the
projects are concerned.

5.0 THRUST AREAS FOR R&D

5.1 Pertaining to the Sub-Committee's query regarding thrust areas identified by
JNARDDC for R&D work of Centre projected for the next five years the JNARDDC
management informed the Sub-Committee that in order to expand the present activities of
JNARDDC - steps have been taken regarding process monitoring and modeling , process
development and product development . Process monitoring and modeling include
mathematical modeling of electrolytic cell; simulation of Bayer process for alumina production;
process monitoring and technological auditing of alumina plants; simulation and optimisation of
alumina precipitation circuit ; technology audit of raw materials for the manufacture of anodes;
development of a technique to determine metal pad velocity in aluminium electrolysis ;
prediction of anode effect for aluminium smelter. The process of development covers,
evaluation of bauxite deposits from modern technological point of view for alumina as well as
non-metallurgical industries; bauxite benefication studies; double digestion study for Central
Indian Bauxites; extraction of alumina from flyash; microbial beneficiation of bauxite and red
mud; recycling of anode butts; and technological studies of Maharashtra and Gujarat bauxites.
Apprising the Sub-Committee of product development JNARDDC management stated that
efforts are being envisaged for development of low soda and high purity hydrate ; development
of new alloys and metal matrix composites; development of value-added special alumina
products; developing value added bauxite products such as various calcined, sintered bauxite
materials and alumina based chemicals for specific uses; utilisation of aluminium industry wastes.

5.2 The Committee understands the significance of adopting the practice of process
monitoring and modeling to carry out the research work in a result oriented manner .
The Committee, while noting the steps taken by JNARDDC regarding the
process development and product development, recommends that JNARDDC
should carry on such research work which may help aluminium industry in
developing new designs of products with the help of product mix. The research
work should — lead to evolution of process development for cost reduction.
JNARDDC should make a survey of the market demand and engage itself in
such research work which might lead to development of products in accordance
with market demands. The new initiatives being envisaged may be taken up at
the earliest.

5.3 The management of JNARDDC pointing out the undergoing rapid transformation of
industrial scenario unleashed by the process of globalisation and implementation of
liberalisation and disinvestment policy of the Government , stated that Aluminium Industry
has to gear up itself to function in an effective manner. The Sub-Committee was informed that
JNARDDC is playing its part to assist the Indian Aluminium Industry to meet the challenges.
The management of JNARDDC stated that the globally emerging trends that need to
implemented in the Indian Aluminium Industry include high and supér-high amperage potlines


for aluminium smelting ; use of inert anodes and non-wet table cathodes in the smelter pots; near
net shape processing; squeeze casting; modern precipitation techniques ; tube digestion
technology; use of pressure decanter technology ; hyper baric filtration for red mud disposal ;
and development of special grade alumina products.

5.4 The Committee desires that JNARDDC should involve itself in such research
work which would provide better quality, speed design engineering and cost effective
production for the ultimate survival and growth of indigenous Aluminium industry in
the changing scenario caused by globalisation and liberalisation. The globally emerging
trends that need to be implemented in aluminium industry may be addressed on a
emergency basis in collaboration with aluminium industry .

6.0 DIVERSIFICATION PROGRAMMES OF JNARDDC

6.1 Replying to the Sub-Committee’s query regarding the diversification programme of
JNARDDC the management stated that in keeping with the changing time and needs , the
Centre is diversifying its activities through downstream processing , waste recycling ,
emphasizing on the emerging field of mathematical modeling and process control; and
exploring new area for development of technology suitable for setting up small and medium
capacity alumina and aluminium plants.

6.2 Regarding the diversification programmes of JNARDDC , the Department of Mines
informed the Sub-Committee that the experimental _ facilities at the Centre have been entirely
oriented towards aluminium process metallurgy. Further, many of the existing facilities in
principle may also be used for R&D work related to other non-ferrous metals, particularly
titanium and magnesium. Scope, therefore, exists for diversification into related industries but
this is to be cleared by the Governing Body of the Centre.

6.3. Pertaining to JNARDDC's role in the setting up of small and medium capacity alumina
and aluminium plants, the Department of Mines stated that the widely held perception is that
only large and very large scale aluminium plants (1-3 million tpa) are viable. However, the cost
of setting up such plants being exorbitantly high, the possibility of such plant coming up in
India in the near future is negligible. However, many small and medium level investors may be
interested in setting up of plants with annual capacity of 20,000-100,000 tonnes. This may be
compared to the situation in China, where more than 80% of the plants are of such small and
medium capacities.

64 The Committee feels that JNARDDC should chalk out its diversification
programme in such away asto benefit the aluminium industry in the short as well as
long term. Since technology for setting up of such plants is not available in India,
SJNARDDC can play a vital role in developing such technologies. The Committee
recommends that research may be undertaken to develop and adapt new technology
which may help setting up of small and medium capacity alumina and aluminium plants.

7.0 . SEMINAR CONFERENCE

7.1. The Sub-Committee was informed that JNARDDC conducts seminars , conference.
It conducted International Interactive Meet on Bauxite and Alumina during December, 2001
with about 15 overseas participants from all over the world and over 100 National delegates.
Similarly during April, 1999 National Seminar on Aluminium Electrolysis was organized in
commemoration of the centre's anniversary celebrations.


72 Department of Mines informed the Sub-Committee that JNARDDC conducts
periodically seminars, conferences and technical programmes of international standards and
generates revenues by charging registration fee for the industrial delegates. For instance, in
December, 2000, JNARDDC had organised an International Meet on Bauxite-Alumina
Technology, which generated funds to the tune of Rs.11 lakhs.

73 The Committee appreciates the efforts made by JNARDDC in conducting
seminars and conferences and recommends that JNARDDC should conduct such
conferences and seminars more frequently . The Committee also recommends that
JNARDDC should make some nominal entry fee from all the participant in order to
raise funds to meet its financial requirements.

8.0 | TRAINING PROGRAMMES AND WORKSHOP.

8.1 JNARDDC management stated that the Centre periodically conducts training
programme and workshops in the field of alumina production , smelter technology,
characterisation of materials etc. In this regard the Centre conducted bauxmet -98.
international conference on aluminium; national workshop on X-ray analysis; workshop on anode
and cathode carbon; aluminium cast house technology- in plant training programme at NALCO,
BALCO ; computer based mathematical modeling of aluminium production process; production
and applications of special alumina chemicals; and alumina technology.

8.2 Conducting of training programmes and workshops provides a platform to
scientists for productive interaction and encourage them to gather knowledge and share
experience. JNARDDC should charge nominal fee from the participants for the training
programme to generate revenue to meet JNARDDC's non-plan financial requirements.
The Committee also recommends that JNARDDC should give wide publicity to its training
programmes.

9.0 | CONSULTANCY AND TESTING SERVICES

91 The Sub-Committee was informed that the consultancy and testing services cell (CTSC)
of JNARDDC was established in August, 1999, in order to streamline and provide efficient
tésting services to the industry. The consultancy and testing: services offered include mine
planning; beneficiation, upgradation, characterisation and technological testing of bauxite;
process monitoring of aluminium electrolysis cell; characterisation of carbonaceous raw
materiajs; energy auditing and process modeling using ASPEN plus software; failure analysis;
chemical, physical and physico chemical analysis. CTSC's services are regularly used by
primary aluminium producers like NALCO, BALCO, HINDALCO, INDAL and MALCO;
public sectors like HAL, SAIL, ordnance factory etc; carbon manufacturers like rain calcining
Itd., Bharat calciners, Goa carbon; R&D institutions like NEERI; private industries like L&T ,
Hindustan Lever Ltd., GIMPEX, CUMI, ESSORCTS, Ashapura, Trimex and many others.

9.2 The details of the resources raised by consultancy, projects and testing during the
Syears are given below:-

(Rs in lakhs)

टला [AT at ee



9.3 The Committee, while taking note of consultancy and testing services offered by
JNARDDC , is of the opinion that JNARDDC should generate sufficient fund to meet its
requirement of non-plan expenditure by opening avenues for generating revenue by
providing consultancy services. JNARDDC may stress on service mix and service
endowment by giving due importance to diversification in consultancy services and
exploring new ideas for generation of new project. The centre should try to provide
consultancy services out side the country as well.

10.0 SERVICE TO DOWNSTREAM SECTOR

10.1. |The Sub-Committee was apprised that the Ministry of Mines has been stressing upon the
need of secondary and downstream aluminium industry to improve the performance indices and
quality of products of the downstream sector. The downstream sector can be serviced by the
JNARDDC after the establishment of a Downstream Processing Laboratory (DSP). A project for
this purpose has been approved by the Ministry of Mines and a partial grant of 1.88 crores has
been granted. The DSP is scheduled to be set up by Dec. 2003. The manpower presently with the
Centre would also have to be adequately trained and sufficient time to be given for development
of expertise in this sector before it could cater to this new segment. The Core areas identified and
visualised for downstream sector may inter-alia include improvement of Aluminium Extrusion
process and alloy development; aluminium recycling (improvement of quality and yield;
innovation of casting technologies for automotive and general engineering application;
aluminium product development and application engineering; providing assistance to defence
agencies such as ordnance factory, Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, DMRL etc. in development,
production and processing of defence related aluminium alloys.

10.2. The Department of Mines informed the Sub-Committee that downstream processing
laboratory is still in the process of establishment. Department of Mines, Government of India
has recently sanctioned Rs.188 lakhs for the establishment of facilities/equipment for this
laboratory. Some of the facilities are being procured and will be operational shortly. in the
meanwhile, utilizing the existing facilities the centre has offered following services:

(i) Conducted studies related to pinhole porosities problem faced in the production
of AI-Si alloy fan blades. Suitable remedial measures were suggested.

(ii) Peripheral Grain Growth in the extruded products of 2014 alloy at OFAJ was
studied and recommendations to avoid the problem were given.

(iii) Texture related studies for 3004 alloy for the development of beverage cans
were conducted for BALCO.

(iv) Gujarat Aluminium Extrusions was helped in eliminating Die Lines in the
production of 6063 alloy profiles.

10.3. The Committee is of the opinion that JNARDDC with its experience can provide
quality service to the down stream sector. Efforts for establishing the downstream
processing laboratory (DSP) may be accelerated and the staff be imparted necessary
training and expertise.


11.0 POLLUTION CONTROL AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENT

11.1 The Sub-Committee was informed that the most challenging task for aluminium
industries is to reduce the environmental damage caused by the production process because of
emissions of CFs (8) and CO2(g) contributing to global warming. The Centre can collect World-
wide information on various aspects of pollution/waste management and control related to
aluminium industries and prepare realistic specifications for pollution control that may be
presented to the statutory bodies of local and Central Governments. The Centre can explore areas
like fluorine contamination (major pollutant in aluminium industry) in air, water and land
development of analytical method and procedure for estimation of fluorine, PAH etc.;
development of disposal and treatment standards for various waste generated in the aluminium
industry; development of various indigenous utilisation processes for waste from aluminium
industry; environmental auditing for various aluminium industries; environmental impact

11.2 The Sub-Committee gathered that to meet the above mentioned targets the Centre
should be provided with statutory powers in the field of environment and waste treatment and
Jawaharlal Nehru Aluniinium Research Development & Design Centre should be entrusted with
task of monitoring pollution and waste disposal methods employed by Indian aluminium
Industries on behalf of Central Government in order to safe guard national interest. Besides a
laboratory for environment and waste treatment may be set up with initial investment from
Government of India with sufficient funds. Initial training program may be provided to the
Scientist and sufficient time period may be given to develop any kind of expertise in the field.

11.3. However. the Department of Mines stated that IJNARDDC is engaged in developing
useful products from aluminium industry waste samples (glass and glass ceramics). It has also
worked on a project to develop guidelines for disposing of red mud. JNARDDC scientists are
members of the National task Force for Environmental Issues of Aluminium Industry constituted
by CPCB. JNARDDC is thus eminently placed to undertake study of various forms of
pollution in aluminium industry. This has helped further the availability of expertise at the
National Environment Engineering Research Institute ( NEERI), Nagpur.

11.4. The Committee observes that the problems of pollution is one of the threat
being faced by human society. JNARDDC can make significant contribution for
environmental impact assessment. Central Goveramenot may consider to entrust with
JNARDDC to undertake study on various forms of pollution and develop mechanism for
pollution/waste management and control. The Centre should be regularly in touch with
other related Ministries.

12.0 FORMATION OF CORE GROUP OF INDIAN ALUMINIUM INDUSTRY

12.1. The Sub-Committee was apprised of the fact that facilities and funds are required to
generate data through numerous laboratory experiments and monitoring at the plant for the
development and validation of models for the operations involved in alumina and aluminium
production. Services from the experienced Centres like IIT Kanpur, 1[Sc-Bangalore, EIL etc. are
also essential. Formation of core group of Indian aluminium industry, Centre and academic
institutions at the working level is need of the hour for development of industrially useful
mathematical models. Two project proposals were submitted to Department of science and
technology but they were turned down, further efforts with help of Government are to be taken to
get the funds from the aluminium industries. Once the complete models are developed and
validated, they are going to be useful for Centre in generating enormous funds through
improvements in the plant by optimisation of the plant parameters. The said core group may
cover modeling of aluminium electrolytic development of software packages for unit


operation/process like precipitation, digestion, red mud washing etc; software packages for
energy/mass balance of alumina plant; development of mathematical simulation package for
bayer process using ASPEN simulation package.

12.2. .The Committee is of the view that regular interaction of Scientists of the centre
with the experienced professional from IIT, EIL, TISL ete. to enhance the knowledge

13.0 ANNUAL BUDGETARY REQUIREMENT OF JNARDDC

13.1 The Sub-Committee was given an understand that the sustenance of JNARDDC
is becoming difficult due to lack of fund flow to meet the plan and Non-plan
expenditure. JNARDDC was setup by the Ministry of Mines with the assistance
from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) with the total establishment
cost of Rs.36 crores. The Development of India provided Rs. 19 crores while UNDP
provided Rs.17 crores. During the project establishment (1989-96) the annual
budgetary requirements of the Centre were met from "Aluminium Development Fund"
through Government of India (Ministry of Mines) . The UNDP input was mainly for
equipment and training programmes. Salaries and recurring expenditures were to be met
by Government of India input.

13.2. The Sub-Committee was apprised of the possible means for raising the fund to
meet the centre's plan and Non-plan expenditure which might be explained as below:-

(i) There already exists an "Aluminium Development Fund" under the Ministry of
Mines. There is adequate balance in this fund and even the annual interest earnings on
the balances in this fund is adequate to take care of the recurring expenditure of this
Centre which is only 2 crores per annum. In the past when the founder Director was
offered to take care of this fund, he refused to take care of it due to lack of adequate
experienced manpower at the construction stage. Now with sufficient and experienced
manpower available with the Centre the possibility of transferring this fund to the
Centre may be explored which will help the Centre to concentrate on its primary
objective of R&D work instead of struggling for financial sustainability for most of the
time.

(ii) The Centre can provide its services by being funded from Indian Aluminium
companies collectively such as a certain percentage of net profit or on a basis like 0.1
% of selling cost per tonne of the aluminium produced. Training for the fresh recruits
for the industries can also be done by the Centre along with meeting the R&D needs of
the Indian aluminium industry.

13.3 The Department of Mines clarified that the present annual financial requirement of
JNARDDC is about Rs.180 lakhs which is expected to increase @ 5% annually. It is met from
Grants-in-aid from the Department of Mines to the tune of 80% of the salary expenditure;
Internal resource generation through project work, consultancy, testing, organization of
seminars, etc.; support from AMDF to meet the shortfall. The budgetary support given by the
Government to JNARDDC is in the nature of grants-in-aid to meet 80% of the salary budget
only. The salary budget amounts to approximately 50% of the total budget. Internal resource


generation being inadequate, shortfall is being met by support from the Aluminium

13.4 The Committee is constrained to express its concerns over the languishing and
pathetic condition of Centre like JNARDDC due to lack of sufficient fund flow from the
Government where all research work pertaining to aluminium industry might be
carried on successfully . The situation emerging out of the development is really pathetic
and requires immediate attention. JNARDDC has an excellent layout with required
equipment and technology for research workin aluminium industry, therefore, the
Sub-Committee is of the view that such an extra-ordinary Research centre should not
languish because of financial crunch. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of
Mines should take stock of actual financial requirement of JNARDDC to meet its plan
and non-plan expenditure . The Committee further recommends that since JNARDDC is
a research centre and does not generate substantial revenue of its own except from
consultancy and services, JNARDDC should be allowed budgetary support to meet at
least its non-plan expenditure so that the scientist should remainin peace while doing
research work and have not to bother for their future survival. The Committee further
recommends that the Ministry of Mines should explore the possibility to
generate/appropriate funds out of Aluminium Development Fund and also from Indian
Aluminium companies to meet the plan-expenditure of JNARDDC. At the same time,
JNARDDC management and the Ministry of Mines should propagate the utility of
SJNARDDC for aluminium industries. The aluminium industries can refer to the Centre for
all of their R& D problems as their invgjvement would definitely help in the development of
technology packages for future expansion programmes. If the Central agency like
Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research Development & Design Centre is involved in
importing technology for green field as well as brown field expansions there is a possibility
of saving a lot of foreign exchange by avoiding duplicate transfer of technology.

REPORT
INDIAN BUREAU OF MINES

The Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) established in 1948, is a multi-disciplinary
government organization under the Department of Mines, Ministry of Coal and Mines, engaged
in promotion of conservation and scientific development of mineral resources other than coal,
petroleum & natural gas, atomic minerals and minor minerals. During the first two years of its
existence, the IBM functioned mostly as an Advisory Body and helped the government in
framing the mineral legislation viz. the Mines and Minerals (Regulation & Development) Act
1948; Mineral Concession Rules 1949 and Petroleum Concession Rules 1949. Later Mineral
Conservation & Development Rules 1955 (MCDR) and Mining Leases (Modifications of terms)
Rules 1956 were framed. With the enactment of the MM (R&D) Act 1948; the IBM was
entrusted with a set of additional functions in August 1950. Accordingly, inspection of mines
and mineral prospects became a regular activity. By 1953, the IBM was entrusted with an
additional function of undertaking detailed exploration of Mineral deposits. Al! the mineral
deposits which were to supply raw materials to the Public Sector Steel Plants established in the
Second and Third Five Year Plan Periods, were proved by the IBM. Accordingly, IBM under-
took exploration for coal, iron ore, limestone, base metals, magnesite, pyrite, tungsten etc. With
the formation of National Coal Development Corporation, the prospecting of coal was transferred
to it from IBM.

2.0 CHARTER OF FUNCTIONS OF IBM

2.1. The Sub-Committee was apprised by IBM management that with the expansion of
mining industry and gradual adoption of updated technology in large mines, the functions of IBM
were reviewed and revised in 1966 and more recently in 1981.

1. The current Charter of functions of the IBM is as follows:-

(a) Enforcing conservation and systematic development of mineral resources
through inspection of mines, beneficiation plants, and mineral-based
industries;

(b) Conducting geological, mining, beneficiation and other related techno-
economic field studies and applied research on mining-geological problems.

2. Approval of mining plans in respect of mining leases granted/ renewed as well as
for existing mining leased on behalf of the Central Government.

3. Conducting studies on environmental protection and pollution control in regard
to the mining and mineral beneficiation operations.

4. Preparation of mineral maps and the inventory of mineral resources of India.

5. Providing technical consultancy services on suitable terms within the country and

abroad in connection with:

(i) Appraisal and exploitation of deposits ‘including ore dressing
investigations and analysis of ores and minerals and preparation of
feasibility reparts and detailed project reports of mines/ore dressing
projects.

(ii) Improving efficiencies and reducing operation costs.
(iii) Market surveys.

(iv) Financial analysis of capital requirements, and charter.


(v) Matters related to any of the functions enunciated in the charter.

6. Conducting under the departmental programme testing and analysis of ores and
minerals, mineral beneficiation and related technological studies on samples
obtained from land and sea; research on fundamental aspects of mineral
beneficiation. 33

7. Collection, processing and storage of data on mines, minerals and mineral-based
industries, collection and maintenance of world mineral intelligence, foreign
mineral legislation and other related matters.

8. Publication of bulletins, monographs, information circulars and reports of
investigation relating to mining, mineral beneficiation and mineral-based
industries.

9. Publication of statistics relating to mineral production in India, mineral stocks,
exports, local consumption, etc. rendering assistance to the mineral trade in the
marketing of minerals.

10. Advising on matters in regard to the mineral industry particularly on planning for
exploitation and utilization of the country's mineral resources and those of the
sea, infrastructure requirements, environmental protection and pollution control,
export and import policies, trade, mineral legislation, wages, taxes, royalty and
related matters.

11. Training of scientific, technical and other cadres of the department and persons
front the mineral industry and other agencies in India and abroad.

12. Promoting awareness regarding the conservation and systematic development of
mineral deposits through museums, exhibitions 5.10 other audio-visual media

13. Undertaking such other activities as may become necessary in the light of the
developments in the field of mining, mineral beneficiation an related technology.

2.2 The Committee takes note of functions envisaged in the charter of functions of IBM
and hopes that IBM would be able to accomplish its task as enshrined in the charter of functions.
The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should take steps towards further
empowering IBM so that IBM would be able to discharge its functions and responsibility in
efficient and effective manner. IBM from time to time should monitor mining plan of all the

* Mines.

23 The Committee further recommends that" since IBM has been entrustea with the
function of approving mining plans in respect of mining leases granted on behalf of the Central
Government as well as conducting studies of environmental protection and pollution Control, it
is pertinent on the part of IBM management that while approving the mining, plans the issue of
environmental protection should be given due importance. The Committee is also of the
opinion that the time-gap between the environmental clearance and app oval of mining lease
should not be too large as to hamper the: growth rate of mining industry.

44 Replying to the Sub-Committee's query as to what extent IBM has been successful in
its aims of preparing and updating of mineral maps of major minerals, the management stated
that the geographical area of the Union of India is about 328 million hects. Of these almost
2/3" are under agricultural cultivable pastures and grazing land. The total area under forest is of
the order of 68.80 m. hects. constituting about 21% of the total geographical area. The mining
lease area constitutes 6,73,425 hects. i.e. 0.200% of the total geographical area. As on date there
are 8870 mining leases in the country with the mining lease area of 6,73.425 hects. The mining
activity is restricted to 21 States in the country for 63 different minerals. The IBM initiated the
preparation of mineral leasehold maps from 1977 and has prepared the mineral leasehold maps on
1 :50,000 scale for 17 important minerals namely. chromite, iron ore, manganese, copper, lead,
zinc, bauxite. rock phosphate, kyanite, sillimanite. wolframite. magnesite. fluorite, soapstone.
graphite, barytes and limestone. The total leasehold covered in these mineral lease hold maps is
of the order of 1950 and the total lease area covered in these maps is of the order of about 3 lakh.
hects. constituting 44.55% of the total leasehold area of the country. In the process of preparation
of mineral leasehold maps, a total of 294 index maps has been prepared thereby covering about
500 Survey of India top sheets on 1 :50,000 scale. Looking to the environmental and ecological
problems due to mining and other activities and thereby causing degradation of land. the IBM


promptly decided to prepare the forest cover maps in the form of transparencies for these index
maps from 1986. These forest overlay maps are prepared based on the Survey of India toposheets.
the forest atlas of India. So far 162 forest overlays have been prepared for the above minerals and
387 Survey of India toposheets has been covered. Very recently, the IBM in collaboration with
Forest Survey of India and Ministry of Environment and Forest has procured 27 forest overlays
maps for some of the districts and minerals. of MP, Chattisgarh. Bihar states. These forest
overlays are based on the latest satellite imageries and the details are given and plotted after
computer analysis and are all ia digitised forms. These maps show the mining leases and also
some of the freehold deposits located in these toposheets.

45 The mineral maps with forest overlays will be used to process the Mining Lease cases by
the respective State Governments and State and Central Forest Departments. The use of these
maps may help to cut down delays in obtaining forest clearance for ML and PL.

4.6. | The Committee is happy to note that IBM has taken up the to provide the specialised
and customized data, preparation of Minerals maps and forest overlays. The Committee hopes
that the IBM__ in tandem with Forest Surveys of India and Ministry of Environment and Forests
would continue to take up latest forest overlays maps. Forest overlays maps used by State
Governments and Central Forest Department would help to cut-down delays in obtaining forest
clearance for ML&PL.

5.0 DIVISION WISE FUNCTIONS
5.1 IBM has following divisions to discharge its functions :~

5.1.0. Mines Control and Conservation of Minerals Division (MCCM Division):-

5.1.1. The Division office is located at Nagpur and headed by the Chief Controller of Mines. It
has three zonal offices; 12 Regional and 2 Sub-Regional offices spread all over the country. The
Division is the primary wing of the IBM and responsible for enforcement of systematic
development of mineral deposits and conservation of mineral resources of the country through
inspection of mines, conservation studies, special studies and approval of mining plans, through
its Zonal, Regional and Sub-Regional Offices. This Division through its Regional Offices gives
approval for registration to recognized qualified persons for preparing mining plans an mining
schemes. It also monitors prospecting activities in prospecting licence and lease areas, prepares
and up-dates Mineral Maps and takes up model field studies as an adjunct to the National Mineral
Inventory.

5.1.2 The Committee feels that MCCM division of IBM would be able to function effectively
once IBM is made as a regulatory body because MCCM is entrusted with enforcement of
systematic development of mineral deposits and conservation studies.

5.1.3. The Committee further recommends that MCCM should keep on up-dating mineral maps
and cover all minerals through the country.

5.2.0 ORE DRESSING DIVISION (0.D DIVISION)

5.2.1 The ore dressing Division is an applied research and development set-up. It provides
research, consultancy and training support in mineral processing to the mineral industry in India
& abroad. From a small beginning in Delhi, to a Laboratory & Pilot Plant set-up in Nagpur in
early ‘60s, and later with opening of two Regional centres in Ajmer and Bangalore in early '80s,


the Division has now become a centre of excellence in mineral processing with the world-class
Mineral Processing Laboratory and Pilot Plant established in Nagpur with UNDP assistance for
equipment, fellowship training and expertise services. The R&D infrastructures of OD Division
consists of the Modern Mineral Processing Laboratory and Pilot Plant located at Nagpur for Ore
dressing Laboratory for bench scale studies with comprehensive and versatile 2 tonnes/hour
capacity pilot plant ; Analytical Laboratory situated at Nagpur and has Chemical Analysis
Laboratory , Mineralogical Laboratory, Physical Characterization Laboratory, Environmental
Sample Analysis Laboratory ; Regional Ore Dressing Laboratory and Pilot Plant at Ajmer and
Bangalore with Ore dressing Laboratory & Pilot Plant, Chemical Analysis Laboratory,
Mineralogical Laboratory; Mineral Processing for development of process know-how by testing
on batch laboratory and continuous pilot plant scale on low grade, ferrous, non-ferrous and
precocious metal ores as well as industrial minerals, establishment of process flow sheet and
design parameters for commercial concentrators, trouble shooting jobs and implant studies of
mineral processing plants , technological auditing with a view to improve plant performance,
preparation of techno-economic feasibility reports for beneficiation of low-grade ores; Chemical
Analysis with the facilities of rapid and precise elemental analysis including precious elements,
wet and instrumental analysis of ores, minerals and ore dressing products, analysis of
environmental samples such as air, water and solids from mines, processing and metallurgical
plants; Mineralogy for mineralogical studies on ores, rocks, sinters, slag, etc., quantification of
minerals for size, shape, interlocking, etc.; Mineral Characterization of Particle size analysis,
surface area measurements, brightness and Zeta potential, viscosity, density

5.2.2. The Ore Dressing Division of the Bureau has three well equipped laboratories and pilot
plants at Ajmer, Bangalore and Nagpur to carry out mineral beneficiation and agglomeration
studies on a variety of ores/minerals. These centres also have facilities for mineralogical and
chemical and environmental analysis. Considering the expertise already developed the
Government of India decided to establish the Modern Mineral Processing Laboratory and Pilot
Plant, as a centre of excellence in Nagpur. The pilot plant was formally commissioned on
28.8.1994. Construction of Analytical Laboratory at Nagpur has been completed and is now
functional.

5.2.3. The Ore Dressing Division of Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM) has well equipped
laboratories and pilot plants at Nagpur, Ajmer & Bangalore with its headquarters at Nagpur.
These laboratories are equipped with latest technology and equipment for-achieving its set target.
The Modem Mineral Processing Laboratory and Pilot Plant at Nagpur is well equipped with most
sophisticated equipment and scientific expertise and is regarded as "Centre of Excellence" in the
field of Mineral Beneficiation. This has been established, at the cost of Rs. 18.2 crores with
partial assistance (2.41 million US$) from UNDP. This is a core center to cater to the needs of the
mining/mineral industry for beneficiation test work. The pilot plant has flexible capacity ranging
from 0.5 to 2.0 tonnes/hour for confirmation of the process evolved in the laboratory as well as to
generate additional process and design data before commercial application and also if need be to
produce adequate quantity of concentrate for end use testing. This R&D centre is also expected to
meet the requirement of other countries in Asia, Pacific Region, Middle East, and African
countries directly or through national/multinational companies/consultancy firms etc.

5.2.4, The Committee recommends that IBM management and the Department of Mines should
ensure that R&D wings of IBM may be well equipped for mineral beneficiation. The Sub-
Committee further recommends that Ore Dressing division of IBM should undertake such
research work pertaining to beneficiation of low -Ore content mineral in cost effective manner
for viable and commercial production of metals.


5.3.0. MINERAL ECONOMICS DIVISION (MLE. DIVISION)

5.3.1 This Division is located at Nagpur. The Division complies National Mineral Inventory,
conducts market surveys on mineral commodities, demand projections, information circulars,
renders assistance in framing mineral legislation including modifications and brings out a
prestigious Indian Minerals Year Book.

5.3.2. The Committee feels that M.E. division of IBM should undertake adequate market
survey and research for procuring demand for cost/projection so that IBM would function in
right direction.

5.3.3. The Committee further recommends that M.E division should undertake study of
comparative mining loss and suggest reforms in Indian Mining legal framework, including
modifications in the provision of MM (D&R) Act, 1957, MCR, 1960, MCDR, 1958 and
Coastal Regulation Zone ( CRZ) Notifications, if required.

5.4.0. TECHNICAL CONSULTANCY DIVISION (T. ८. Division)

5.4.1. This Division is located at Nagpur and undertakes consultancy work in the fields of
geology, mining and environment. Technical Division provides following services;

A. GEOLOGICAL SERVICES:-

(i) Survey of mineral properties and preparation of mine plans & sections.
(ii) Preparation of geological plans and preliminary geological appraisal of
mineral properties, formulation of scheme of detailed exploration with
: estimate of cost.
(iii) Supervising exploratory drilling done by contract agencies.

(iv) Logging and sampling of bore holes, evaluation of exploratory date
including Geostatical evaluation and preparation of detailed reports on
exploration.

(v) Collection and preparation of samples for laboratory/ pilot plant tests.

(vi) Geostatistical computer evaluation of mineral deposits.

B. MINING SERVICES

6) Preparation of feasibility reports.

(ii) Preoperational of mine development scheme.

(iii) Preparation of environment management plan.

(iv) _ Evaluation of feasibility reports on behalf of financial institutions

(v) Financial analysis of mining projects

(vi) Determination of productivity & fuel consumption norms for mining
ventures

(vii) production., Planning and grade control on given process parameters
(viii) Re-modeling of old mines for introduction of advance mining technology

(ix) Supervision and management of assorted mining services


5.4.2. The Sub-Committee was informed that the Technical Consultancy Division is equipped
with the latest technology and equipments for the set targets excepting the field equipments.

5.4.3. The Committee notes that the functions and responsibilities entrusted to T.C. Division
of IBM and hopes that T.C. division of IBM would leave no stone untumed in accomplishing
its task. The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines in tandem with IBM
management would estimate the requirement of field equipments Technical Consultancy
division and accordingly, manage funds for purchase of those equipment in the financial year (
2002-2003), itself.

5.5.0. DIVERSIFICATION OF CONSULTANCY SERVICES.

5.5.1. Pertaining to the issue of overall scope of diversification of consultancy services
imparted by IBM, it was informed that IBM offers technical services to mining industries in
surveying, exploration, geology, mining feasibility studies, mineral processing and
environmental related issues on payment of charges approved by the Government from time to
time. The management stated that certain areas where diversification opportunities are there
include areas like Geo-technical Investigation for non-mining projects like National Highways,
Hydro-electric Power, State Highways etc., Design of Excavation including Geo-technical
aspects in Tunnels for Hydro-electric Power projects and other non-mining projects; Hydro-
geological Surveys inclusive of Ground Water Modeling; Remote Sensing; ISO Certification
including Environmental Auditing; Assignments outside India particularly in the under
developed countries, Techno-economic scrutiny of Foreign investment proposals in the
Mining sector of India; and Design of Blast Parameters for optimisation of blast operation. The
management further stated that in the field of minerals benefication, diversification may be
initiated through creation of a new Business Promotion Cell to obtain jobs on charge basis;
extending activities to other neighbouring countries in South East Asia and Africa;
Enforcement of regulatory functions under Rule 20 of MCDR, 1988 for the development of
mines; organising R&D meets with the representatives of the industry; Publicity of the facilities
and capabilities; Credibility and improvement in the standard of work; and Dissemination of
information on the work carried out. The management stated that in order to diversify the
activities of consultancy services, the additional resources in terms of manpower, equipment
and training are required.

5.5.2. The Committee, appreciating the wide scope for diversification, desires that IBM
management may explore diversification of consultancy services which might be imparted by
IBM in the areas like Geo-technical investigation for non-mining projects and techno-
economic scrutiny of Foreign Investment proposals in the Mining sector in India. The
Committee also recommends that the requirement of IBM in respect of manpower , equipment
and training to enable it to diversify consultancy services may be fulfilled.

5.5.3 The Committee further recommends that IBM should create the business promotion cell
for procuring work order from developing countries particularly South-East-Asia and Africa.
IBM should charge for providing consultancy services ‘and thus generate revenue.

5.6.0. PLANNING AND CO-ORDINATION DIVISION

5.6.1. This Division is responsible for common services, i.e. Administration, Technical Co-
ordination, Training, Press and Hindi Anubhag. The Training Centre which is under the charge


of a Director (Training) imparts training both to in-house and industry as well as overseas
participants.

5.6.2. The Committee is of the view that IBM should impart training to Geology students of
various Indian university on nominal fee basis which would serve the purpose of injecting geo-
logical insight into students of Geology as well as generation of revenue for IBM. In this
regard, the Committee recommends that training unit of IBM should be strengthened. If
necessary, the Department of Mines should approach University Grants Commission for
incorporation of compulsory geology training for students of geological to be imparted by
IBM.

5.7.0. MINING RESEARCH CELLS

5.7.1. Mining Research Cell of IBM of Mines was established in 1972 with a view to conduct
applied mining research to serve the growing needs of mining industry, with its rich experience in
conducting various types of research investigations in environmental, geo-technical projects. The
mining research cell has developed a strong technological base comprising pool of highly trained
man power to conduct investigations on various mineral based industries.

5.7.2. Keeping in view the growing technological needs of mining industry, the Mining

(ii) Performance studies in mechanised mines; copper, iron ore an d limestone

provided consultancy services on Environmental and Geo-technical problems in open case and
underground mines. The important projects handled so for include;

the efficiency of dust contro! measures: Iron ore and diamond.

(ii) Generation of environmental baseline data for preparation of environmental
management plans: Base metals, iron and limestone.

The Committee understands that IBM draws its strengths from its charter of functions

coupled with statutory provisions. However, in order to inject new vision and trained hands in
the system it is essential that IBM should go for pruning of surplus manpower from non-core
sector and recruit scientists/staff as per requirement. By adopting the policy of rationalisation
of manpower in non-core sector and recruitment of scientists in desirable field would keep the
non-plan expenditure under control with the added advantage of having manpower as per
requirement.

COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE

CHARTER OF FUNCTIONS OF IBM ,

The Committee takes note of functions envisaged in the charter of functions of IBM
and hopes that IBM would be able to accomplish its task as enshrined in the charter of functions.
The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should take steps towards further
empowering IBM so that IBM would be able to discharge its functions and responsibility in
efficient and effective manner. IBM from time to time should monitor mining plan of all the
Mines.

(Para 2.2)

The Committee further recommends that since IBM has been entrusted with the
function of approving mining plans in respect of mining leases granted on behalf of the Central
Government as well as conducting studies of environmental protection and pollution Control, it
is pertinent on the part of IBM management that while approving the mining plans the issue of
environmental protection should be given due importance. The Committee is also of the
opinion that the time-gap between the environmental clearance and approval of mining lease
should not be too large as to hamper the growth rate of mining industry.

(Para 2.3)
BUDGETARY SUPPORT

The Committee, taking note of the need of the enhanced budgetary support for IBM,
recommends that the Department of Mines in tandem with IBM management would estimate the
actual need of budgetary support and take it up with the Ministry of Finance.

(Para 4.3)

The Committee is happy to note that IBM has taken up the to provide the specialised
and customised data, preparation of Minerals maps and forest overlays. The Committee hopes
that the IBM_ in tandem with Forest Surveys of India and Ministry of Environment and Forests
would continue to take up latest forest overlays maps. Forest overlays maps used by State
Governments and Central Forest Department would help to cut-down delays in obtaining forest
clearance for ML&PL.

MINERAL EXPLORATION CORPORATION LIMITED

1. MECL was established on 21.10.1972 to undertake detailed systematic mineral
exploration and allied works in order to establish reserves of various minerals/ores in shortest
possible time, to curtail the large time gap entailed between discovery of a prospect and its
eventual exploitation. The corporation has been carrying out these functions by steadily enlarging
scope of activities during last 29 years. It is the premier exploration agency in the country and
undertakes exploration work on behalf of Government of India, Public Sector Enterprises, State
Governments and private organisations. It has taken up coal sampling and analysis work and it is
also planning to diversify into commercial mining of selected minerals.to increase its revenue

1.2 At present the authorized capital of the Company is Rs. 100 crores and the paid- up
capital is Rs. 67,75 crores.

2.0 OBJECTIVES OF MECL

2.1 During the course of Interaction with the management the Sub-Committee was apprised
of the objectives of MECL which is mentioned below:-

(i) To plan and execute exploration programmes and prepare evaluation reports

(ii) To undertake geological, geo-chemical and geophysical surveys at optimel cost
to the customers to establish exploitable reserves of various minerals.

(iii) To achieve cost effectiveness through improved productivity, optimum utilisation
of human and physical resources ‘and technological up-gradation.

(iv) 10 obtain PL/ML for potential mineral deposits in India for the purpose of
development of the deposit either individually and or jointly with other parties.

(v) To achieve consistently increasing growth through diversification and joint
ventures, strategic partnership and expansion into solid fossil fuels etc. to become
a dividend paying Company.
3.0 ACTIVITIES OF MECL

3.1 MECL is the premier exploration agency in the country and carries out exploration
activities under two major heads, viz. (a) ‘Promotional’ on behalf of Govt. of India, in which
projects are funded by Central Govt. on the basis of detailed exploration schemes formulated by
the Company, in the perspective ‘of the demand vs. availability as well as national priorities (b)
‘Contractual’ on behalf of other agencies including Public Sector, Private Sector and State
Governments as per contract executed by MECL with them.

32 The Committee understands the vital role of MECL in carrying out detailed
systematic mineral exploration and hopes that MECL management would be guided by the
management by objectives ( MBO) and make its eamest efforts for achieving the cherished
goals.

4.0 ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE

4.1 As regards the organisational set up of MECL, the management informed the Sub-
Committee that MECL with its registered office at Nagpur carries out its operations all over
the country through separate division with specific functions. The operational division comprise,
Geology, Drilling and Mining. Support services are provided by Finance, Materials
Management, Personnel & Administration, planning & Business Development Division. It also
has a full fledged information Technology Centre at Nagpur. It manages its functions at projects,


facilitate =] Prompt maintenance of plant and machineries deployed at the projects it has 3
Regional Maintenance Centres at Ranchi, Nagpur and Hyderabad, Technical guidance to
projects, finalisation of geological reports and close liaisoning with the clients is carried out
through the Regional Exploration Centres located at Ranchi, Korba, Nagpur, Hyderabad,
Neyveli and Barmer. To Promote the commercial activities, Commercial Centres are located at
Delhi, Ranchi, Guwahati and Calcutta,

zonal offices and whether the zonal offices are profit making units. The management stated that

5.0 Co-ordination and Co-operation between MECL and GSI/ merger of MECL
with GSI

5.1 The MECL management stated that MECL was carved out of GSI with a specific
mandate of conducting detailed exploration in the identified Prospects of GSI. Over a period of
30 years, these activities have been almost completed and GSI is not able to identify many new
Prospects for MECL to carry out detailed exploration. In this context, it is essential that
funding and efforts of GS! should continue, so that they can search and identify more prospects
for MECL for detailed exploration.

5.2 Further, the major role of MECL has been in Promotional coal exploration which is also
now getting reduced since the majority of area has already been explored during VIlIth and
IXth plan period, The level of revenue now available for next ten years is merely of the order of
1.00 lakh meteres/annum equivalent to Rs.25.00 crores.


$.3 The Department of Mines informed the Sub-Committee that there is a close cooperation
between the GSI and MEC. Objective of MECL and GSI are different. GSI does the
preliminary geological search whereas MEC has been created for detailed exploration of the
promising proposals at indicated mainly by GSI. MEC takes up the detailed exploration
activity on commercial lines, 051 is Government organisation and MEC is a commercial
organisation created in 1972 for above purpose. At. present MEC has diversified its field of
operations and specialised manpower, due to which MEC is able to manage its affairs by
undertaking contracts from various departments/clients.

5.4 The Committee is of the view that GSI should undertake honest effort for searching
and identifying new prospects for MECL for detailed exploration,

$5 The Ministry of Mines may explore the possibility of merger of MECL with
Geological Survey of India (GSI) for better co-ordination and continued prospect for MECL
for detailed exploration. MECL could work as a separate division in GSI structure. The
synergy so achieved due to merger and brand endowment of GSI would open new areas for
MECL as a separate wing of GSI for detailed exploration and promotion and would enable it to
work in domestic market as well as foreign market. Besides, these measures would reduce the
administrative expense .

8.0 PHYSICO-FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE OF MECL

8.1 Since inception of MECL, upto 1988-89, there was an upward trend in total productivity
and tumn- over df the Company. The Company had been making profit and generating surplus
from 1976-77 upto 1989-90 except for the period of 1980-81 to 1982-83. But after economic
liberalisation in India it had to face constraints and has been incurring losses from 1990-91. With
the change of policy after liberalisation, the allocation of funds for mineral exploration was
reduced considerably resulting in reduction of direct support to MECL in terms of promotional
projects from a level of around Rs. 20 crores per annum during late eighties to around Rs. 5-8
crores per annum in the recent years, The contractual work which was being awarded by various
public sectors has also reduced considerably on account of financial crunch faced by other
organisations.

9.1 In this scenario, in 1995 Government of India chalked out a revival plan based on

performance level without appreciable loss. MECL implemented the recommendations of the
Revival Committee, which resulted in improvement in physico-financial performance -

clean balance sheet. of the company would enable the company to obtain loan from bank
easily other-wise obtaining loan from banks even for promotional purpose becomes difficult

15.0 FUTURE THRUST AREAS OF MECL

15.1. With the economic liberalisation policy of Government of India and frame work of new
mineral policy, the funding for core activity has started showing declining trend. At the same
time, contractual work on behalf of major traditional clients has also drastically reduced. This has
prompted MECL to Identify certain non- traditional areas for its diversification programme.
Some of the important thrust areas for diversification are mentioned below;

15.1.0 EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF COAL BED METHANE

15.1.1 Coal Bed Methane (CBM) is emerging as a promising source of clean energy and now is
recognised as a legitimate, low risk and environmental friendly source of energy, associated with

vast known coal and lignite deposits in India. MECL, has emerged as one of the leading agencies
in the field of CBM exploration.


= The Department of Mines stated that the liberalisation of CBM has helped MECL in
procuring orders for slim hole drilling. MECL has already completed first phase of drilling of
Rs.9 crores for ONGC and additional work of Rs.2 crores has been awarded recently, Further
work of Rs.10 crores is expected soon from ONGC. Private parties like ESSAR and Reliance
have been approaching for similar job.

15.1.3 The Committee is happy to observe that MECL is emerging as one of the leading
agencies in the field of CBM exploration. As the Government of India has also liberalized the
CBM policy recently and seven CBM blocks has been auctioned, association of MECL with
prospective Indian/ foreign entrepreneurs will go a long way in developing the CBM resources.
MECL should not leave any stone unturned in getting orders for exploration . Government
also should give priority to MECL. y

15.2.0 COMMERCIAL MINING OF MINOR MINERALS

15.2.1 Besides mine development, commercial mining of certain minor minerals would be
beneficial for the sustainable growth of MECL. Rail ballast stone mining and supply tb Railways
has been the major thrust area identified by MECL recently and efforts are being made to carve
its position in this field. Since the demand of Rail ballast for Railways is expected to increase
manifold in future, Government should evolve a mechanism for awarding supply of Rail ballast
by MEOL to Railways on continuous basis.

15.2.3 The Department of Mines stated that MECL has undertaken mining of blast stone
initially in the State of Jharkhand whereas efforts are being made for obtaining mining lease of
bauxite in Orissa and Chattisgarh and mineral sand in the State of Tamil Nadu.

15.2.4. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Mines should extend its all possible
guidance to MECL for commercial mining of minerals. At the same time MECL management
should approach the Ministry of Railways for receiving work-order for supplying of Rail
blast to Railways.

15.3.0 COAL SAMPLING AND ANALYSIS

15.3.1 MECL has already been identified as third party agency for sampling of coking and non-
coking coals by various clients. Government's help in awarding the work by various
clients/power plants would be very vital for revenue generation in future.

15.3.2 The Committee is pleased to note that that MECL has made its presence felt in the field
of coal sampling and analysis. The Committee recommends that MECL management should
make effects for procuring work order in this field.

15.4.0 MINING & BENEFICIATION. OF BEACH SAND

15.4.1 Beach sand mining and beneficiation for production of Titanium dioxide pigment is
another diversification programme of MECL, for which it has gone ahead With application of
Mining Lease in the state of Tamil Nadu. Once the lease is granted, MECL could attract private
parties for purchase of mineral concentrates for production of pigment. This activity could be a
source of additional revenue for MECL on sustained basis and Government's assistance is needed
in granting mining leases, the Sub-Committee was informed.

15.4.2, The Committee recommends that Government may grant the lease at the earliest.

10



15.5.0 GROUND WATER EXPLORATION

15.5.1 Besides mineral resources, ground water is a vital resource for the development of the
nation. Due to rapid industrialization and population explosion on one hand and depletion of
shallow ground water resources on the other, hamessing the water resources from deep seated
aquifers and its effective utilisation is of paramount importance in the present day scenario. In
view of the above, MECL has now identified ground water exploration and development as the
vital area under diversification programme.

15.5.2 The Sub-Committee was informed that MECL has succéssfully undertaken the ground
water exploration and tube well development in different geological terrain. Having required
infrastructure and capabilities, MECL is geared up to accept the challenging task of deep drilling,
so that assessment and exploitation of ground water resources from deep seated water bearing
strata can be made for water management planning in future.

15.5.3 The Committee understands that harnessing the water resources and its effective
utilization is essential for proper water planning and management, The Committee feels that
MECL , with its rich experience in deep drilling and exploration , should be able to play a
positive role in'exploring ground water which is gradually becoming scarce resource.

REPORT
 
            The Offshore Areas Mineral (Development And Regulation) Bill, 2001 was referred to the Committee on
Industry by the Hon'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha on  7
th September, 2001 under  Rule 270(b) of the Rules of Procedure
and Conduct of Business in Rajya Sabha for examination and report thereon.
2          The Bill aims to provide for development and regulation of mineral resources in the territorial  waters,
continental shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India and   to provide  for matters connected
therewith or incidental  thereto.
3          According to   the statement of objects and reasons of the Bill, the need was felt to have  proper legal   frame
work for   regulation and  development of minerals occurring  in the offshore areas, that is,  territorial waters,
continental shelf, exclusive  economic zone and other maritime zones of  India, in order to develop the offshore  areas
scientifically and  systematically.   India  has approximately 3.3 million square kilometres  of land area  with a coast line
of 8041 kilometres. The area of the Exclusive Economic Zone is 2.02 million square kilometres and  in terms of the UN
Convention on the Law of the Sea, 1982,  the coastal states have specific rights and jurisdiction, inter alia,  for exploring
and exploiting the natural resources over the continental margin, which will add about 0.80 million square kilometres in
addition to the area of Exclusive Economic Zone. In  India, beach placer deposits have been economically exploited
since long. The mining and processing of different minerals obtained from these placer deposits into valuable products

69th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/69threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:13:34]
are also well established. India is richly endowed in mineral sands in the Eastern and Western Coasts. Heavy mineral
sand containing mostly  ilmenite with some rutile, leucoxene (a decomposition product of ilmenite), garnet, zircon,
monazite and aluminium silicates like silimanite and kyanite occur in isolated to extensive spreads all along the sea
coast.
4          The proposed legislation would enable streamlining of mineral exploration and development in the offshore
areas and ensure systematic and scientific exploitation of mineral reserves (except petroleum, natural gas and
hydrocarbon resources) for attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
5.         Under the Law of the Sea  convention, 1982, the coastal states   are  entitled to territorial sea (12 nautical miles), 
contiguous zone (24 nautical miles) exclusive  economic zone (200 nautical miles) and   continental shelf (200/350
nautical  miles) drawn from normal base-line, which is the low-water line along  the coast,  over which the  coastal
States have specific rights and Jurisdiction, including for  exploring and  exploiting the natural  resources.  The
Convention   came into effect  on 16
th November, 1994 and became part of the  International Law, India has ratified the
Law of the Sea Convention on  29th June, 1995.  Article  297 of the Constitution of India was amended by the  40th
Amendment to the Constitution and according to amended Article 297 , all lands , minerals and other things of value
underlying the  ocean within the   territorial water, or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone of  India, 
shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes  of the Union.  In 1976, the Parliament passed the Territorial
Waters, Continental Shelf , Exclusive  Economic zone and other Maritime Zones Bill, 1976 delineating therein the
limits of the zones and rights and obligations in maritime zones.
6.         Entry  54 of   List-I of the Constitution gives powers to the Central Government for regulation of mines and
mineral development to the extent to which such regulation and  development under the control of the   Union is
declared by  Parliament by law to be  expedient in the public interest.  The Bill has been introduced accordingly. 
Further, the  clauses 16 and 17 of the Bill provide that royalty and fixed rent shall be payable to the Central Government
and, therefore, in accordance with Article 117 (1) of the  Constitution of India, which requires  that any Bill making
provision for any of the matters specified in sub-clauses (a) to (f)   of clause (1)  of article110   [Definition of   "Money
Bills."] ,  recommendation of the President has been obtained prior to introduction of the Bill.
7.         As per amendments  made  on November, 10, 1992 to the  Allocation of  Business Rules,  1961, legislation for
regulation  of mines and development of minerals underlying  the ocean within the territorial waters, or the continental 
shelf of the exclusive   economic zone and other maritime   zones of India has been placed under the charge of the
Department of Mines.  In May,.  1993 a working group was constituted, headed  by the Joint Secretary, Department of
Mines, for finalising the legislation for offshore areas .  Terms of reference of the working group were  (i) to suggest a
suitable legislation and rules for regulating prospecting and mining in the  Territorial Waters, c Continental Shelf and
Exclusive Economic Zone of India after examining the existing legislation of the  subject viz.  the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957  (MMDR Act) , and the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive
Economic Zone and other Maritime Zone Act, 1976 and other related matters; and (ii) to make any  other
recommendations as may be considered necessary.  The working group    has taken into consideration the opinion
expressed  by Ministry of Law, ( January, 1974) that if, by virtue of special requirement of minerals in the offshore
areas, it is considered necessary to lay down conditions or restriction which are at variance with the existing statutory
provisions in the MMDR Act, 1957 , then under such circumstances, it would not be legally permissible to do  so
without first   amending the statute, i.e. MMDR Act, 1957  itself suitably.  It was  also observed that by virtue of Article
297 of the Constitution, the ownership of minerals in the offshore areas vests  in the Union and if the MMDR Act were
to be used for  framing rules applicable to offshore areas  it would require extensive amendments.   The Wording Group
also  examined the possibility of framing Rules under section 15 of the Maritime Zone act, 1976.  It was observed 
however, that the Maritime Zones  Act   is in the nature of umbrella legislation and if Rules are to be framed under this
Act, provisions normally included  in the Act will   have to  be  necessarily provided for in the Rules,   This  could be a
doubtful course of action, as it would amount to "excessive delegation"  through the rules which is not desirable in  any 
legislation.  The Working  Group, therefore, came to the conclusion that it would be advisable to frame a new Act for
mineral exploitation in offshore areas and submitted its report and draft of the proposed legislation accordingly in
December, 1995.   The Report and the proposed draft legislation was further examined in  extensive consultation with
all Departments and Ministries in the Government of India who have  stakes in off shore areas.  Accordingly the Bill has
been prepared, duly addressing the concerns of all stake holders.

details of  short title and commencement, Declaration  as to  expediency of Union control, Application, Definitions.

3.         The Committee was given to  understand  that  the   need to have a proper legal framework for regulation and
development of  minerals  occurring  in the offshore areas. i.e. territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic
zone and other maritime zones of India. Replying to the Committee's  query  whether  the existing  legal framework on
the subject viz.  the Mines and Minerals ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 (MMDR Act) and the Territorial
Waters, Continental Shelf, exclusive Economic Zone and other  Maritime Zone Act, 1976 proved  deficient for making
rules for  development of offshore areas in a scientific and  systematic manner so much so that the need of separate  and
fresh legislation was felt the Department of Mines  stated that  in May 1993 a working group  was constituted  headed
by the Joint Secretary, Department of  Mines for finalizing the legislation for offshore areas.  The working group was 
asked  to suggest  a suitable legislation and rules  for  regulating, prospecting  and mining in the  territorial waters,
continental shelf AND EEZ  of  India after examining the existing legislation on the  subject, namely,  the Mines and
Minerals  ( Regulation and Development) Act,  1957 , the  Territorial Waters, Continental  Shelf, Exclusive Economic
Zone and other Maritime Zones Act, 1976 and other related matters.     The  Ministry  of Law  had advised that  if by
virtue of  special requirements  of minerals in the  offshore areas, it is considered necessary to lay down  conditions or
restrictions which are at variance with the existing statutory provisions in  the MMDR Act, 1957, then under such
circumstances, it would not be legally permissible to do so without first  amending the Principal Act.  The features 
unique to development of mineral resources in  the offshore   areas  were different    in the environment, the nature of
operations and  the equipments required and hence it was  felt  that rules framed under the MMDR Act would   not be 
adequate in  the matter. The other possibility was framing rules under   section 15 of the Territorial  Waters, Continental
Shelf, Exclusive Economic Zone and other Maritime Zones   Act, 1976.  Maritime Zones Act is in the nature of
umbrella legislation and  therefore if rules were to be framed under this Act, the provisions normally  included in the
Act were to be necessarily provided for in the  rules.  This could be  a doubtful course of action, as it would amount to
excessive delegation through  rules.  Accordingly, therefore, the Working Group came to the conclusion that it would
be  advisable to   frame a new  Act  for mineral exploitation in Offshore areas, which has  formed the  basis of the
Offshore Areas Mineral (Development and Regulation) Bill.    Further more the purpose of the Territorial Waters,
Continental Shelfs, Exclusive Economic Zones and other Maritime  Zone Act, 1976 is  mainly to define  and determine
the limit of the territorial water continental  shelf, exclusive    economic zone and other maritime zone of India and to
regulate certain other  limited matters relating to them.  The said Act   does  not specifically provides for  grant of
reconnaissance permit exploration license  or production lease  for the  purposes  of  extracting minerals from sea land. 
The Mines and Minerals  ( Development and Regulation) act, 1957 was enacted mainly for  the purpose of development
and regulation of mines and minerals under the  land only.  It was  not intended to regulate and develop the mines and
minerals in the offshore  areas.  The development and regulation of mineral resources in the  territorial water,
continental shelfs, exclusive economic zones and other maritime zones  need a different expertise, technical ability  and
separate methodology of operation performed or carried out by the use of vessel, erection, appliance, artificial island
and platforms, etc.  The measurement of wave tides, hydrography etc.  are required   for which separate conditions of
licenses and permits are  required to regulate the licenses, permits and leases of quite different nature   specifically for
