4.         The  Committee feels that in order to develop the offshore areas scientifically and systematically it is pertinent to
have a proper legal frame-work for regulation and development of minerals occurring in the offshore areas, that is,
territorial waters, continental shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India. The proposed
legislation would enable streamlining of mineral exploration and development in the offshore areas and ensure
systematic and scientific exploitation of mineral reserves (except petroleum, natural gas and hydrocarbon resources) for
attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
5.         The Committee  observe  that  under the law of the sea convention, 1982 , the coastal states  are entitled to
territorial sea (12 nautical miles), contiguous zone (24 nautical miles) exclusive economic zone (200 nautical miles) and
continental shelf (200/350  nautical miles) drawn from normal base-line, which is the low-water line along the coast,
over which the coastal States have specific   rights and Jurisdiction, including for exploring and exploiting the natural  
resources.  The Conventional came into effect on 16
th November, 1994 and became part of the International Law,  India
has ratified the Law  of the Sea Convention on 29th June, 1995.  The Department of  Mines  informed the Committee
that   Article 297  of the Constitution of   India was amended by the 40th Amendment to the Constitution and according
to amended Article 297, all lands, minerals and other things of  value  underlying the ocean within the territorial water,
or the continental shelf, or the exclusive economic zone of  India,  shall vest in the Union and be held for the purposes
of the Union.  In 1976, the  Parliament passed the Territorial Waters, Continental Shelf, Exclusive Economic  Zone and
other  maritime zones  Act, 1976 delineating therein  in the limit of the zones and  rights and obligations in maritime
zones.  Entry 54 of List-I of  the Constitution gives powers to the Central Government for  regulation of mines and
mineral development to the  extent to which such regulation and development under the control of the Union is declared
by Parliament by  law to be expedient in the public interest.  The Bill has been introduced accordingly.
6.         The Committee is of the  view  that  the proposed legislation  have sufficient legal  frame-work for making rules
necessary for development and regulation of offshore areas . Some of highlights which  takes care of all required legal-
framework  are as follows: —
There will be three types of operating rights, namely, Reconnaissance permit (non exclusive), exploration licence and
production lease.
The offshore areas will be released periodically for grant of operating rights only after inter-departmental consultation
with the Ministries/Departments  which have parallel interest in the offshore areas.
Exploration licence or production lease will be granted to any person over an area only upon submission of a work
programme for the exploration operation, or development of the mineral deposits in that area. This would ensure that
exploration and mining operations in the offshore areas are conducted on a scientific basis with due regard to
conservation.
No operating right shall be granted to any person unless such  person is an Indian national or a company as defined in
sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Companies Act, 1956 (1 of 1956).
The holder of the reconnaissance  permit shall commence work within a period of six months, the holder of the
exploration licence shall commence work within a period of one year and the holder of the production lease shall
commence commercial production within a period of two years from the date of grant.
Reconnaissance permit will be granted for a maximum period of two years with the provision for renewal for another
maximum period of two years. Exploration licence shall be granted initially for a  maximum period of three years with a
provision for renewal so that the total period of exploration does not exceed five years. Production lease shall be granted
initially for a period not exceeding thirty years with the provision for renewal for twenty years.
The Central Government is being authorised by notification in the Official  Gazette to prescribe norms for the safety and
health of persons and safety and security of  property in offshore areas.
There is a provision  for payment of royalty and in order to discourage the speculative acquisition of large areas, there 
is also  provision for payment of fixed rent. The rate will be prescribed by notification, with the proviso that  royalty and
fixed rent shall not be enhanced more than once during any period of three years.
In order to safeguard defence and security of the country,  the provisions of the proposed legislation shall be in addition

to and not in derogation of any other law for the time being in force in the offshore areas.
There is  an enabling clause for making rules to address problems of pollution of offshore environment and security and
safety of marine life including fin and shell fish, coral and other species. Every holder of the operating rights shall be
liable for any pollution or damage to marine environment resulting from  activities in the offshore areas.
7.         The Committee notes and endorses the contention  of the Department of Mines  that  the proposed  legislation  
would be able to  provide  for regulation and development of mineral resources in the territorial waters, continental
shelf, exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India  and to provide for matters connected therewith or
incidental thereto.  The Bill when enacted would help in streamlining mineral exploration and development in the
offshore areas for attracting private investment in the mineral sector.
8.         The Committee is of the opinion that  the procedure for grant of operating rights in the  proposed Bill is
considered reasonably flexible.  The Offshore Areas are repository of variety of natural  resources.  In order to exclude
overlapping of granting of operating rights   for exploration and mining of non-petroleum mineral resources   and
petroleum  resources, or for excluding areas rich in fishing     and for excluding areas sensitive  from security and
strategic point of view,  it  is  necessary    that the areas which  would be released for grant of operating rights under the
proposed legislation, are  released periodically in consultation with  all the concerned Departments/Ministries.  In
particular, the procedure for grant of reconnaissance permit is totally flexible, since reconnaissance permit is envisaged
as a non-exclusive permit and   any number of persons could be granted reconnaissance permit over the same area or
even for the same minerals.
9.         The Committee  notes that the offshore areas  would be released periodically for grant  of operating rights for
systematic development of mineral resources of the offshore area.  In order to exclude  overlapping of granting of
operating rights for exploration/mining of non petroleum mineral resources and petroleum resources,   or for excluding 
areas   rich in fishing , the  areas would  be notified for  grant in consultation  with the Ministry of Petroleum  and
Natural Gas, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, and the Department of  Animal Husbandry and Dairying. 
Similarly, in order to  ensuing that the areas used  by the Indian Navy, Coast Guard, Indian Space Research
Organisation (ISRO) for exercises/firing  etc. and areas for traffic separation routes, maritime safety routes and the like
are  not notified for grant.  Consultation would be done with the Ministry of Defence before  notifying areas for grant.
10.       Replying to  the Committee's query regarding to  what  extent the proposed  legislation provides  encouragement 
to private sector  in the field of  offshore  areas the Department of Mines stated that   the Bill has been formulated to
provide  a legal  frame  work for entry of private sector in the offshore areas.  The Offshore Areas Mineral (
Development and Regulation ) Bill, 2001 provide equal emphasis on the development and  regulation aspects of
minerals as both aspects are essential.  The Mines and Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957  also has
similar provisions for  ensuring conservation and regulation measures.  Provisions like, power of the  Central
Government to authorize entry, inspection, search and seizure, power to issue directions for conservation and systematic
development of offshore  Minerals, pollution, marine environment, coastal erosion, etc. are essential in the  national
interest and in the interest of mineral  conservation.  The proposed Bill  also  provides  that notwithstanding anything 
contrary contained in the legislation,  if the Central Government is  of the opinion that in the interest of offshore
mineral  development, it is necessary to do so,  it may in any specific case, authorize grant, renewal or transfer of any
operating right to any person on such terms and  conditions as it  may specify in this behalf.  This enabling clause
underlines the  intention of the Central Government that  development of minerals in the offshore areas is its primary
concern.
11.       The Committee observes that  the Offshore Areas Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Bill, 2001 empowers
the Central Government to make rules in case of pollution of offshore   environment and  security and  safety  of  
marine life including fin and  shell fish,  coral and other species.  Sub-clause 2 of  the clause  20 of the proposed Bill 
provides that  every holder of the operating right shall be liable for any pollution or damage to marine environment
resulting from his activities in the offshore areas.  Once the law is enacted, the rules would be framed in consultation
with the Ministries/Departments concerned.
12.       The representatives of  Legislation Department , Ministry of Law, justice and Company Affairs  impressed upon
the Committee that proposed legislation adequately safeguards the national interest in  all respect.      in order to
safeguard defence and security   interests of the  country, the  provisions  of   the  legislation are in  addition to and not
in derogation of any other law for the time being in force in the offshore areas.  Further, the offshore areas would  be
released periodically for grant of operating rights only after inter-Departmental consultations with the 
Ministries/Departments ( including the  Ministry of  Defence)  who  have parallel interest in the offshore areas, and in 
order to  ensure that the areas   used by Indian Navy Coast Guard, etc. for  exercising, the areas for traffic separation
routes,  and maritime safety routes, are not notified.

15.       The Department of Mines  impressed on the  Committee that   the opinion/comments of Departments and

sought while discussing and finalising the Bill.   The Department of Mines  had  consulted the Ministries of Defence,

Departments  of    Ocean Development, Atomic  Energy , Animal Husbandry and Dairying, Science and Technology,

proposed Bill.
16.       Justifying  the criterion  for royalty and fixed rent as  indicated  in Schedule -I and Schedule-II of the proposed

in the Mines and Minerals ( Development and Regulation) Act, 1957.The rates of royalty under section 9 of the Mines
and Minerals ( Development and Regulation ) Act, 1957 have been notified last on 12

of royalty in Offshore Areas Mineral ( Development and Regulation) Bill, 2001 have been indicated at the same level.
Fixed rent  is basically the minimum royalty expected from a lease hold.  Rate of fixed rent for a standard block of 5

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman of the Department Relat ed Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Industry, having been author ised by the Committee to present on its beha lf, present this 
Seventh Report of the Committee on the working of Bharat Gold Minies Limited which falls 
under the jurisdiction of Ministry of Mines. 
2. The Committee at its meeting held on 15th June, 1993 identified 'Bharat Gold Mines' as 
one of subjects for indepth study and report. The Committee directe d the Secretariat to obta in 
a detailed Background Note on the subject from the Ministry of Mines. 
3. At its sitting held on 28th June, 1993 the Committee held a general discussion on the 
note furnished by the Ministry on the subject and finalised a questionnaire for furth er 
clarificatiOns by the Ministry. 
4. The Committee also heard the oral ev1aence of the Secretary of the Ministry alongwith 
the representat ives of Bharat Gold Mines Limited at its two meetings held on 30th September 
and lOth November, 1993 respectively for clarifications. 
5. The Committee at its meeting held on the 9th November, 1993 also heard the oral 
evidence of the representatives of the Workers' Unions operating at Bha rat Gold Mines Limited 
witl;l a view to eliciting their views on the functioning of the company. 
6. In its meeting held on 11th November, 1993 the Committee decided to constitute a Sub­
Committee to visit Kolar Gold Fields, Karnataka for an on the spot study of the working in 
Bharat Gold Mines Limited . The Chairman of the Committee accordingly constituted a Sub­
Committee of the following Member s for the purpose. 
1. Shrimati Suseela Gopalan - Convenor 
2. Shri J.P. Javali 
3. Shri K. K. Veerappan 
4. Shri K. H. Muniyappa 
5. Shri V. Dhananjaya Kumar 
6. Shri Tej Nar<tyan Singh 
7. Shri P.G. Narayanan 
7. The Sub-Committe e visited the Kolar Gold Fields on 5th and 6th January, 1994. The 
Sub-Committee heard the oral evidences of the repre sentatives of the worke rs unions operating 
at Kolar Gold Fields and also the representatives of Bharat Gold Mines Limited Management 
and the Ministry of Mines. The Sub-Committee submitted a study report on its visit. The study 
report was considered by the Committee at its meeting held on 22nd Febr uary, 1994. After 
some discussion the Committee unanimously adopted the report submitted by the Sub­
Committee. 
8. The Committee at its meeting held on 23rd February, 1994 heard and considered the 
views of Shri S. Natarajan on the subject as recommend ed by the Sub-Committee. 
9. The Committee considered the subject in 11 sittings and ado pted the draft report at its 
meeting held on 30th March , 1994. 
10. The study report of the Sub-Committee is annexed (Annexure 1). 
11. On the basis of the documents furnished by the Ministry of Mines, the oral evidence of 
the representatives of the Ministry, workers unions management of Bharat Gold Mines and the 

study VISit of the Sub-Committee to Kolar Gold Fields as stated above the Committee 
recommends that:-
11.1 It is necessary to allay the fear of imminent closure of BGML at Kolar which is 
looming large on the workers and their families and other inhabitants of the area. 
They are living under a fear psychosis as the sword of closure is hanging over their 
heads. To remove this fear psychosis it is necessary to declare in unequivocal terms 
that the Company will not be allowed to close down and every effort will be made to 
revive it at the apex nation,al level. 
11.2 The Company has been referred to BIFR. Now it can not take any action for the 
revival without the prior permission of BIFR. Hence it is necessary that the reference 
of BGML, Kolar to BIFR be revoked forthwith and taken out from the purview of 
BIFR. 
11.3 To bring the company on rails· requisite funds should be given to establish a plant for 
recycling the huge stock of tailing so as to extract gold therefrom. The Committee 
observes that once the plant is established and it starts running within two to three 
years not only the company will wipe out its losses but it will also start earning 
profits. To boost the morale of the company the Ministry of Mines must come 
forward. The Government may either make available 41 crores of rupees as 
Budgetary support or soft loan to the company or stand as a gurantor to enable the 
company to get loans from banks and financial institutions. The management can also 
explore the possibility of hypothecating its surplus land to raise the funds for the 
plant of course with the prior approval of the Government. 
11.4 The management can raise the requisite funds for its revivial by selling its surplus 
land at the existing market rates as the land can fetch good prices but this step should 
be resorted to as the last step because the land can be utilised for agricultural 
pruposes particularly the cashew growing. Presently the management has planted 
eucliptus in parts of the surplus land and expecting to get some revenue therefrom 
but keeping in view that this variety makes the land infertile its plantation may be 
discouraged. 
11.5 The Security network of the company should be streamlined and every effort should 
be made to prevent pilferage of gold produced by the company. Frisking be mae 
compulsory for everyone coming out of the premises where gold is produced 
irrespective of his status. The Security personnel be provided modern gadgets to 
detect pilferage of gold. A vigilance wing should also be established to keep overall 
watch over the movements in the premises including that of security personnel. 
Surprise checks should be conducted and activities of the goldsmiths living around 
Kolar be monitored to prevent passing of pilfered gold. 
11.6 Survey of the gold deposits in the area should be counducted in more and more 
scientific way. BGML is presently wholly dependent on Geological Survey of India 
for this purpose. The management may have its own team to do this job. Technology 
from other countries like South Africa and Australia can be obtained in this field as 
they have the latest know-how in this area. South Africa in particular have the 
resembling conditions as that of Kolar and doing very well. Their co-operation can be 
more helpful. 
Technology from countries like South Africa, Australia etc. can be explored who can help in 
modernising the existing techniques of BGML on profit sharing basis. 
11.7 The BGML is undertaking diversification activities to earn more revenue. It is 

manufacturing mmmg equipments and also providing mmmg consultancy services. 
The Government can help BGML by securing orders from other departments. Export 
possibilities should also be explored. The diversification activities should be encour­
aged to create more job opportunities. 
11.8 BGML being a Government of India enterprise it is the onus of the Government to 
provide funds for the modernisation of the mills and mining techniques of the 
company. The funds may be in the form of long term loans with reasonable interest 
thereon. Since it is the only one establishment engaged in production of precious 
yellow metal in the country phasing out is not advisable at all. If proper investments 
are made in this company and new era of hopes and dedication is generated the 
company can run smoothly for the next fifty to sixty years. But there must be a will 
on the part of the Government to run this company. 
11.9 The BGML is spending a substantial portion of its earnings on power tariff. 
Understandably the Karnataka Electricity Board had established a power house 
exclusively for BGML. The production cost pe~; unit in that power house comes to few 
paise but the Board is charging exorbitant tariff from BGML. The State Electricity 
Board should be apprised of the gravity of the situation and persuaded to reduce the 
power tariff to reduce the burden of BGML. Similarly the State Government is 
charging royalty from BGML without extending any facility. The State can also be 
persuaded to forgo charging royalty from BGML. 
12. The ·Committee has come to conclusion that the past performance of the present

Kolar Gold Fields have a vast area consisting of gold ore banks stretching over 200

GOLD PRICE FORMULA 
The Sub-Committee has gathered that till the formation of the company the gold was bought 
by the Government at IMF prices. In April, 1974. the pricing policy underwent a change and the 
old was to be sold at London Metal Exchange Rates The pricing policy further underwent a 
change during 1976-88 as per details given below:-
(i) The subsidy payable is equal to the difference between the IMF Price (Rs. 84.40 per 10 
grams) and the cost of production of 10 grams of gold in 1975-76 plus 12% on capital 
and reserves. 
(ii) Government could review from time to time the cost of produ ction and take into 
account any inescapable increase in cost of production. 
(iii) This price was subject to a minimum of the average international price in the prccedmg 
month and a maximum of the average international price in the rrc ceding month plus 
25%. 
(iv) The Government of India from November, 1982 fom1ulatcd the following formula: 
"Bharat Gold Mines Limited (BGML) and .Butti Gold Mines Limited (HGML) each 
be allowed to meet half of the total industrial demand for gold at the prevailing 
domestic price. The production of BGML and HGML over and above this quantity as 
well as the ehtire production of Hindustan Copper Limited would be taken over by the 
Mint at an average international price during the preceding month plus 12.1/2% or the 
average domestic price during the preceding month whichever is lower.·· 
(v) From 1.4.1984, the pricing policy of Government for BGML gold was LMc price 35% 
or Indian Market rate whichever is lower. 
However with effect from 1.4.1988 the Government permitted BGML to sell gold in the 
open market. BGML has nominate-.! ag..!nt~ in the open market and 10% commission in terms of 
value of agents had been fixed. There have been cases of irregularities in terms of commission 
paid to these agents and the company had to bear some losses on this account. Thus it is 
apparent that the Ministry of Mines prescribed the terms and conditions in the matter of gold 
selling policy. Government of India had released a sum of Rs. 172.24 crorcs as subsidy, Rs. 
132.26 crores as prices differential, Rs. 24.81 crores as Non-Plan loan and Rs. 54.28 crores as 
Plan loan respectively during the years 1972-73 to 1992 91. The Management feels that b;td the 
company been given the market price for gold it would have had a surplus of Rs. 5.02 crores on 
31.3.1985 even after taking the unprecedented Joss of Rs. 6.62 crores in the years 1984-85 into 

account. Now the Company has started selling its gold in the open marke t without any pre­
condit ions and it hopes to get reasonable market price for its gold. 
WORKER'S REHABILITATION 
As per the figures place before the Sub-Committee the BGM.L manp ower which was 11,026 
at the end of 1988-89 has come down to 8448 in 1992-93. As on 20.6.1993 the company had 
manpower of 7828 which has further reduced to 7607 as on 31.8.1993. Out of these 2159 persons 
are surplus for whom VRS of the Company is applicable. The latest figures during the visit show 
that the present strength of company is around 7000 persons. According to the Management the 
existing mines are getting fast depleted and efforts have been made to deploy surplus manpower 
in other activites. In addition over the years the workers have developed expertise in other 
activit ies like manufacturing components of equipment and mine construction activities. 
The workers unions arc of the view that despite reduction in number of employees the 
company has maintained the steady production rate of ore. Though no mechanisation is taking 
place. the employees have been forced to go on retirement on the plea of moderni sation. A 
number of equipments are lying used due to callous attitude of the Management towards its 
manpower and these equ ipments are likely to become junk in due course. A lot of talent has 
been thrown out of the company which has resulted into 40% loss of gold. By excess placement 
of people at unviable deep mining sites ignoring the manpower at profitable sites the 
Management has enjoyed free hand in declaring people surplus. Even Voluntary Retirement 
Scheme is not being implement in letter and spirit. G_old mine expert retiring or VRS is included 
and shown in salary figure. The Nat ional Renewal f-'und meant for rehabilitation and retraining of 
workers has been diverted to some other heads. The Manage ment has shown indifferentness 
towards its employees. fhey arr bring charged very high monthly instalment for the dwelling 
units (huts) which were built about 50 to 60 years back by the Britishers. 
'The Management has however projected their two point formula for rehabilitation of 
displaced workman as below:-
(i) To allot a house site at reasobale rate adjacent to Municipal area and permit them to 
dismantle and carry present house materials on payment of reasonable price and pass 
on the liability of maint enance of civic amenities to the Municipality. 
(ii) Agricultural Finance Corporation has been engaged at the instande of Government of 
Indi a to study the land available with BGML at KGF and to suggest an utilisation plan 
which includes utilisat ion of some land for rehabil itating the workmen who may be 
affected due to restructur ing of the company. 
The Sub-Committee after hearing the workers living in KGF and passing through the localities 
of the workers found that the workers are liviP.g in small houses ·in inhuman conditions. They are 
getting electricity for not more than one hour a clay that too at a very low voltage. Similar is the 
case of potable water. Sanitary condit ions are also not satisfact ory. Their localities are stinking. 
The workers have no other options but to live there with their families. The management is 
charging ren tals for these small houses, electricity and water from the low paid workers whereas 
the officers of the company are perhaps enjoying rent free accommodations. The Sub-Committee 
was told that rehabilitation measures are not take n for the dependent of those workers who die 
while in service. Their depend ents are not given suitable jobs on compassionate grou nds as a 
result such families are forced to live in agony and miseries which can be avoided 
if adequate welfare measures are undertaken by the BGML management. After talking to the 
local people at KGF the Sub-Comrr.ittee found that majority of the people do not know any 
other profession except mining because they are in this field generation after generatio n and 
when these peo ple are not given jobs in KGF they remain unemployed and loiter around in the 

hope of getting job. It is, therefore necessary to create more job opportunit ies in KGF or the 
Sub-Committee is afraid that the unemployed youth of the area may join hands with an~i socials. 
As such the BGML management has to initiate welfare measure in a systematic way and on a 
larger scale to benefit the work ers and their families. 
The Sub-Committee was shocked to learn that scanvenging by scavengers is still in existen ce 
in KGF despite its abolition at the national level and a law coming into force banning scavenging. 
The management showed a will to remove this inhuman practice but it appears that Governmen t 
has not provided adequate funds to the management for this. The Sub-Committee is of the 
opinion that Ministry of Mines should bring this matter before the Ministry of Welfare and obtain 
adequate funds for the rehabilitation of scavengers of KGF. 
REVIVAL OF THE COMPANY 
Finally the Sub-Committee is of the opinio n that following measures need to be taken for the 
revival of the BGML by the Governmental and BGML managemen t:-
(a) It is necessary to allay the fear of imminent closure of BGML at Kolar which is looming 
large on the workers and their families and other inhabitants of the area. they are living 
under a fear psychosis as the sword of closure is hanging over their heads. To remove 
this fear psychosis it is necessary to declare in unequivocal terms that the · Company will 
not be allowed to close down and e very e ffort will be made to revive it at the apex 
national level. 
(b) The Company has been referred to BIFR. Now it can not take any action for the revival 
without the prior permission of BIFR. Hence it is necessary that the reference of 
BGML , Koar to BIFR be revoked forthwith and taken out from the purview of BIFR. 
(c) The management must be given a chance to bring the company on rails. It should be 
given the requisite funds to establ ish a plant for recycling the huge stock of tailings to 
extract gold therefrom. The management is confide nt that once the plant is established 
and it starts running within two to three years not only the company will wipe out its 
losses but it will also start earning profit s. To boost the morale of the manag e ment the 
Ministry of Mines must come forward. The Government may either mak e ava ilable 41 
crores of rupees as Budgetary support or soft loan to the compan y or stand as a gurantor 
to enable the company to get loans from banks and financial institutions. The 
management can also explore the possibility of hypothecating its surplus land to raise the 
funds for the plant of course with the prior appr oval of the Government. 
(d) The management can raise the requisite funds for its revival by selling its surplus land at 
the existing market rates as the land can fetch good prices but this step should be 
resorted to as the last step because the land can be uitlised for agricultural purposes 
particularly the cashew growing. Presently the management has planted eucliptus in parts 
of the surplus land and expecting to get some revenue therefrom but keeping in view 
that this variety makes the land infertile its plantation may be discouraged . . 
(e) The security network of the company should be streamlined and every effort should be 
made to prevent pilferage of gold produced by the company. Frisking be made 
compulsory for everyone coming out of the premises where gold is produced irrespective 
of his status. The security personnel be provided modern gadgets to detect pilferage of 
gold. A vigilence wing should also be established to keep overall watch over the 
movements in the premises including that of security personnel. Surprise checks should 
be conducted and activities of the goldsmiths living around kolar be monitored to 
prevent passing of pilfered gold. 
(f) Survey of the gold deposits in the area should be conducted in more and more scientific 

way. BGML is presently wholly dependent on Geological Survey of India for this 
purpose. The management may have its own team to do this job . From other countrie s 
like South Africa and Australi a can be obtained in this field as they have the latest know 
how in this area. South Africa in particular have the resembling conditions as that of 
Kolar and doing very well. Their Co-operat ion can be more helpful. 
(g) Technology from countries like South Africa, Australia etc. can be explored who can 
help in modernising the existing technique s of BGML on profit sharing basis. 
(h) The BGML is undertaking diversification activities to earn more revenue. It is 
manufacturing mining equipments and also providing mining· Consultancy services. The 
Government can help BGML by securing orders from other departments. Export 
possibilities should also be explored. The diversification activities should be encouraged 
to create more job opportunities. 
(i) BGML being a Government of India enterprise it is the onus of the Government to 
provide funds for the moderni satio n of the mills and mining techniques of the company. 
The funds may be in the form of long term loans with reasonable interest. thereon. Since 
it is the only one establishment engaged in proauction of precious yellow metal in the 
country phasing out is not advisable at all. If proper investments are made in this 
company and new era of hopes and dedication is generated the company can run 
smoothly for the next fifty to sixty years. But there must be a will on the part of the 
Government to run this company. 
(j) The BGML is spending a substantial portion of its earnings on power tariff. Understand­
ably · the Karnataka Electricity Board had established a power house exclusively for 
BGML. The production cost per unit in that power house comes to few paise but the 
Board is charging exorbitant tariff from BGML. The STate Electricity Board should be 
apprised of the gravity of the situation and persuaded to reduce the power tariff to 
reduce the burden of BGML. Similarly the State Government is charging royalty from 
BGML without extendi.ng any facility. The State can also be persuaded to forgo charging 
royalty from BGML. 
The Sub-Committee has come to the conclusion that the past performance of the 
present management has been quite dismal and the change of the management, as a test 
case, could be a better future of the company. 
The Sub-Committee is of the opinion that if the above mentioned steps are taken by 
the Government and BGML there is every possibility of the revival of BGML and 
certainly it will prove to be a national asset. 
The Committee may consider.

INTRODUCTION

1, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry, having been authorised by the Committee, hereby present this Seventieth Report on
the Demands for Grants (2002-03) pertaining to the Ministry of Steel .

2. The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary and other representatives of the
Ministry of Steel on 4" April, 2002.

3. While examining the Demands for Grants, the Committee also examined and
considered the Action Taken Notes of the Ministry of Steel on the recommendations contained
in the Committee’s 57" Report on Action Taken Notes on the recommendations contained in
the Committee's 517 Report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) pertaining to the Ministry of
Steel. The Committee also examined the relevant Documents and papers furnished by the
Ministry.

4. The Committee is thankful to the representatives of Ministry of Steel who appeared
before the Committee . The Committee also wishes to thank the Ministry for furnishing the
replies to the questionnaire and the points raised during the course of oral evidence.

5. The Committee at its meeting held on 29" April, 2002 considered and adopted the
Report.

April 29, 2002 Chairman

Standing Committee on Industry

Gi)


REPORT

1. The Ministry of Steel has to play a crucial role in ensuring harmonious and integrated
growth of steel sector. The main functions of Ministry of Steel are as under :-

(a) co-ordination of the growth of the Iron and Steel Industry (including Re-rolling Mills,
Alloy Steel and Ferro Alloy industries, Refractories) both in the Public and Private
Sector.

(b) formulation of policies in respect of production, pricing, distribution, import and
export of iron and steel and Ferro alloys;

(c) planning, development and control of and assistance to the entire iron and steel
industry in the country; and

(d) development of input industries relating to iron ore, manganese ore, refractories etc.,
required mainly by the steel industry.

1.2 Besides the Secretariat, the Ministry of Steel has an attached office viz. the office of the
Development Commissioner for Iron and Steel (DC I & S) located at Calcutta and its four
Regional Offices located in New Delhi, Calcutta, Chennai and Mumbai. Under the administrative
control of Ministry of Steel the following Public Sector Undertakings are functioning :-

i. Steel Authority of India Ltd. (SAIL).

ii. Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. (KIOCL), Bangalore

iii. National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. (NMDC), Hyderabad.
iv. Hindustan Steel Works Construction Ltd. (HSCL), Calcutta

v. MECON Ltd., Ranchi.

vi. Manganese Ore (India) Ltd. (MOIL), Nagpur.

vii. Sponge Iron India Ltd. (SIIL), Hyderabad.

viii. Bharat Refractories Ltd. (BRL), Bokaro.

ix. Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd. (RINL), Visakhapatnam.
x. MSTC Ltd. Calcutta.

xi. Ferro Scrap Nigam Ltd. (FSNL), (A subsidiary of MSTC Ltd.).

xii. Kudremukh Iron and Steel Company Ltd., (KISCO), Bangalore (A Joint Venture
Company of KIOCL, MECON and MSTC Ltd.

xiii. Bird Group of Companies, Calcutta, a Government managed company.

1.3 Consequent on acquisition of the shares by the Bird Group of Companies Ltd. 8
companies of the Bird Group related to the steel industry came under the administrative control of
the Ministry of Steel which inter-alia include Eastern investment Ltd. (EIL); Orissa Mineral
Development Co. Ltd. (OMDC); Birsa Stone Lime Co. Ltd. (BSLC); Karanpura Development
Co. Ltd. (KDCL); Scot & Saxby Ltd. (SSL), (a subsidiary of KDCL), Kumardhubi Fireclay &
Silica Works Ltd. (KFSW); Borea Coal Co. Ltd.; and Burraur Coal Co. Ltd. out of which on four
companies (OMDC, BSLC, KDCL and SSL) are now operational.

1.4 The Committee notes the structural and functional aspects of the Ministry of Steel and
PSUs under its administrative control and hopes that all wings of the whole structure would make


their respective/allocated duties and responsibilities with due co- ordination and inter PSUs
cooperation in such a manner that steel sector in general may contribute to economic growth and
national development.

(Rs. in crore)

6.1.1 The Non-Plan loan of Rs.89.44 crore is to be used for partially clearing arrears of wages
& salaries and statutory dues of the employees of HSCL. It is expected that this entire amount
will be used for this purpose. The large arrears on account of unpaid wages & salaries and
statutory dues have been a source of industrial dissatisfaction among the employees of the
company. This has led to the industrial relations situation being vitiated and has adversely
affected the productivity of the company. Further, the company is also handicapped in
aggressively pursuing the separation of surplus employees through VRS in the face of large
arrears of wages & salaries. The separation of at least 5000 employees through VRS is critical for
the improvement of the operational margins available to the company. It is felt that the non-plan
loan outlay of Rs.89.44 crore will go a long way in solving the above stated problems. However,
it may be noted that the amount of Rs.89.44 crore sanctioned is much below the actual arrears on
account of wages & salaries and statutory dues which, as on 1* March, 2002 stands at Rs.207
crore approximately. To this extent the present non-plan assistance will only be partially
beneficial. As stated above the provision of this loan assistance will be crucial for persuading
employees to accept VRS in large numbers. It has been computed that for the company to
generate positive margins, there is a need to separate at least 5000 employees. The separation of
5000 employees will enable the company to generate positive gross margins. Given the slow
down in the steel sector and low margins in the non-steel sector the prospects of improvement in
physical performance is less. However the Company is striving to diversify its activities in non-
steel sector and is trying to improve its competitiveness by cutting costs.


6.1.2. The Committee is pleased to note that HSCL management and the Ministry of Steel are
making earnest efforts for clearing arrears of wages and salaries and statutory dues of the
employees of HSCL.. Ata time when the rationalisation of manpower in HSCL is going on
payment of dues or arrear will act as a deterrent factor to the successful implementation of VR
Scheme. Therefore, Government took a proper decision to accept the proposal of Ministry
of Steel for the second revival package for HSCL which would take care of clearing of arear of
wages & salaries and all statutory dues.

6.1.3. The Committee, however, recommends that the Government should provide complete
and comprehensive revival package to HSCL at one go so that all envisaged strategy come
true in the scheduled time frame.

SAIL is failing in generating extra budgetary internal resources as per the set target as a result
of which capital projects/schemes get either scuttled or delayed. The Committee is constrained
to express its concern over the financial performance of SAIL as SAIL suffered a loss of
whopping 1290.00 crore in the first nine month of financial year 2001-02. Among SAIL
PSUs only BSP is doing well and DSP is trying to catch up with the stabilization of
modernisation programmes. Performance of RSP is miserable. Investors' mood is shaking as
SAIL issue price is coming down. The debt instrument of SAIL has already been rated by
CRISIL as inadequate safety for fixed deposit programme and Bond programme. The debt-equity
ratio stands at 5.52: 1 as on 31.12.2001 and SAIL cannot raise resources on “stand alone" basis.
The Committee feels that the status of ‘Nav-Ratan' is at stake if the proposed business and
financial restructuring of SAIL does not fructify in time, the Committee fears against the
possibility of sinking of SAIL and wants to call the immediate attention of Government.

12.1.17. Progress in implementation of business and financial restructuring of SAIL

Ministry of Steel informed the Committee that while the financial restructuring of SAIL
has been completed, substantial progress has been made in many areas and the assigned tasks
completed. Organisational tasks such as redesigning incentive structures, redesigning key
corporate processes have been completed. All the tasks in the marketing areas such as strategic
marketing, tactical marketing, including introduction of KAM process, improving sales force
effectiveness etc. have also been completed. The capital expenditure has been restricted 10 Rs.426
crore in 2000-01. Till December 2001, the actual capital expenditure has been throttled to Rs.244
crore only-and the year 2001-02 is likely to end with Rs.500 crore. The process of redesigning
the capital expenditure procedures and manuals have made good progress and is more or less
complete. In the area of operation management, Rs.505 crore was saved through cost reduction
in 2000-01. In the current year Rs.306 crore have been saved till January 2002 and by the end of
this financial year, Rs.400 crore is expected to be saved. The progress on purchase cost reduction
and sale of idle assets have been satisfactory. Further efforts in this regard will continue.
However, in a few cases constraints have been faced affecting progress and needing a re-look.
As regards the change from a Functional to Business Unit Structure, a detailed study has been
undertaken with consultation from a reputed management consultant. The basic blueprint for the
restructuring has been made ready and implementation plan is presently under preparation.
Considering the scope of such a major organisation restructuring in a large organisation like
SAIL, and the implications with respect to location of head quarters of SBU, Board Structure etc.,
it has been decided to take up the implementation in two phases. In Phase-I, many critical
changes such as separation of branches and stockyards, enhanced KAM process, revised cash
management system, modified system of MIS, improved reward and punishment system etc. will
be taken up for implementation. Implementation of all these major activities in Phase-I is
expected to start in April 2002 and completed in two month’s time i.e. by end of May 2002. The
2™ Phase will be taken up later for implementation.

12.1.18. The Committee is of the view that while the business and financial restructuring
package for SAIL as approved and sanctioned by the Government contains the element for

28


substantial sustenance and survival of SAIL PSUs but the progress made in the implementation
is not ata satisfactory pace as a result of which SAIL is failing in sailing through the rough
weather. Although the financial restructuring of SAIL has been completed alongwith the
organizational task i.e. re-designing incentive structure, re-designing key corporate process,
strategic and tactical marketing as and so forth, however all these efforts seems merely a
"Paper-work" in the absence of measures undertaken for posting a marked impact on the
performances of SAIL in general. The Committee gets some solace with the performance of
SAIL in the field of operation management where Rs.55.00 crore was saved through cost
reduction measures and a further saving of Rs.400.00 crore is expected on this count during
the year 2001-02. The Committee hopes that , with the implementation of restructuring i.e. the
change from an officialdom to Business unit structure whose basic blue print is ready and its
implementation plan is under preparation, the fate of SAIL may move in the right direction. The
Committee hopes that organisational restructure would be completed in two phases and the
first phase being going to be completed by May, 02 the Committee expects that the Ministry of
Steel , while furnishing Action Taken Note on the present Report , would also furnish the details
of actual impact on the physical and financial performance of SAIL as a results of
implementation of first phase of organisation restructuring.

The incentive schemes in RINL have been designed on production volume of major

ii Liquid Steel improved from 97% to 100.9% of rated capacity.
iii  Saleable Steel improved from 94.4% to 101.4% of rated capacity.

operation and financials. The concerted effort in all the areas have resulted in significant
improvement in the performance of the company during the year 2000-01 and is being continued
thereafter. The distinctly improved performance levels achieved so far provide confidence that
the company, without any further investment can turnaround by 2003-04 to a net profit making
company by achieving production beyond the rated capacities. In the next 3 to 4 years to come,
no capacity expansion by incurring capital expenditure has been envisaged except the installation
of the 4" Coke Oven Battery at an estimated capital cost of around Rs.360.00 crore. The company
is expected to make net profits from 2003-04 onwards subject to steel market continuing the
revival trend.

workers/trade union resulting into production volumes beyond the steel capacity i.e. hot metal

13.4. Replying to the Committee's query as to what extent the conclusion arrived at from
completed R&D project , have been successful in removing the problems being faced by Steel
Industry , the Ministry of Steel informed that Of the twenty-seven R&D research projects
sanctioned by Empowered Committee for financial assistance from Steel Development Fund
(SDF) three projects have been successfully completed so far. One project was to study
measures for energy efficiency improvement in secondary steel sector. By implementation of
some of the recommendations, many Electric Arc Furnace based steel plants have been able to
reduce energy consumption to some extent. Many more recommendations are being
implemented to reduce energy consumption further. The progress of implementation is, however
slow because of financial constraints. The second project was to develop on line expert system for
continuous casting system (Billets/Blooms/Slabs). By implementation of this system the
continuous casting machine can understand its environment and modify its behaviour accordingly
in order to achieve desired goal. The off line system has been developed and for implementation
of the expert system in actual operation (on line), the Empowered Committee has approved
additional SDF contribution. The results are awaited. The third project was to develop a teaching
package on structural design for department of Civil/Structural Engineering. The introduction of
this package in civil engineering institutions will improve knowledge and competence of fresh
civil/structural engineers so that they can confidently specify usage of structural steel in
construction with the ultimate goal of increasing steel intensive construction in India. Four
workshops have been conducted in different parts of the country. Participants found the teaching
material very useful for enhancement of the knowledge and expertise in the structural steel
design. The follow up of action has been initiated with different institutes/universities who are
teaching design of steel structural.

13.5. The Committee is happy to note that the decisions arrived at from the completed R&D

in secondary sectors, improvement in the continuous costing system and development of civil
engineering.

15.0 GALVANISING COMPLEX IN NORTH-EASTERN REGION.

15.1. Setting-up of a Hot Dip Galvanizing Line (HDGL) Project in North-east at an estimated
cost of Rs.42.85 crore was approved by the SAIL Board in Jan’97. The work was awarded on a
turnkey basis to MECON in Jul’97 with a completion schedule of Jan’99. Civil work for the
project was in advanced stage of completion and equipment supply had also started. However,
due to delay in completion of the approach road & the bridge over river Chasa by Govt. of Assam
and stoppage of work due to heavy rains & floods in the area, the project has been delayed.
Moreover, some of the facilities and concessions to be extended by the Govt. of Assam were not
made available in time. All these factors delayed the Project activities and affected the financial
viability of the Project adversely. Considering the fund constraints of SAIL, SAIL Board
desired in Jan’99 that the possibility of divesting the Project to other interested party with the help
of North-East Development Bank be explored and no further expenditure be incurred till Assam
Govt. provides the various facilities and concessions.

15.2. On the request of SAIL, M/s IFCI reassessed the financial viability of the Project in
Oct’99. They concluded that the Project was not viable with the existing financing pattern and
suggested measures to improve the viability of the Project such as: exemption from excise duty &
income tax, transport subsidy, and obtaining funds from external sources. Efforts were made by
SAIL to obtain funds from external sources but without success. Keeping this in view, it was
decided by SAIL Board in Mar’00 that the project be kept in abeyance and alternate strategies,
including identification of suitable party who may be interested in owning and executing the
project, may be examined.

15.3. Accordingly, the work was suspended in Apr’00 and in May'00, M/s PNB Capital
Services Ltd. were appointed as the Adviser for selection of a Joint Venture (JV) partner. Tenders
were issued to three agencies but only one bid from M/s North East Steels (NES) was received in
Jan’01. NES were selected as Prospective JV partner on preliminary basis in Jul’01 and the

required security deposit of Rs.15 Lakh has been received from them in Dec’01. NES have been

15.4. The Committee is pleased to note that M/s North -east Steels (NES) has come forward

17.0 | GENERAL AND CURRENT ISSUES AFFECTING STEEL INDUSTRY
17.1. Impact of the imposition of tariffs by USA

17.1.1 The US administration has selectively imposed duties and quota restrictions on various
categories of imported steel under the safeguard provisions of the World Trade Organization
(WTO). The announcement of safeguard action is disturbing to the extent that it would accentuate
instability in the global steel market. The unilateral closure of the US market to a large number of
exporters will result in diversion of some of the global surplus into the markets of other importing
countries. This would further depress the market price of steel items and encourage dumping of
steel into other open markets, thereby risking the progressive closure of world markets by resort
to unilateral trade defense measures. This would be particularly unfortunate in the context of the
round of trade liberalization recently agreed upon by WTO member countries in their meeting at
Doha last year.

55


17.1.2. USA exemption to Indian steel from new levy:-Indian steel exporters are already
suffering under the heavy burden of anti-dumping and countervailing duties imposed by the US
Government on CTL Plates, HR Coils and Wire rods, which have seen our exports of these items
plummet rapidly in 2001. India has even taken the issue of imposition of anti-dumping duty on
CTL places to the WTO dispute settlement panel and a decision is expected soon. Nonetheless,
India’s exclusion from imposition of additional duty on account of safeguard action provides our
steel industry with an export opportunity in a wide range of flat and long products, which are not
under anti-dumping duty. The total import of steel products by the US is around 36 million tons
and India ranks 11" in terms of volume of steel supplied by countries to the US. Among the other
top ten countries Canada (placed at no. 1) and Mexico (placed at no. 3) being members of
NAFTA have been totally excluded from the Safeguard Action. Brazil, which is placed at number
2, has also been ostensibly excluded as a developing country. However its export of slabs to US,
which constitutes 80% of its total exports, have been brought within the ambit of safeguard
action. Safeguard actions on the remaining countries like China, Ukraine, Russia etc. may thus
provide Indian exporters with a fresh opportunity to expand their share of the market in the US.

17.1.3. Replying to the Committee's query as to whether it was a fact that price hike is expected
in the domestic market as cascading effect of exclusion of India Steel manufacturers from
safeguard duties by USA the Ministry of Steel informed that It is too early to give an accurate
assessment on.the impact of safeguard measures on the domestic steel industry. However price
hike does not seem to be a possibility. On the contrary as a result of the US action, about 18-20
million tons of steel may get redirected to other unprotected markets like India and further
depress the market.

17.1.4. .India has been totally excluded from the scope of safeguard action taken by the US
Government except for the category of export of carbon flanges. India exported Rs. 60 crore
worth of carbon steel flanges in the year 2000 as against a peak level of Rs.1865 crore worth of
total steel exports to the US. Since the export of carbon steel flanges from India to the US has
been small, the inclusion of this product under safeguard action may not have significant
implication for the Indian industry.

17.1.5.Ministry of Steel has requested Department of Commerce that in view of the threat to the
domestic industry arising due to the safeguard measures taken by the US, the following steps may
be considered for immediate implementation:

(i) The floor price for import of seconds/defectives steel products operative under the
current EXIM Policy 1997-2002, under Notification No. 31(RE-99) dated 1*
November, 1999 should be incorporated in the new EXIM Policy which is to be
announced shortly.

(ii) A strong surveillance system needs to be introduced to prevent an anticipated rise in
steel imports. We could adopt a system like the one notified by the EU. Under the
system, imports are monitored on a quarterly basis through an automatic surveillance
document. The document is issued free of charge, to all importers, for any quantity
requested. Such a system could monitor import arrivals and help identify any surge in
import of steel item.

17.1.6. The Committee appreciates the efforts of Ministry of Steel for taking up the matter of
imposition of US tariff on steel industry and offsetting its adverse impact on Indian domestic
steel Industry . The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Commerce should consider
speedily the suggestion of the Ministry of Steel seriously with a view to help the steel industry of
the country which is alternatively passing through a rough phase .

17.4 Advanced Licence Scheme

17.4.1. Under the Export- Import Policy in -force, an advance license is issued (by Directorate
General of Foreign Trade) under the Duty Exemption Scheme to allow import of inputs/raw
materials duty free for actual use in the export product. Advance License as the name implies is
issued in advance for import of inputs/ raw materials against specific orders in respect of Physical
Exports, Intermediate Supplies and Deemed Export. It can also be issued on the basis of projected
annual requirement for exports/ supplies in accordance with the specified conditions.

17.4.2.The scheme has been found beneficial by the industry including the Iron and Steel
industry, as they are able to import duty free raw materials/inputs for export production.
However, large-scale import of iron and steel items particularly, seconds and defectives of flat
rolled products at very low prices have been adversely affecting the interest of the iron and steel
industry. The Ministry has noticed this abuse of the scheme. Since the Ministry of Commerce
monitors the scheme, this lacuna has been brought to their notice.

17.5. Export Incentive

17.5.1. Commenting on the suggestion that the export incentive (WTO compatible) that clearly
establish a nexus between import of raw materials and export of finished products are introduced
as has been done in USA and EU the Ministry of Steel agreed to the suggestion. An export
incentive scheme, which is WTO compatible, will help Indian Steel Exporters by removing the
threat of imposition of CVD duties on their exports. It will simultaneously help them to be
competitive in the international market and also help them boost their exports.

17.6. Planning to raise prices of steel products

17.6.1. There are reports that the Indian steel companies are planning to raise prices of their
products in the range of Rs. 500- Rs.1000 per ton in the domestic market in response to the rise in
prices of the same in the international market. The Indian steel prices are to be influenced by the
following factors as well.

(a) Rise in domestic demand for steel

(b) Depreciation of the rupee, that makes imports expensive at a given dollar
denominated price.

(c) Reduction in inventory

17.6.2. The Committee recommends that Indian Steel PSUs, while keeping an eye to the world
price index of steel products , should keep on revising the price of Indian steel products under a
definite marketing strategy.

17.7. Progress made in regard to consideration of the "Buy Indian Steel Act" in order to protect
Indian Steel Industry.

59


17.7.1. Ministry of Steel is proposing enactment of a legislation - “Buy India Act” with the
objective to encourage growth and development of indigenous industry by giving preference to
indigenous steel producers in Government procurement. The legislation would apply to all
projects, industrial or business enterprises set up or to be setup with the grant and aid of public
money. The act stipulates that all such industrial and business enterprises would procure iron &
steel material indigenously for their requirement unless such materials are not available in the
country in the specified quality or within required delivery schedule or contrary to public interest
or detrimental to the project. The use of non- indigenous iron and steel materials for such projects
are to be cleared by Ministry of Steel, Government of India.

17.7.2. The Draft Legislation was circulated for comments to Ministry of Commerce & Industry,
Department of Finance and DGFT. While DGFT as proposed a few modifications in the Draft
Legislation, Ministry of Finance have stated that they do not support the proposed legislation,
Ministry of Commerce have suggested to pend the proposal for the time being. In the meantime,
since the legislation is based on the lines of ‘Buy America Act’ inputs from EOI/Washington on
the operational aspects of the Act have been sought to examine the proposal further.

17.7.3.The Committee feels that the Buy Indian Steel act’ would prove a long way in the
promotion of domestic steel industry and the Government of India in general and Ministry of
Finance in particular should not hesitate in the enactment of the legislation.

17.8 Future Outlook of Indian Steel Industry vis-a-vis emerging Global Steel Scenario.

17.8.1. There are tentative signals that the global steel market is on its way up. The prices of
most steel products in the international markets have increased. For example, the export prices of
HR coils, as per information available from World Steel Dynamics and other market intelligence
reports, have increased from about $165 per tonne to about $195 per tonne. The prices for
Japanese mill products are still higher. There are reports that this price increase has been backed
by definite increase in demand/consumption. In response to the increased demand and prices, the
crude steel production globally has also risen.

17.8.2. There are reports that steel consumption in India in the recent months have
increased. As per the latest report of the Joint Plant Committee, the consumption of
finished steel during April- February 2001-02 have increased by 1.9 per cent over the
corresponding period last year. Exports of finished steel have also increased 2.7 percent.
Stock of steel with the main producers has also dropped marginally during February
2002. The steel makers are reportedly planning price hikes in response to the
strengthening of the market within the country as well as outside it.

17.8.3. The demand for steel is expected to increase by 6 per cent in the coming year ( 2002-03 ).
According to the study of the 10" Five Year Plan Working Group on Minerals, carbon steel
demand in the country is expected to maintain an annual growth rate of 6 per cent over the plan
period. Demand for steel will be supported by increased investment on infrastructure, increased
demand for consumer durables and automobiles and residential and industrial construction.

17.8.4. The growth rate of steel consumption in India is expected to remain higher than the global
average in the coming years. Despite increased threat of protectionism worldwide, the Indian
industry will remain dependent on the conditions in the world market. Increased export
opportunities and the emerging competitive strength of the industry will also shape the growth
pattern of the Indian industry

17.8.5. The Committee is pleased to note that global steel scenario is improving and thus
coming out of recession.

without any tangible outcome has resulted. The Committee is of the view that while other steel
plants have undergone modernisation process, IISCO continues to operate through conventional
method with outdated and traditional machinery and equipments. Physical and financial
performance alongwith various financial ratios and liabilities of the company against its assets
are indicative of the fact that ISCO is reeling & reins amidst adverse financial scenario
and is only awaiting a gloomy future unless some substantial steps are taken immediately.
The Committee observes that SAIL and Government has already taken unreasonably time only
in coming up with a final rehabilitation package, although revival of IISCO is also a part of
the Financial and Business restructuring package for SAIL which, inter-alia envisaged write off
of loans and advances of SAIL/GOI to IISCO for Rs.1946.17 crore as on April, 1, 1999. The
Committee has been given to understand that M/s TYZHPROMEXPORT (TPE) remains the
sole contender for joint venture and a simultaneous revival proposal prepared by SAIL is also

1.         History  is a witness to the fact  that  minerals  have  been the  basis of classification of human  civilization.   A
civilization undertakes development  in consonance with a pattern of physical  endowment of valuable minerals like Copper,
Iron Ore,  Aluminium,  Zinc, Lead, Gold,   Cobalt, Manganese, Graphite, Lime Stone, platinum etc.    Since minerals resources
are wealth hidden   beneath the earth-curst and are wasting assets    their conservation and planned   exploitation is of
paramount importance to  national economic development and growth .  As a matter of fact,  mineral resources not only provide
the basic inputs to domestic industry,  but also account for sizeable export and foreign exchange earnings.  Henceforth, the
development and regulation of the mineral sector is concomitant to the optimal utilisation of resources which ensures all round
development and growth of national economy.
1.1.      The Department of   Mines is  responsible for development and regulation of the mineral sector including  the mining
and metallurgy     of all non-ferrous metals both in private and public  sectors, but excluding   natural Gas, Petroleum, Coal and
Atomic   minerals.  As per the Annual Report (2001-02) of   the Department of Mines  has been   allotted subjects  as under:-
Legislation for regulation  of mines and development  of    minerals within the territory of  India, including   mines    and
minerals  underlying the ocean within the territorial waters  or the continental shelf, or the Exclusive Economic zone and other
Maritime Zones of  India as may be specified from time to  time by or under any law made by Parliament.
Regulation  of mines and development of minerals   other than coal,  lignite and sand  for  stowing and any minerals declared as
prescribed substances for the  purposes  of the  Atomic Energy Act, 1962 (33 of 1962)  under the control of the Union as
declared by law,   including   questions concerning  regulation and development of minerals in various states and the matter
connected therewith with or incidental thereto.
All other metals and minerals not  specifically allotted to any  other Ministry/ Department  such as aluminium, zinc , copper,
gold, diamond and nickel.
Planning development and control of  and assistance to all industries dealt with by the Department.
At the Secretariat level  the  Department of Mines is  mainly engaged in direction, supervision and coordination of five
divisions which inter-alia include Survey and Exploration,  Mines, Metal, General Administration and Finance and Accounts
Division.   Survey and Exploration has two principle agencies i.e. Geological Survey of India (GSI) and Mineral Exploration
Corporation Ltd. (MECL) for the implementation of the programmes of this division while Mines Division has one  subordinate
office to implement the programmes of the division, viz. Indian Bureau of Mines (IBM). Metal division of the Department of
Mines deals with the planning, exploration, development, monitoring of programmes and research in respect of non-ferrous
metals both in the public and private sectors General Administration Division is mainly concerned with the establishment and
administrative matter of the Department and Finance and Accounts Division is concerned with the budget, financial scrutiny of
projects and other proposals, rendering financial advice and maintenance and compilation of accounts.
Department of Mines has two  subordinate offices, namely :-
Geological  Survey of India ( HQ Kolkata)
Indian Bureau of Mines (HQ Nagpur)

1.7.      The Committee notes the structural and functional pattern of the Department of   Mines,   the  Secretariat  for the 
Department of  Mines and  is of the  view  that structural aspect must  match the functional requirements and working   of  the 
organisation with adequate degree  of co-ordination and collaboration   among  various units  thus contributing as their  part    in
the overall functioning of the organisation in the interest of national  economy .
1.8.      The Committee, in view  that Bharat Gold Mines Ltd. has  been closed since 14
th March, 2001,  SMC stands transferred
to Department of  Development of  North Eastern Region,   BALCO since, March, 2001 and Hindustan Zinc Ltd. since April,
2002 has already been    disinvested  and NALCOs  and HCL   are   on the  verge of disinvestment, it is  the right  time  for the
Government  to undertake   the programme for  massive  rationalisation of  manpower not only at the level of  PSUs but also at
the level of Department  of Mines .
1.9.      The Committee was informed that the Department of Mines is enjoined to legislate for regulation of mines and
development of minerals within the territory of India including mines and minerals underlying the ocean within the territorial
waters or the continental shelf or the exclusive economic zone and other maritime zones of India as may be specified from time
to time by or under any law made by the Parliament.   Further, the Department is enjoined the task of regulation of mines and
development of non-fuel and non-atomic minerals including questions concerning regulating and development of minerals in
various States and the matter connected therewith or incidental thereto. The Department further has the responsibility for
overall development of all metals and minerals not specifically allotted to any other Ministry or Department (i.e., development
of aluminium, zinc, lead, copper and diamond, etc.). The Department has been allocated the work of Geological Survey of India
which is the premier agency in earth sciences in the country. The Department enforces the regulatory measures on all mines
pertaining to subjects under its charge including iron ore, through Indian Bureau of Mines.
 
1.10.    The Committee was further informed the Department of Mines is enjoined to look after planning, development and
control of and assistance to all industries dealt with by the Department including the Public Sector Undertakings.  It is obvious,
therefore, the role of the Department of Mines is not restricted to direct, supervise and coordinate the PSUs, which is only a
part  of its overall role and function  in the Government. Therefore disinvestment of PSUs, closure of BGML and transfer of
SMC to the Department of  Development of North Eastern  Region will allow the Department of Mines to focus on its areas of
core competence, i.e.  survey and exploration of all minerals other than natural gas,  petroleum and atomic minerals, administer
the mining statutes as well as enter into new areas and develop competence in, after the Off Shore Areas Mineral (Development
and Regulation) law comes into effect. The Bill stands  already introduced in the Parliament.
1.11.      The Committee understands the  core  function of Department of Mines , however,     the real  question arises  
whether  a separate Department is required for discharging the  core function only .  The Committee is of the  firm view  that
the  existence  of structure of any  department   presently  the   Department of Mines, must  justify itself  through  discharging  
its corresponding duties and function since  this involves substantial  financial implications. 
1.12.    When the Committee  asked the Department  of Mines  to comment on the  proposal of transferring National Mineral
Development  Corporation Ltd.  (NMDC) , Kudremukh Iron  Ore Company Ltd., Manganese Ore  (India) Ltd. and
Metallurgical  &  Engineering Consultants India Ltd. (MECON)  from Ministry of Steel to Department of Mines  in order to
rationalise the allocation of business of Government. The Department of Mines stated that since the subject matter relating to
legislation, regulation and concessions of manganese and iron ore is allocated to the Department of Mines and level playing
field between public and private sector companies are to be ensured therefore it is anomalous that public sector undertakings in
this area namely; NMDC, MOIL, Kudremukh Iron Ore Company Ltd. are dealt with by the Ministry of Steel whereas all the
private sector companies and necessary legislative and regulatory work be dealt with by the Deptt. of Mines.  A proposal
therefore has been submitted to the Cabinet Secretariat for transfer of these public sector undertakings, which are also slated to
be disinvested in due course of time, to the Deptt. of Mines, Ministry of Coal & Mines. 
1.13.    Reacting  to the proposal of  integration / merger of  Geological Survey of India, Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd.
and India  Bureau of Mines  (IBM)  and the same is transferred either to  Ministry of Steel and  Coal or Petroleum with suitable 
change in the name of the Ministry Department of Mines explained that Geological Survey of India, Mineral Exploration
Corporation and Indian Bureau of Mines are mandated to take up different and specific responsibilities which cannot be
merged. GSI is a scientific organization serving as the principal provider of basic Earth Science information to Government,
Industry and general public.  MECL is a commercial organization for mineral exploration, whereas IBM is an arm of the
Government to enforce the legislations and regulations pertaining to MMRD Act and Rules thereunder.   Geological Survey of
India’s areas of activity include scientific survey and research for locating mineral resources and geological studies while IBM
is primarily responsible for promotion and conservation of scientific development of mineral resources of the country.  The
basic aim of MECL is to bridge the gap between preliminary exploration of mineral prospect and its commercial exploitation. 
From this   it is clear that these are responsible for development and regulation of mineral sector including the mining and
metallurgy of non-ferrous metals both in private and public sector excluding natural gas, petroleum and atomic minerals and
this cannot be transferred to the Ministry of Steel, Coal or Petroleum as these Ministries have been allotted specific charters.
1.14.    The Committee  understands  that GSI, IBM and MECL have their specific charter  of function but it is also true that
MECL  is   an  offshoot of GSI and later on created a separate body to supplement GSI .Moreover, GSI, and  MECL  work  not
only for the    Department of Mines  but also for  Department of Coal and  Ministry of Petroleum  .  The Committee is  of the
view that possibility of integration of  GSI, IBM and MECL may be explored and the  efforts may be made for  rationalising 
of  non-plan expenditure.  The Committee is of the further view that GSI  MECL and IBM may  co-exist  under one organic

71st Report

unit and may remain either in the Department of  coal or petroleum  or Mines discharging  their  roles as mentioned  in their
respective  charter   of function   intact and in original  form.  The Committee opines   that GSI, MECL  and IBM  may be
integrated with  their   differential roles under one  umbrella  and which would not only rationalise   the  non-plan  expenditure 
but also  inject synergy  and enhancement of  brand  endowment.
1.15.    Under the circumstance, the  Committee recommends that  Government should immediately constitue  a  Task Force
having representatives from Department of Coal, Mines, Petroleum   and Steel   to examine the following issues:-
Determination of continuation of Department of Mines with a view  to discharge its  core function;
Feasibility and desirability of integration/merger of GSI, IBM and MECL  and  transferring of  same to either   of  Department
of Coal, Petroleum or Ministry of  Steel.
Transfer of  NMDC, KIOCL, MOIL and MECON from the Ministry of Steel  to Department of Mines.  
Merger of Department of Mines , coal and steel.
1.16.    The  Committee recommends that the Committee be apprised of the  findings    of Task Force and thereafter  the
Committee would   form its final opinion after examination the  findings of the   task force.  The  Committee recommends that

2.2       The Committee is pleased to note that the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Department of
Mines is broadly based on the principle that extensive survey and investigation should be carried out in the field of minerals in
which the country is deficient or which are of strategic importance for the country.  Besides this, the need for advance
exploration and prospecting techniques in the field of geophysical and geo-chemical methods has been envisaged and
participation of domestic and foreign private explorators  and prospectors has been stressed.  Simultaneously, the need for
modernisation and upgradation of technical skills of the organisations like GSI, MECL, IBM and some of the State Department
of Mines and Geology has been planned. In the field of mineral output , stress has been laid on recycling of metal scraps and
enhancement of smelting capacities of metals like aluminium, lead & zinc, copper, steel and Ferro alloys has been taken into
consideration.  Stress has also been laid on development of dimension and decorative stones, mining and processing industry,
minerals required for advanced ceramic and glasses, abrasive minerals and materials, high purity metals alloys and electronic
materials based on minerals. Development of infrastructure is another important issue on which stress has been laid on annual
plan 2002-03.  States are being encouraged to ensure proper linkage of raw material to the industry along with development of
necessary basic infrastructure. In the field of mineral administration, with the desired level of amendments in the Acts and
Rules governing mineral sector, the environment is highly congenial for both domestic and foreign investors. With these
measures, the budget proposals for the year 2002-03 pertaining to the Department of Mines, are expected to prove as an
instrument to march forward towards the national goal of overall development in the era of liberalised and globalised economy.
