7.1.1.   The Geological Survey of India (GSI), a premier National Scientific Survey and Research Organisation is the principal
provider of basic earth science information to the government, industry and the general public, as well as responsive participant
in international geo-scientific fora .Set up in 1851 with the sole direction to locate coal for the railways, the GSI over the years
has expanded its role particularly after independence towards elucidation of the geo-scientific set-up of the country, locating
and harnessing the mineral  resources , providing geo-scientific information for the power (thermal, hydro, geothermal and
nuclear), agricultural, irrigation etc. sectors ,management of risks due to natural hazards such as floods, landslides and
earthquakes
defining and delineating areas prone to environmental degradation , providing geological inputs to optimise developments in
the transport and communication sector , geo-scientific studies and inventory of resources in the Exclusive Economic Zone
(EEZ) as well as in extended continental shelf in the surrounding ocean and also the icy continent of Antarctica glaciological
study ,dissemination of Information through map and publication ,training of scientific manpower. The prime activity of GSI
has resulted in coverage of 98.23% of the country (out of total map able area of 3.146 million sq. km.)  by geological mapping
in 1:50,000/63,360 scale 96% of Exclusive Economic Zone in the surrounding ocean (2.02 million sq. km.) 1.5 million sq. km
by aero-geophysical survey .
7.1.2.   GSI has been associated with discovery of almost all major mineral deposits in the country other than oil, gas and
atomic minerals Several Public Sector Undertakings, like HZL, HCL, NALCO, BALCO, Coal & Nevyeli Lignite Corporations,
NMDC etc. were established to exploit the mineral resources discovered by GSI. The vibrant Steel, Coal, Cement, Aluminium,
Copper-Lead-Zinc, Fertilizer, Chemical industries which expanded phenomenally in post-independence era, bear eloquent
testimony to GSI’s sustained efforts towards augmentation of mineral resource base. Value of mineral production increased
from Rs. 7 crore in 1951 to more than Rs. 25,300 crore (excluding petroleum and natural gas) presently, which may mainly be
attributed to the continuous efforts of GSI in augmenting the resource base of the country. Identification of off-shore resources
like heavy mineral placers, lime mud, phosphate rich sediments, micro nodules, calcareous sediments, etc. having mining
potentiality. GSI is conducting site specific environmental impact assessment studies in mining projects. The major mineral
sectors were brought under public control and primary responsibility of mineral exploration (except that of Oil, Gas and Atomic
minerals) was entrusted to GSI. In this context it may be mentioned that the nucleus of the ONGC and the Atomic-Mineral
Division were created in GSI, and later developed into independent organisations .The contribution of GSI in mineral industry
alone runs to enormous magnitude in terms of monetary value. Considering only 10% of resources estimated by GSI, the

augmentation of mineral resources since independence is worth more than eleven hundred thousand crore of rupees. Several
PSUs like HZL, HCL, NALCO, BALCO, COAL & Nevyeli  Lignite Corp., NMDC etc. were established to exploit the mineral
resources discovered by GSI. Major organised construction programmes in the country since independence have been for
harnessing rivers for irrigation, power and flood control. All of them have depended on geological ADVICE  from GSI.
Outstanding examples are Bhakra dam, Yamuna Valley Project, Tungabhadra, Nagarjun Sagar, Indravaty and many more. GSI
is presently associated with major projects like Tehri, Thein, Naptha Jhakri, Sardar Sarovar, soil  erosion of Ganga etc. and
several micro-hydel projects of North Eastern Region. As such GSI contributed its mite to this paramount national endeavour,
which ushered in the Green Revolution.

10.6.    Pertaining to the Committee's query  as to what extent the research projects does stress the generation and development
of indigenous technology  to lessen the technology-import syndrome the Department of Mines stated that the criteria for
selection of S&T projects is to cater to the national requirement and develop technologies which are not available for import
due to either strategic or commercial reasons. The details of major projects are given below:-
Development of technology for extraction of nickel from chromite overburden of Sukinda:- Sukinda Valley in Orissa is the
only known source for nickel in the country. Even in this the nickel content is less than 1% and the ore is oxidic in nature.
Nowhere in the world such an ore is exploited commercially. A process has been developed indigenously and the critical
parameters of the process have been tested in a pilot plant established at RRL, Bhubaneshwar. National Aluminium Company
under the Department of Mines is examining further the commercial viability of the process.
Setting up of a national facility for semi solid forming at IISC, Bangalore:- The semi-solid forming technology is the latest
technology used for manufacturing aluminium auto components. The technology is closely guarded and is available for import
only at a very high price, though the components made using this technology are available freely for import at high prices. A
National facility is being set up to develop semi solid forming  technology indigenously. Various auto manufacturers and
research organizations like Indian Space Research Organisation, DMRL have been involved in the development of the project
to ensure gainful use of the facilities.

10.10.  The Committee  reiterates its recommendations made in  its  38
th Report  on Demands for Grants (2000-01) that while   
it  is rational for  grants in aid to research projects  and provision of funds for awards  but at the same time opines that
autonomous and scientific  bodies should generate revenue to meet non-plan expenditure.  In  this regard  JNARRDC, 
National  Institute of  Rock Mechanics (NIRM) and  National Institute of Miner's Health (NIMH)  should generate sufficient
fund to meet their requirement of non-plan  expenditure.  In today's  commercial world service is regarded as product so these
scientific  institutions should open avenues  for  generating revenue by providing consultancy services.  By  diversification and
exploring the possibility of service  mix, these  institutions may go for  service endowment  in the field  of  consultancy,
training and ideas for project generation.  They should become the  seller of    ideas  and once the measures click they may
reign and  rule  in the    world   market of ideas.  On the  whole the committee is of the  view  that scientific institutions  should 
create  opportunity for extending consultancy service and help Government  in pruning  of non-plan expenditure.
10.11.  The Committee is aware  that research and development is an on-going   process, however, the  outcome thereof should
benefit the present civilization and that is  possible  only when adequate degree of intellectual honesty is involved  in the
research process.  Research  is  carried  out not just  for the sake of research but for the  benefit and welfare of human being. 
Research  and  development in mining field can  not  only provide cost  effective  tools and technology but may  go in a long
way for   management  of    eco-friendly environment.  The Committee would like to recommend that the  Department of
Mines  should have definite  "Research & Technology Mission"  which should act as the   storehouse of mining  related
`experiments and  observations'  and knowledge   and experience skimmed of such  Mission would be helpful in removing the
problems being  faced by mining sector.

12.0.    Entry of foreign investors in non-ferrous mining sector 
12.1.    Besides a number of domestic entrepreneurs, a large number of foreign investors have shown interest in the non-ferrous
metals, precious metals and diamond-mining sector in the country.  With the introduction of the concept of aerial geophysical
prospecting over large area the mineral policy and the Acts and Rules governing mineral survey were modified to allow
Reconnaissance Permit over large areas to ascertain the possibilities of these minerals.  Till February 2001 65 Prospecting
Licences for aerial prospecting over 90,000 sq. km area were granted in 7 states.  Besides 41 Reconnaissance Permits were
approved over an area of 11,200 sq. km in the state of Rajasthan, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
12.2.    Foreign Investment Promotion Board
The Foreign Investment Promotion Board has approved 70 applications for foreign investment in the mineral sector involving
investment of over 770 million US$ which includes 11 proposals from Australia, 5 from Canada, 8 from UK, 8 from USA, 6
from South Africa besides proposals from other foreign countries.
12.3.    The Committee appreciates  the  efforts made by the Department of Mines towards making the  mining sector more  
investor friendly  but  at the same time hopes that  pace of foreign  investment  in the mining sector may be   accelerated.

17.0     Impact of withdrawal of the SSI exemption   on   granite in the budget 2002-03 on the granite industry
17.1.    In the budget 2002-03 Excise Duty exemption available to small scale units upto a  limit of one crore turnover has been
removed and therefore all small scale and cottage scale granite industry come under the net of excise duty @ 16%.  Coupled
with already increased cost, adverse effect of recession in last few years and signing of WTO agreement and dumping of
vitrified ceramic titles and  granite from China had already affected the domestic market.
17.2.The All India Granite and Stone Association has reported that there are approx 5 thousand granite units in small scale and
cottage scale sector/tiny scale entrepreneurs having an investment ranging from Rupees 5 lakhs to Rupees 60 lakhs each.  If
these units have to pay excise duty, many of these would become unviable resulting in unemployment of over 3 lakhs people
working in the industry.   Many of the units in small scale and cottage scale cater to local market directly and export market
indirectly and thus even exports too will suffer.   In larger interest, therefore, restoration of excise  exemption limit up to Rs. 1
crore has been prayed.
17.3.    The Committee observes that the exemption of  excise duty on small scale  and  cottage scale granite  industry upto limit
of Rs.1.00 crore in the  budget 2002-03 has  rendered  5 thousand granite units in  complete  doldrums and employment of  3
lakh workers  is in jeopardy.  The Committee has been given to understand  that SSI  granite industry is already reeling under 
high cost of production, adverse  affect of  recession  and  dumping of  cheaper   product  from China and the  withdrawal of the
SSI exemption  on granite SSI  sector would  further   hit the granite SSI  sector adversely.  Therefore, the Committee
recommends,  that the Government would  take due  note of the provisions  enshrined  in the  budget 2002-03 and  do justice  to
the granite SSI  industry.

REPORT
1          The Department of Heavy Industry is concerned with the development of the Heavy Engineering Industries, Machine Tool Industries, Heavy Electrical Industries, Industrial Machineries and Auto-Industries. The Industries covered by this Department provide goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy, including power, rail and road transport. They also cater to the requirements of equipment for basic industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, textiles, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is responsible for the development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engines, industrial gears and gearboxes. It is also vested with the administrative charge of 49 Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs).
1.1       The PSEs under the administrative control of the Department are engaged in the manufacturing of Engineering/Capital Goods, Consultancy and Contracting Activities. The total investment (Gross Block) in 49 Public Sector Enterprises under the Department of Heavy Industry was about Rs.8052.00 Crores till 31ST March, 2001 employing about 1,46,558 lakh persons.
1.2       The Department holds interactions with various Industry Councils and evolves Plans for their growth. The Department also assists Public Sector Enterprises through policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariffs and trade, technological collaboration, up- gradation and Research & Development, etc.

The Department further informed the Committee that in the event of any shortfall in the requirement of capital investment, additional funds will be sought at the RE stage.  
2.2       Budgeted Plan outlay and Actual expenditure during the year 2001-02 up to January 2002 PSEs-wise for the Department of Heavy Industry for the year 2001-02 has been given in Annexure- I. 
2.3          It was   stated by the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises that the performance of PSEs had been below the projected levels primarily due to the shortage of orders and working capital, high cost of production, inability to face competition and excessive manpower
2.4       The PSEs of Heavy Industry informed the Committee that there are 15 profit making PSEs under DHI such as BHEL, B&R, BRAITHWAITE, BBJ, BHPV, EPI, HPC, HMT (Holding.), HMT (I), HMT (B), HNL, Hooghly Printing Press, REIL, SIL & TSP whereas loss making PSEs under DHI are 34 which include CCI, HEC, HPC, MAMC, RIC, CCIL & TCIL etc.
2.5       The Committee noted that many of the Central PSEs are making losses due to their inability to their face the competition, obsolete R&D, high cost of production, shortage of work orders, etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry should infuse capital, state of the art technology and entrepreneurship into  potentially viable PSEs so as the make these `Modern Temples' capable to face the private sector MNCs in the  consumer economy.2.6       In the wake of growing financial   crunch in many of the Central PSEs, the Committee recommends that the Government should provide financial assistance in the form of working capital, Non-Plan loan, Government guarantee, etc.  to  PSEs which are potentially viable.
2.7     In order to overcome the constraints of the Central PSEs, concerted efforts have been made including restructuring of various Heavy Industry PSEs. The BIFR has sanctioned revival plans   in the case of 12 PSEs, which are under implementation.  On its own Government has approved restructuring in seven other cases. Action has been initiated for converting 28 PSEs into Joint Ventures/disinvestment. As a last resort, seven unviable PSEs have been closed. Unviable units of some of the   PSEs have also been        closed. Government has approved reservation of orders for Hindustan Cable Ltd. from DOT/MTNL and from BSNL for Instrumentation Ltd. Ministry of Railways   has been     persuaded to place orders for wagons on the wagon building PSEs of the Department of Heavy Industry.
2.8       The Department also stated that a White Paper defining the future of the PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry based on the Public Sector Policy of the Government is under preparation.  The Department informed the Committee that Public Sector Policy of the Government has focused on the following areas: -
·
        Restructure and revive potentially viable PSEs;
·        Bring down Govt. equity in all non-strategic PSEs to 26% or lower, if necessary;
·        Fully protect the interests of workers; and
·        Close down PSEs, which cannot be revived.
 
2.9       The Committee recommends that while rationalising the Government   equity in non-strategic PSEs, interests of the workers should be protected fully.
 
REVIVAL PLANS / FINANCIAL RESTRUCTURING OF PSEs
3          The Department informed the Committee that so far as the Central PSEs under the Department of Heavy Industry is concerned, the funds have been provided for as per the restructuring plan approved by the Government/BIFR. It was informed that allocations are being made in the budget for each year based on the requirements projected in the restructuring exercise and funds released.  In the case of any additional requirement, the Department of Heavy Industry stated that funds would be sought/released by way of supplementary grant/re-appropriation.  A  lump sum provision of Rs.150.00 crores has been made in the budget 2002-03 for meeting the funds requirement for the implementation of restructuring plans that may be approved by the Government and BIFR.
3.1       During the oral evidence, the Secretary in reply to a question stated  “Rs.250.00 crores have been earmarked for Voluntary Retirement Schemes and Rs.150.00 crores for revival scheme.”  The Secretary, Ministry of Heavy Industries, informed the Committee  “the revival plan, restructuring/JV formulation exercises move at different pace in each PSE and it is difficult to assume that certain PSEs will conclude the exercise and that this will be the requirement. In earlier years, there used to be company-wise allocation and then we were to go back to the Finance Ministry for re-appropriation. However, this time I had requested the Finance Ministry to give us the flexibility to make allocation PSE-wise.”3.2       The Committee noted that in budget 2002-03, the PSE wise allocations have not been made for various schemes in these PSEs.   This flexibility of lump-sum financial allocations given to DHI is, indeed, a new practice.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should not discriminate while allocating the funds to the Central PSEs.

RESEARCH & DEVELOPMENT OF AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY      
4          The Department stated that R&D and technology development is the backbone of the Automotive Industry. Because of this fact, a cess had been imposed on Automobiles with effect from 1st January 1984 and on tractors from 1st October 1985 at the rate of 18% advalorem to finance R&D in the industry. The cess is being collected by the Department of Revenue and forms part of the Consolidated Fund of India. The Ministry of Finance is allocating a portion of this fund through the Budget to the DHI under the Head of Account ‘Cess’ for the Development Council for Automobile and Allied Industries.
4.1       It was stated by the Department that with the fragmented automobile industry in India, it is not feasible for the individual units to establish full-fledged R&D set up and testing facilitates. Hence there is a need to establish R&D testing facilities, which will cater to the industry as a whole. With the introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards, more & more R&D facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of the Industry.   The Department further added that the Development Council for Automotive and Allied Industry (DCAAI) allocates Cess funds for research and development to establish R&D institutions through a Cess Committee chaired by Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry. 
4.2       The Department has informed the Committee that with progressive introduction of new and stricter emission norms as well as safety standards, more and more testing facilities are needed in the country to meet the demand of  Industry. There is also a need to look at other areas of product and process related research with a view to propelling India’s Automotive Industry into a higher league and for surviving the import surge under WTO regime. The plan-budget will be used to these areas of concern.
4.3       The Department also informed the Committee that the Government has adopted the following Policies to encourage the testing facilities for Auto Sector:
·        Budget enhanced from Rs.8.00 crores in 2001-02 to Rs.25 crores in 2002-03
·        Facilities to be provided at 6 or 7 different Centres in the country at a total cost of Rs.700.00 crores to meet regulations relating to safety and emission norms.
·        Plan component during the 10th Five Year Plan is Rs.350.00 crores and balance will be met from the non-plan from cess fund.
4.4       The Department further added that at present the cess is levied @ 1/8% i.e. 0.125% over and above the excise duty.   In difference to the recommendations made by the Committee last year, Department of Heavy Industry has already taken up the matter with the Ministry of Finance for (i) enhancement in the rate of levy of cess from 0.05% to 0.25% and (ii) for increasing the allocation of collected cess to that Department. While the Finance Ministry has enhanced the allocation of cess from the existing level of Rs.10.00 crores to Rs.25.00 crores in the Budget Estimates for the financial year 2002-03, the rate of cess has not been revised.
4.5       The Committee has noted that the cess to improve R&D in Automotive   Industry has been increased from Rs.10.00 crores to Rs.25.00 crores in the budget estimates of 2002-03.  However, the rate of cess has not been revised from 0.05% to 0.25% over   and above the excise   duty    as earnestly demanded by the automotive sector.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should, at the first instance, take up this matter with the Ministry of Finance and resolve to save the automotive industry.
4.6       The Department further stated that there is an urgent need to ensure higher commitment on research and development activities by the industry in the emerging circumstances. At present industry is spending only about 0.2% of their sales turnover on research and development. In most developed countries the spending on R&D in automobile sector ranges between 3% to 4%.  Realising this fact the Government has provided for special incentives to research and development activities in the Auto Policy, which has been announced recently.
4.7       The Committee is constrained to note that the Indian Automotive Industry is spending only 0.2% of their sales   turnover on R&D as against 3% to 4% spent by most auto industries in the developed Countries.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should create a separate corpus of funds to meet the emerging requirements of R&D of the auto industries.
4.8       It was informed by the Department that the cess funds have been used to create necessary infrastructure for the automotive sector. The infrastructure created includes facilities for testing of vehicle for the purpose of assessing their conformity to the Central Motor Vehicles Rules. The objectives of the Cess funded projects range from testing vehicles for roadworthiness, to testing of components and sub-assemblies from the angle of safety and environmental protection. Keeping in view these objectives, cess funds have been utilized over the years to strengthen the capability of the research institutes in Automotive Sector-particularly Automotive Research Association of India (ARAI), Pune; Vehicle Research Development Establishment (VRDE), Ahmednagar and Central Institute of Road Transport (CIRT), Pune, which undertake testing of new vehicles for their homologation i.e. testing of various components and vehicle parameters to check compliance with Central Motor Vehicle Rules (CMVR) requirements and road worthiness. This Department is working on National Testing facility in consultation with concerned agencies like Society of Indian Automobile Manufacturers (SIAM) etc. to meet the emerging requirements.4.9       The Department informed the Committee that DHI has taken the following efforts to enhance the R&D facilities:
Ø
                  A National Project on `coal gasification’ for power generation has been included in Budget 2002-03. Development of this technology will result in: -
·        Better utilisation of high ash content Indian coal.
·        Improvement in efficiency.

4.10     The Committee notes that cess funds have been   utilised over the years to strengthen the infrastructure of the research institutes of ARAI, VRDE, CIRT, etc.  for testing of various   auto components to meeting regulations relating to safety and emission norms.  The Committee recommends   that Department of  Heavy Industry should analyse the results achieved by these Institutes in the field of testing new vehicles for their homologations from the safety and environment point of view and take appropriate measures.
4.11     It may be pointed out that Electric Vehicles (E.V.s) are making their  own contribution towards making our environment free from pollution. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Excise Duty on 3-wheeler Electric Vehicles may be reduced from existing 16% to 1 %. The Committee also recommends that the Basic Customs Duty on components of the Electric Vehicle may be reduced from the existing 15- 35% to 5%.
4.12     In the Auto Policy, compatible with WTO guidelines, which were announced by the Government on 7th March 2002 it has been indicated that as an impetus for the development of electric vehicles, an appropriate long term fiscal structure shall be put in place to facilitate their acceptance vis-à-vis vehicles based on conventional fuels. Already Scooters India Limited, a Public Sector Enterprises, is running a pilot project with financial assistance from the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources for establishing commercial viability of the battery run three wheeler vehicles.
4.13     The objectives of the Auto Policy as announced by the Department of Heavy Industry on 7th March, 2002 are as under: -
·        Promoting a globally competitive Auto Industry and developing India as a major source of World class auto components.
·        100% Foreign Direct Investment without any minimum capitalisation norms now permitted in this Sector.
·        other significant objectives of the Policy are higher value addition through appropriate fiscal measures, promotion of low emission fuel technologies, alternative fuels and hybrid vehicles.
4.14     The Committee has noted that Auto Policy was approved after a long period. The Committee also took note of the  criticism of the Policy by the media mainly for non-prescribing specific fiscal measures for growth of the Industry.  The Auto Policy talks of India emerging as a hub for small car production but  has not made  any  proposal which will achieve this objective. The Committee noted that Brazil and Japan have extended substantial fiscal incentives in the form of tax relief to encourage small car production in their countries which has helped them raise their annual production level by 2 to 3 times. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government may consider extension of similar fiscal incentives for strengthening of the small car industry.
4.15     The Committee recommends that the Government should give impetus to develop and promote the indigenous technology in the auto-sector. The Committee also recommends that the government should   be cautious in inviting the 100% FDI in the auto-industry by protecting the interests of the domestic auto industries.VOLUNTARY SEPARATION SCHEME AND STATUTORY    DUES

th July 1999; it was informed by the Department of Heavy Industry that the Department had earlier taken up this matter with the Ministry of Finance on the basis of request from the players in the Capital Goods Sector. This issue was once again taken up with the Ministry of Finance pursuant to the recommendations made by Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 45th Report for expediting the decision in the matter. Pre-Budget proposals of the Department for Union Budget (2002-03) included rescinding of Notification No. 85/99 dated 6th July 1999 to provide a level playing field to the domestic industry. But so far it has not found favour with Ministry of Finance. In this connection the Department of Heavy Industry requested to rescind Customs Notification No.85/99 – CUS dated 6th July, 1999 permitting imports at zero duty & restoration of 15% domestic price preference for projects funded by multilateral funding agencies (Annexure-II).  It was also informed by the Department that …
                     i.            World Bank tenders financed under International Competitive Bidding  (ICB) provide for giving price preference to indigenous manufacturers limited to 15% or applicable import duty whichever is lower for compensating partly the local disadvantages in developing counties.
                   ii.            Through Customs Notification No.84/97 customs dated 11th November 1997 the government of India exempted all the goods imported into India by the United Nations or an International Organization for execution of the projects financed by them and approved by the govt. of India, from the whole of the duty of customs leviable thereon. This exemption was intended for small projects to bring down the costs of these projects being funded by UN/World Bank in the social/welfare sectors like Rural Health, Sanitation, Drinking water, Family planning, Primary education etc. and were low technology items.
                  iii.            The above Customs Notification, which did not affect the competitiveness of domestic capital goods manufacturers, has now been amended through a Notification No85/99 customs dated 6th July 1999. This revised notification stipulates that all projects funded by UN/World Bank/ADB shall attract NIL customs duty & has brought the zero duty regimes to “all the goods imported into India for execution of projects financed by the United Nations or an international organization”. The scope of this zero duty regime has been greatly enhanced to include even large infra-structure/commercial projects in the Power & Fertilizer sectors etc. However, World Bank guidelines provide for compensation to developing economies by allowing 15% price preference to domestic bidders or the rate of applicable customs duty, whichever is lower. Since the customs duty has been brought to zero, the price preference automatically reduces to zero, affecting the competitiveness of domestic industry and negating the compensation provided by World Bank to offset the local Infrastructural disadvantages.
                 iv.            It was therefore requested that Notification No.85/99 customs dated 6th July 1999 might be rescinded so that its scope is restricted to social sectors only. This will ensure continuance of 15% Price Preference to domestic bidders in case of UN/World Bank/ADB funded projects as per their guidelines, ALTERNATIVELY, projects funded by UN/World Bank/ADB should attract customs duty of at least 15% with “NIL” C.V.D. (i.e. CD=15% & CVD=0%).
9.7       The Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry, informed the Committee  "Zero duty is affecting the electrical engineering industry in our country. Companies from various countries are coming to our country with World Bank norms and other things. This thing this Committee have to take up with the Government and the Government has to take into consideration.”
9.8       The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers are not able to avail price preference of 15% for projects funded by international agencies like World Bank, United Nations, Asian Development Bank etc. as imports on such projects is allowed at 'nil' duty as per Notification No.85/99-customs dated 6th July, 1999. The power projects for l0th and 11th Five Year Plans are being finalised. Some of these projects may entail multilateral funding. Additional power projects of 60,000 MW during the 11th plan period are likely to be finalised. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Customs Notification No. 85/99 -custom dated 6.7.1999 should be rescinded to enable domestic manufacturers to effectively compete against foreign suppliers by taking advantage of 15% price preference provided in ICB tenders.
9.9       The Committee views this issue very seriously since it has effected zero customs duty regime applicable to all goods imported into India for execution of projects financed by the United Nations/World Bank or any other International Organisation. This amended custom duty structure has adversely affected competitiveness of the domestic Capital Goods industries.
9.10     The Committee, therefore, recommends that this anomaly needs to be rectified at the earliest possible. The Committee also recommends that if need arises then the DHI should take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance  (Department of Revenue) to revolve the log jam. The Committee further recommends that the un-resolved matter may be placed before the cabinet committee to consider the matter De-novo.
9.11       The Committee is concerned to note that the domestic manufacturers continue to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi, and high cost of finance and infrastructure bottlenecks to the extent of 18-28% while competing with imports. At present custom duty on coal mining, Fertilizer and Power projects is 5% basic custom duty + 16% CVD and 'nil' SAD. Under this structure the domestic industry is unable to claim refund of excise duty and become uncompetitive. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be no duty free import of projects and a minimum of 15% basic custom duty + 'nil' CVD + 4% SAD be imposed to enable the domestic industry to become competitive without increasing the project cost.
9.12      With respect to the special notification extending deemed export benefit of refund of terminal excise duty to projects ordered prior to 1st April, 2000, the Department of Heavy Industry informed the Committee that the Department had earlier taken up this matter with the DGFT on the basis of request from the players in the Capital Goods Sector and pursuant to the recommendations made by the Committee in its 45th Report. DGFT in their response stated that they have re-examined the matter.  In view of the fact that CVD on imports for power projects other than mega power projects has been increased to 16% in the budget announced in February, 2000. All the supplies effected from 1st April 2000 are not entitled for refund of Terminal Excise Duty.  Further, they are also contesting a Court case against M/s Malane Power Company in which the latter as well as BHEL have filed affidavits against Union of India. The matter is subjudiced and DGFT have taken the above stand. In view of these, DGFT expressed their inability to extend the benefit to power projects other than Mega Power Projects even if the Project Authorities have placed their orders prior to 1st April 2000.
9.13     The Committee regrets to note that despite persistent efforts, the issue of refund of Terminal Excise duty has not been resolved. Terminal Excise Duty (TED) to domestic suppliers to projects was provided up to March 2000. But in the Exim policy announced on 31.3.2000, refund of TED was withdrawn. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the issue of withdrawal of refund of terminal Excise duty for contracts finalised before 31.3.2000   (transition period)  may be reviewed by the Government.
9.14        The Committee has further noted very seriously  that the withdrawal of export benefit of refund of Terminal Excise Duty has adversely affected those Central PSEs/Companies whose cycle time for completion of the Projects is normally 3 to 4 years.  With the withdrawal of this refund, the Power Companies are unable to absorb the 16% Excise Duty which is quite substantial. This has been affecting adversely the functioning of all power companies and particularly the BHEL. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Government/DGFT should make a special measure for refund of terminal Excise Duty for those projects/bids, which were finalized (under International Competitive Bidding) before 31.3.2000 for maintaining the continuity of the existing Exim Policy for projects/bids affected.
9.15     The Committee noted that huge amounts of BHEL (Rs.1559.95 crores) are locked up with SEBs payable to Central PSEs causing enormous hardship to the PSE for circulation of working capital. In this regard, the Committee also noted that Montek Singh   Ahuluwalia Committee, while suggesting a one-time settlement   of dues of State Electricity Boards against Central Undertakings, has recognized BHEL’s outstanding dues. The Committee further noted that despite the concerted efforts made by BHEL to realize the amounts, the entire outstanding does not get realized in time mainly because of shortage of funds with the State agencies.
9.16     On this the Department of Heavy Industry has informed the Committee that      Power Ministry has devised a scheme for one time settlement of outstanding dues of SEBs based on the recommendation of Montek Singh Ahluwalia Committee.  Upon the request of DHI, Power Ministry in their proposal to the Government, have proposed to extend the scheme for BHEL. The scheme envisages one time settlement of outstanding dues of SEBs accumulated upto 30th September 2001, which is Rs.1559.95 Crores in the case of BHEL.
9.17        The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, in their 47th Report on Demands for Grants for the year 2001-2002, had stated that settlement of outstanding dues of Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL) from State Electricity Boards (SEBs) may be provided for in the scheme being worked out for liquidation of out standings of CPSEs on the recommendations of the Ahluwalia Committee.
9.18         The Committee, in the first instance, regrets to note that even though the Conference of Chief Minister had resolved to set up an Expert Group to recommend one time settlement of all Power Sector outstanding dues to Central PSEs and dues from Central PSEs to State Power Utilities, the Ahluwalia Committee restricted the scope of their study to one time settlement of dues relating to electricity and fuel supplied to SEBs by Central PSEs excluding Central PSEs like BHEL, PFC etc. as their dues were on the capital account.
9.19        The Committee noted that pursuant to its recommendations and efforts made by the DHI, the Ministry of Power had proposed to include the outstanding dues of BHEL and AYCL also in the scheme worked out by the Ahluwalia Committee. The Committee, however, is disappointed to note that Government has not accepted the proposal of the Ministry of Power, and has excluded BHEL/AYCL from the scheme, presumably on account of the fact that the Ahluwalia Committee had recommended one time settlement of SEBs’ dues in respect of only those Central PSEs which are supplying electricity and fuel to the SEBs.
9.20         The Committee would like to place on record its appreciation of the role played by BHEL and other Central PSEs like Andrew Yule Co. Ltd. (AYCL) over the last 40 years for development and growth of the Power Sector. The health of equipment supplying Central PSEs (BHEL, AYCL etc.) is as important for the Power Sector as that for Central PSEs supplying electricity and fuel. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends to the Government to review its decision and include EHEL and A YCL in the one time settlement scheme for outstanding dues.
9.21       The Committee also recommends that if issue of liquidation of the outstanding dues of BHEL is not resolved, then, it may be placed before the Cabinet Committee.
HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION LTD. (HPC)10        HPC was incorporated in 1970 with the objective of establishing pulp and paper and newsprint mills in the country. It has 2 units and 3 subsidiaries. Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited is in the process of removing bottlenecks and stabilizing production in its units and subsidiaries. A restructuring plan has been sanctioned.  The Committee has been informed that the provision under interest subsidy has been provided for carrying out accounting adjustment for transaction arising out of restructuring of the capital base of HPC Ltd.
10.1     During 2001-02, Rs.85.61 crores has been proposed as IEBR by HPC Ltd. The budgetary support by the Government to it is very marginal i.e. Rs.0.01 lakh. During 2001-02 the interest subsidy allocation was Rs.3.88 crores at BE which was reduced to Rs.2.80 crores at RE. 
10.2     The tentative target of company’s production during the year 2002-2003 is Rs.524.04 crores as against Rs.501.46 crores during 2001-02. The Indian Paper Manufacturers’ Association has done a study particularly on the Hindustan newsprint. If energy consumption is taken as a parameter, the Hindustan Paper Corporation Limited is the most efficient mill in the country.
10.3     The Committee admits that the Company is in dire need of financial assistance to meet its working capital requirements and for other projects in pipeline. The Committee also feels that cut/removal in the budgetary support, interest subsidy, government guarantee, etc. to HPC would adversely affect functioning of the HPC.
10.4     The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should provide interest subsidy, government guarantee, bank guarantee, etc. to fill the gap.10.5     The CMD, HPC, informed the Committee “budget for the financial year 2002-03 will be very disappointing for the paper industry”.  He stated, “The newsprint industry is down in the dumps.  I am happy to inform this august body that HPC is the only newsprint company, which has managed to stay afloat this year with a very nominal profit of Rs.3.00 Crores. As far as writing and printing paper industry is concerned, the duty reduction from 35 to 30 as against the WTO bound rate of 40 per cent is going to affect HPC adversely.” He further stated,  “In this Budget the Finance Minister has also outlined his philosophy towards the duty structure. Manufactured products attract 20 percent raw maters and inputs 10 per cent. Newsprint is still at 5 per cent. The industry has been making persistent representations, supported by various State Chief Ministers, to, at least, enhance the level up to 25 per cent, which is the WTO bound rate.”
10.6     CMD informed the Committee “newsprint today attracts customs duty of 5 per cent.  States like Tamil Nadu have already imposed an industry tax of 10 per cent on newsprint. Therefore, the Budget will encourage the consumers to import all these products.  35 per cent duty has been brought down to 30 per cent. There is a talk that countervailing duty may be taken out which will affect the paper industry adversely.”
10.7     The Committee recommends that while rationalizing the duty structure compatible with WTO guidelines, the Government should protect the interests of the domestic paper industries.
10.8     The CMD, HPC, further informed the Committee that in nutshell the impact of Union Budget for the Financial Year- 2002-03 on Paper Industry will be as under: -
i           Even though the basic customs duty applicable to paper & paperboards has been slashed to 30 % from 35 %, the said move is seen a part of the overall reforms process towards lower import duties, at East Asian rates (20%) in the medium term.
ii         The basic customs duty on newsprint imports continues to be pegged at 5% as against the WTO-bound rate of 25%, indiscriminate dumping of newsprint is taking place.  Ironically, newsprint also does not attract Special Additional Duty (SAD) while domestic newsprint manufacturers have to pay local sales tax, entry tax, etc.  The ‘Disguised Imports’ of writing and printing paper and ‘stock lots’ are still vitiating the domestic paper market and posing difficulties for domestic paper manufacturers, eroding their capability to become globally competitive.  Import duty on newsprint should, therefore, be enhanced to the WTO-bound rate of 25%.  Imports should also be regulated as per the genuine requirements of the newspaper publishers by insisting on a third party certificate from any independent international quality surveyor (not the manufacturer of newsprint).  Newsprint import also should attract SAD as applicable to other products.
iii        The Government of India has treated the Light Weight Coated (LWC) paper as a variety of newsprint since June 1998 for customs duty purposes attracting only 5 % duty.  In the guise of LWC, a lot of coated and uncoated papers are being imported into the country disturbing the market equilibrium.  Even though production capacity exists, domestic manufacturers do not find it worthwhile to produce LWC on account of the non-existence of a level-playing field.  LWC should be classified as paper and not be clubbed with Newsprint.  Import of LWC should attract SAD and Counter Vailing Duty (CVD), as domestic production of equivalent varieties attracts local taxes and basic excise duty (currently 16%).
iv       Excise Notifications issued by the Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance including Notification No. 8/2002-CE and 9/2002-CE both dated 1st March, 2002 allowing continuance of payment of zero excise duty by a section of paper industry up to the first clearance of aggregate quantity not exceeding 3500 tpa of paper of Unconventional Raw Material (UCRM) are causing substantial losses to the Exchequer (estimated to be about Rs.500 crores) as a large number of paper mills are avoiding the payment of excise duty (misusing the said dispensation) and thereby vitiating the market characteristics.  When the imperative is to consolidate and create world-scale (and world-class) capacities, this lop-sided exemption dispensation has acted as a dampener for capacity expansion and technology up gradation, besides breeding unhealthy practices in the market place.
v         The increased outlay earmarked for primary education (especially the ‘Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan’) from Rs.4000 crores to Rs.4, 900 crores is expected to provide the much needed stimulus to growth in demand for paper and paperboard products.
vi       The Union Budget proposal for giving fillip to projects of softwood plantation on degraded non-forest land so as to encourage compensatory afforestation and conservation of natural resources is laudable as the availability and affordability of appropriate cellulosic fiber (raw material) is currently the single most intractable limiting factor in the growth of paper industry in India.
vii      Regarding EXIM Policy, there should be a uniform DEPB rate for all varieties of paper & Paper Boards to provide opportunities to more and more producers to make forays in the export market.
10.9       The Committee views the Government’s Policy of reducing Customs Duty from 35% to 30% as against the WTO bound rate of 40% as a major threat for the domestic Paper Industries. The Committee conceives that the reduction in Customs Duty would definitely encourage import, which, in turn, would adversely affect the paper industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should review its decision and revise the Custom Duty to 35% or 40%.
10.10      The Committee recommends that the Government should stop the `Disguised Import’ of newsprint in order to save the domestic Paper Industries. The Committee also recommends that the DHI should take up this subject with the Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue) for reversing the Custom Duty on newsprint from the present 5% to 15%-20% which is still lower to the WTO bond rate of 25%.
10.11      The Excise duty on writing & printing paper may also be reduced from 16% to 8% ad-valorem.
10.12      Regarding the Hindustan Newsprints Ltd. (HNL), a subsidiary of the Hindustan Paper Corporation on the issue of disinvestments, the Secretary stated, “the Government's policy is to disinvest non- strategic PSUs, and all the PSUs under the DHI are on-strategic. There is no distinction between a loss making company and a profit making Company”. He stated  “initially it will be a joint venture. Later on, the Government will disinvest totally. But, initially, the effort is to find a strategic partner for forming a joint venture.”
10.13      The Committee recommends that an early decision may be taken on joint venture formation of the HNL so as to sustain the profitable operation of the Company and further improve its performance.10.14      The Committee notes that the Nagaland Pulp & Paper Company Ltd. is before the A.A.I.F.R.  and the Company has been referred for its winding up.  The Committee, however, recommends that the Government should formulate a strategy to revive the Nagaland Pulp & Paper Co. Ltd.  as It is the only industry in Nagaland . The Committee feels that the revival   would be an appropriate step since the Government of India have extended the cease fire period by one year as a prelude to a peaceful solution of the insurgency problems in Nagaland.
HINDUSTAN MACHINE TOOLS LTD. (BEARING)
11        The Department stated that the Company has been restructured into HMT Limited, the Holding company with Tractor Business in its fold, and the other Business Groups have been spun off into subsidiaries viz., HMT Machine Tools Limited, HMT Watches Limited & HMT Chinar Watches Limited. Besides, the company has two wholly owned subsidiaries HMT (Bearings) Ltd. and one partly owned subsidiary, Praga Tools Ltd.
11.1     The major elements of financial and organizational restructuring are: -
(i)
            Fresh infusion by Government of India to the extent of Rs.395.00 crores.
(ii)          Closing 5 unviable units and offering VRS to all employees.
(iii)         Conversion of Rs.39.70 crores government loan into equity.
(iv)        Manpower reduction by 6947 under VRS by 2001-02.
11.2     It was also informed by the Department that the process of Disinvestment/Joint Venture has been initiated for Tractor Group, HMT Machine Tools Limited, HMT Watches Limited, HMT Chinar Watches Limited, HMT Bearing Limited and HMT (International) Limited.11.3       The Committee has noted that the Government has decided to close down 5 unviable units of HMT under its restructuring programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should give impetus to the schemes/programmes for training and rehabilitation of retired workers under VRS/VSS.
11.4     HMT (Bearings) Ltd. (erstwhile Indo-Nippon Precision Bearings) was established in the year 1964 as a state public sector company. In the year 1981, this company became a central public sector enterprise as a subsidiary of HMT Ltd. The production of the Company during the year 2001-02 is anticipated to be Rs.45.10 crores. Efforts to locate a joint venture partner for the company have been initiated as a part of the restructuring.
11.5     The acting CMD, HMT, informed the Committee “as far as the Budget is concerned, the company does not have any direct impact. But the HMT   is suffering due to other reasons. The tractor industry which was growing in the last 22 years at the rate of almost 15 to 20 per cent and, at an average rate of 14 per cent showing a negative growth of 20 per cent. This is a very serious situation. We are able to reach the farmers, but their capacity has gone down and they are not able to purchase the tractors. So, the Government should provide liberal loans to the farmers. Then only farmers will be able to purchase the tractors and the mechanization process will start.”
11.6     The Committee recommends that the DHI should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance, Banking Division, so as to provide soft loans to enable the Land Development Banks (LDBs), Central Cooperative Banks (CCBs), etc to enable the farmers to purchase Tractors.11.7     As regards watches he also stated “we don’t have that mechanism process in the country. We manufacture only 10 million watches and the consumption of watches in our country is much more than that. We have the capacity to manufacture a watch for Rs.75. But the smuggled module costs Rs.30 or 40 only. Ours is a social and national oriented organization. The cost of our module is Rs.110. Of course, we have taken a lot of measures and the cost of the module can be reduced to Rs.75. But still we are not able to compete because the smuggled module costs only Rs.35 to 40.  I agree with your point that we have to make efforts to compete, but there are some limitations. Some mechanism should be adopted by the government, so that the organized sector like HMT are little bit protected”.
11.8     The Committee recommends that the Government should take-up hard measures to control the smuggled watches/module so as to save the domestic watch companies.
11.9     He further added,  “The Company is able to manufacture about 475 lakh tractors, but are selling only 10,000 tractors. So not only HMT, but even other tractor manufacturing companies also should try and boost export of tractors. This time we are sure to have a 15 per cent growth in our exports. There is one company called the HMT International, it has made progress to the extent of 50 per cent”.
11.20   The Government of India has decided to disinvest most of the businesses of   HMT– watches, tractors, etc. The process is going on. The company has been making losses continuously for the past few years. The Company’s Turnaround plan approved by the government in July 2000 envisaged Organisational Restructuring by conversion of Business Groups into separate subsidiary Companies and disinvestments in these subsidiaries.
11.21   The Committee recommends that the Government should make concerted efforts to improve the financial positions of the HMT subsidiaries as per the restructuring plan. The Committee also recommends that, wherever possible, joint venture partners should be invited to infuse the required funds in the subsidiaries.11.22   It has also been observed that the tractor industry, which had been growing at the rate  of almost 15-20%, is presently showing a negative  growth.  The farmers are reluctant to purchase new tractors due to their decreasing purchasing power and increasing   running cost of tractors.  This is a very serious situation, which the farmers are facing at present.  In the long run, it will adversely affect the agricultural production.
11.23   Secondly, since farmers are increasingly depending on tractors for the purpose of transportation, the decreasing sale of tractors will lead   to a depressing situation in the rural economy.  It is, therefore, felt that both public and private sectors in the tractor  manufacturing  should  introduce  Battery Driven Tractors  for the rural market, which will drastically reduce the running cost of tractors, which , in  turn, will push-up the sale of tractors  if the  Ministry of Non- Conventional Energy Sources subsidises these tractors. A common facility centre for  recharging the batteries with the help of  photovoltaic system may be made in the cluster of 5-10  villages to help the farmers  to have tractors  with minimum running cost.
11.24   The Committee recommends that the Department of Heavy Industries, in consultation with the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources should make a proposal in this regard for Government's consideration.

13        Hindustan Cables Ltd. (HCL), a Government of India Undertaking is the pioneer in the field of Telecom Cables in India.   The company was set up at Rupnarainpur, West Bengal in 1952 to make the country self-reliant in the    manufacture and supply of various types of telecom cables.  Over the years the Company with an investment of about Rs.537 crores, has grown from a single unit, single-product organization to multi-unit, multi-product entity with Units located at Hyderabad in Andhra Pradesh and Naini in Uttar Pradesh, besides Rupnarainpur Unit in West Bengal.  The company’s main products are Jelly Filled and Optical Fibre Cables.  It has a capacity of 107 LCKM of Jelly Filled Cables and manufacturing capacity for Fibre Optic Cables is 70,000 FKM per annum.  The Company has manpower of 4,341 as on 1
st June 2000.
13.1     HCL has been a profit making Company right from its inception. The performance of the company, however, started declining from 1995-96 mainly due to inadequate capacity utilization, acute shortage of working capital, higher finance charges and salary and wages disproportionate   to the volume of production following economic liberalization. In order to improve the performance of the company, the cabinet in its meeting held on 27th January 1999, approved a package of assistance together with financial restructuring.  The package   comprised the following: -
                     i.            Non-Plan budgetary support in the form of equity of Rs.75 crores towards partial reimbursement of cash losses.
                   ii.            Assistance in the form of grant of Rs.40.00  crores in 1998-99 and Rs.28 crores during 1999-2000 for implementation of Voluntary Retirement Scheme subject to revision as per new scheme which the Government may announce.
                  iii.            Capital restructuring involving the following: -
§         Conversion of outstanding Government loan of Rs.167.12   crores (as on 1st October, 1998) into equity;
§         Waiver of outstanding interest on Government loan amounting to Rs.109 crores as on 1st October, 1998; and
§         Waiver of interest of Rs.13.66 Crores accrued on Danida grant.
                 iv.            Government Guarantee for raising Rs.35 crores by way of bond/commercial loan from Financial Institutions/ Banks/Trusts/Corporate Bodies etc. for a period of six years with exemption from guarantee fee.
                   v.            Extension of Government Guarantee for Rs.112 crores with exemption from guarantee fee in favour of banks covering the overdrawal of the cash credit account for a period of four years up to 31st March, 2003 on yearly basis, and also exemption from guarantee fee from October 1996 to June 1999.
vi.   Reservation of orders of annual requirement of telecom cables of DOT/MTNL in   favour of HCL-30% in the first year and 25% in the second year, along with advance of 50% gross value as available to ITI and HTL.   The policy of reservation of orders is to be reviewed thereafter, as directed by the cabinet.
13.2     In pursuance of the package of assistance, HCL received order of 87.12 LCKM of Jelly Filled cables and 4615 K.M. of Optic Fibre Cable during 1999-2000 along with 50% advance from DOT and MTNL.  The Company surpassed all past records of production and sales during the year 1999-2000.  In physical terms, the production of Jelly Filled Cables was in the order of 85 LCKM and that of Optic Fibre Cables was 4663. The Turnkey Division of the company also achieved an all time high turnover of Rs.203.00 crores against a target of Rs.160.00 crores.  With this the company achieved a record turnover of Rs.804 crores during the year.  The loss for the year 1999-2000 has been brought down to the level of Rs.40.00 crores from Rs.139.00 crores incurred during the year 1998-99.  This is against a projected loss of Rs.51.00 crores for the first year of the implementation of the package assistance approved by the   Cabinet.  The company slashed 385 employees under VRS during 1999-2000.  The Company raised a fund of Rs.35.00 crores from the market through private placement of bond, which helped the company to augment its working capital resource.  The financial institutions were persuaded for relief and concessions.  Accordingly, UTI, LIC and IFCI waived penal, overdue and compounded interest amounting to the tone of Rs.27.50 crores, reduced the interest and rescheduled the loan amount. Thereafter, the Company received work orders of 30.31 LCKM of Jelly Filled Cables under reservation policy for the first six months of the current year.  Orders of Optical Fibre Cables from DOT and PIJF cable from MTNL are awaited. 
13.3     In connection with the continuing restructuring process in the Company, the CMD of HCL elaborated to the Committee  “in 1999 a package of assistance was given by the Cabinet, where some restructure was allowed to the Company. In this package one important provision was made regarding reservation of orders along with the advance by the BSNL. During the year 1999-2000, which was the first year of the implementation of package, the results were very good. Due to this the Company’s turnover went up to the level of Rs.803.00 crores. The loss has also come down from Rs.138.00 crores to Rs.39.00 crores. It was the net loss. In fact, the operating profit was to the level of Rs.80.00 crores. In the subsequent year, i.e., 2001, the effect of the package continued.  The efforts were on the same lines and the turnover increased further from Rs.803.00 crores to Rs.975.00 crores. This was the highest production in the Company and it was the record turnover”.
13.4     The Committee is happy to note that with the concerted efforts of the Government by applying restructuring plan, the Company’s  decline has stopped and its turnover increased from Rs.203.00 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs.975.00 crores in 2000-01. The Committee feels that this record turnover of the company has been possible mainly due to `reservation of orders’ for the Company by the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should continue making provisions of work orders for the Company.

CUSTOMS DUTY ON IMPORT OF PHOTO-SENSITIVE GOODS
21.         The Committee was concerned to note that Budget 2002-2003 has not announced any tariff related measures for development of the integrated manufacturer of Photo Sensitive Goods, which has brought contemporary technology to the Country. Photo films technology is a closely guarded secret of a few MNCs who are exploiting the policies to their advantage and as a result, the domestic industry is reduced to a make packaging industry.
21.1.      The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should provide following fiscal incentives to promote integrated manufacture of Photo Sensitive Goods in the country: -
(i)         Customs Duty on raw material specific to the Photo Sensitive Goods Industry is reduced to 'nil' to ensure fair competitiveness with importers of semi-finished/finished goods who are mere converters/Traders.
 
(ii)        The Basic Customs Duty on import of semi-finished and finished photographic goods be raised to WTO bound rates.
 
(iii)       The Government may also consider imposing 'nil' Excise Duty on Photo Sensitive Goods actually manufactured within the country vis-à-vis those merely converted from Jumbo rolls.

(Para: 10.11)
 
 
The Committee recommends that an early decision may be taken on joint venture formation of the HNL so as to sustain the profitable operation of the Company and further improve its performance.
(Para: 10.13)
  
            The Committee notes that the Nagaland Pulp & Paper Company Ltd. is before the A.A.I.F.R.  and the Company has been referred for its winding up.  The Committee, however, recommends that the Government should formulate a strategy to revive the Nagaland Pulp & Paper Co. Ltd.  as It is the only industry in Nagaland . The Committee feels that the revival   would be an appropriate step since the Government of India have extended the cease fire period by one year as a prelude to a peaceful solution of the insurgency problems in Nagaland.
(Para: 10.14)
           
The Committee has noted that the Government has decided to close down 5 unviable units of HMT under its restructuring programme. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the DHI should give impetus to the schemes/programmes for training and rehabilitation of retired workers under VRS/VSS.
(Para: 11.3)
 
The Committee recommends that the DHI should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance, Banking Division, so as to provide soft loans to enable the Land Development Banks (LDBs), Central Cooperative Banks (CCBs), etc to enable the farmers to purchase Tractors.
(Para: 11.6)
 
            The Committee recommends that the Government should take-up hard measures to control the smuggled watches/module so as to save the domestic watch companies.
(Para: 11.8)
The Committee recommends that the Government should make concerted efforts to improve the financial positions of the HMT subsidiaries as per the restructuring plan. The Committee also recommends that, wherever possible, joint venture partners should be invited to infuse the required funds in the subsidiaries.
(Para: 11.21)
 
            The Committee recommends that the Department of Heavy Industries, in consultation with the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources should make a proposal in this regard for Government's consideration.
(Para: 11.24)
 
             The Committee views RIEL as a potentially viable PSE, which needs fresh infusion of funds so as to update its R&D, and projects. The Committee is, therefore, in conformity with the DHI to invite a joint venture partner for the Company.
(Para: 12.2)
           
            The Committee is happy to note that with the concerted efforts of the Government by applying restructuring plan, the Company’s  decline has stopped and its turnover increased from Rs.203.00 crores in 1999-2000 to Rs.975.00 crores in 2000-01. The Committee feels that this record turnover of the company has been possible mainly due to `reservation of orders’ for the Company by the Government. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should continue making provisions of work orders for the Company.
(Para: 13.4)
 
            The Committee recommends that the Government should take into consideration interests of the workers and Company as well while diverting the equity base of the Government up to 26%.
(Para: 13.6)
 
            The Committee, however, noted that recently the price of the jell filled cables, Main Product of HCL, has gone down by 17 % which has adversely affected the profit of the Company.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the company should drastically reduce its cost of production.
(Para: 13.7)
 
            The Committee notes that the Company, which has been slated for disinvestment, is presently facing the problem due to fall of prices of cables.  Private Sector is also facing the same problem but they are able to cope up with the situation as they have less manpower and the workforce is mostly on contract basis with low wage cost.  The Committee therefore, recommends that HCL should further trim its present workforce. The DHI should provide the Company grant for VRS purpose on liberal terms. The Committee further recommends that the Company should continue its efforts for diversification of its products.  It should also approach Telecommunications Consultants of India Ltd. (TCIL) to tie up the synergies.
(Para: 13.10)
 
The Committee further recommends that provision  of reservation of work order for the Company  should  continue  two years  after it is  disinvested.
(Para: 13.11)
            The Committee recommends that the Government should make concerted efforts to locate joint venture, partners for BHPV and TSPL so that the companies may be put back to full operations and start earning operations.
(Para: 14.10)
 
            The Committee recommends that the DHI should make efforts to get work orders for the BYNL group of companies under the Policy of Purchase Preference so as to maintain their viability.  The Committee further recommends that the DHI should take up the matter with the oil sector PSEs, Ministry of Fertilizer, Railways and State Governments for placement of orders on subsidiaries of BYNL.
(Para: 14.11)
 
            The Committee recommends that the Government should provide adequate financial assistance to TSPCL, TSL and R & C so as to enable these to Trim their excessive manpower under their Voluntary Retirement Schemes (VRS) undergoing in these subsidiaries.  The Committee also recommends that the Company’s request for margin money in   the form of equity and counter   guarantee to   raise   funds should be considered by the Government.
(Para: 11.12)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should assist the Companies wherever and whenever the Companies under the DHI are facing working capital problem and are not able to execute the orders in hand. The Government should assist the companies under the DHI to meet the shortage of working capital in the form of Bank Guarantee, Non plan loans, etc. The Committee further recommends that the DHI should help these Companies by getting advances from the client PSEs for the execution of the work orders. The Committee also suggests that under one time settlement, all the cases of Liquidity Damages up to March 2001 may be considered and settled. The Committee recommends that both the Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises and the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas should make joint efforts to resolve the issue relating to the Liquidity Damages and placement of work orders on the BYNL group of Companies.   
 
(Para: 11.14)
 
The Committee recommends that till the revival plan is implemented, the Government should provide non-plan support for meeting the expenditure of salary and wages of employees.
(Para: 15.1)
 
Praga Tools Ltd.  was referred to the BIFR and the Company was declared sick.  BIFR has directed the operating agency (IDBI) to submit a revival plan.  The Committee recommends that the budgetary support as non-plan loan and VRS grant should be provided to the Company till the revival plan is finalised.
(Para: 16)
 
 Department of Disinvestment has already constituted an Inter-Ministerial Group of the Joint-Venture Corporation in respect of BSCL and BCL.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that these two Companies should be restructured as a prelude to disinvestment to attract prospective bidders.
(Para: 17)
 
NEPA Ltd. is listed for disinvestment but so far the proposal has not been implemented.  The Committee reiterates its recommendations made in the 59th report that in case the disinvestment of NEPA is not possible in six months, its revival plan should be implemented without further delay.
(Para: 18)
 
Scooters India Ltd.  is one of the Companies which has successfully come out of BIFR.  The Committee reiterates its stand made in the 59th report for reduction in Customs and Excise Duties on the imported components used for electric vehicles keeping in view the electric vehicles’ contribution towards making environment pollution free.
(Para: 19)
 
            The Committee therefore recommends that this ban should be lifted immediately  and registration of two-stroke dedicated CNG mode three wheelers should also  be restored. 
 
(Para: 19.2)
 
The Committee recommends that the examination of the report may be expedited so that necessary group restructuring may take place at the earliest.  The Committee in its earlier report had recommended that the Government should find a suitable joint-venture partner for the engineering and electrical division of the Company, keeping in view the success the Belting Division had achieved.  The Committee recommends that Department of Heavy Industry should continue its effort to locate a suitable joint-venture partner for the Company. 
(Para: 20.1)
 
Presently, the Company is facing the problem of working capital and as a result, it has become difficult for the Company to execute its orders. It has substantial work orders in its hand but it is not able to execute orders as its funds are locked up with the State Electricity Boards (SEBs) to the extent of Rs.50.00 crores. The Government should assist the Company by enhancing its existing Bank Guaranty  to enable it to execute the work orders. The Company may also be provided Plan Fund to undertake capital expenditure for modernization of its plants and machineries and fund for crucial balancing. It may also be provided VRS grant for trimming their large work force.
 (Para: 20.2)
 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should provide following fiscal incentives to promote integrated manufacture of Photo Sensitive Goods in the country: - 
(i)   Customs Duty on raw material specific to the Photo Sensitive Goods Industry is reduced to 'nil' to ensure fair competitiveness with importers of semi-finished/finished goods who are mere converters/Traders.
 
(ii) The Basic Customs Duty on import of semi-finished and finished photographic   goods be raised to WTO bound rates.
 
(iii)The Government may also consider imposing 'nil' Excise Duty on Photo Sensitive Goods actually manufactured within the country vis-à-vis those merely converted from Jumbo rolls.
(Para: 21.1)

PREFERENCE FOR DOMESTICALLY MANUFACTURED GOODS
 
1.         The Borrower may, with the agreement of the Bank, grant a margin of preference in the evaluation of bids under ICB procedures to bids offering certain goods manufactured in the country of the Borrower, when compared to bids offering such goods manufactured elsewhere. In such cases, bidding documents shall clearly indicate any preference to be granted to domestic manufactured goods and the information required to establish the eligibility of a bid for such preference. The nationality of the manufacturer or supplier is not a condition for such eligibility. The methods and stages set forth hereunder shall be followed in the evaluation and comparison of bids.2.         For comparison, responsive bids shall be classified in one of the following three groups:
a.
       Group A: bids offering goods manufactured in the country of the Borrower if the bidder establishes to the satisfaction of the Borrower and the Bank that (i) labor, raw material and components from within the country of the Borrower will account for more than 30 percent of the EXW price of the product offered, and (ii) the production facility in which those goods will be manufactured or assembled has been engaged in manufacturing/assembling such goods at least since the time of bid submission.
b.      Group B: all other bids offering goods from within the country of the Borrower.
c.       Group C: bids offering the goods from abroad and to be directly imported.
3.         The EXW price quoted by a Group A bidder shall include all duties and taxes paid or payable on the basic materials or components purchased in the domestic market or imported. Similarly, prices quoted by Group B bidders shall include all duties and taxes on components and raw materials. The price quoted by Group A and B bidders shall exclude the sales and similar taxes on the finished product. The price quoted by Group C bidders shall be on CIF or CIP border point or other destination, exclusive of customs duties and other import taxes.
4.         In the first step, all evaluated bids in each group shall be compared to determine the lowest evaluated bid in each. Such lowest evaluated bids shall then be compared with each other and if, as a result of this comparison, a bid from Group A or Group B is the lowest, it shall be selected for the award.
5.         If, as a result of the comparison under paragraph 4 above, the lowest evaluated bid is a bid from Group C, all Group C bids shall be further compared with the lowest evaluated bid from Group A after adding to the evaluated bid price of the imported goods offered in each Group C bid, for the purpose of this further comparison only, an amount equal to: (i) the amount of duties and other related import charges which a nonexempt importer would have to pay for the importation of the goods offered in such Group C bid; or (ii) 15 percent of the CIF or CIP bid price of such goods if said duties and charges exceed 15 percent of such price. If the Group A bid in such further comparison is the lowest, it shall be selected for the award; if not, the lowest evaluated bid from Group C, as determined from the comparison under paragraph 4, shall be selected.
 
6          In the case of single responsibility, supply and installation or turnkey 45 contracts in which a number of discrete items of equipment is grouped into one contract package, the preference margin shall not be applied to the whole package, but only to the locally-manufactured equipment within the package. Equipment offered from abroad shall be quoted CIF or CIP, and equipment offered locally EXW (free of sales and similar taxes); all other components, such as design, works, installation, and supervision, shall be quoted separately. Bids should not be classified into groups A, B, or C. In the comparison of bids, only the CIF or CIP price in each bid of the equipment offered from outside the Borrower's country shall be increased by the applicable duty and other taxes payable by a non-exempt importer or 15 percent, whichever is less. If duties vary from item to item within a package, the appropriate tariff for each piece of equipment shall apply. No preference shall be applied for any associated services or works included in the package.

 REPORT
 
            The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all PSEs and assists in policy formulation pertaining to the
policy guidelines on performance improvement and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel management and in related areas. It
also collects, evaluates and maintains information on several areas in respect of PSEs. In fulfilling its roles  it associates itself with
other Ministries and Organizations.
 
1.1               The important role and tasks of the Department of Public Enterprises are: -
 
(i)                 General policy relating to Public Sector Enterprises;
(ii)               Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and Guidelines to    Public Sector Enterprises;
(iii)              Formulation of Policy Guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs) in areas like performance
improvement and evaluation, financial   management, personnel management, board structures, wage settlement,
training, industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.;
(iv)
             All matters relating to Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between the    Public Sector Enterprises and the
Administrative Ministries/ Departments.;
(v)                Matters relating to  the delegation of powers   to the  Board of Directors;
(vi)             To undertake in-depth studies in respect of significant areas of functioning             of central PSEs.;
(vii)            Matters relating to International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE);
(viii)          Matters relating to Standing Conference of Public Enterprises (SCOPE);
(ix)             To monitor and evaluate the performance of PSEs and to act as a repository of data and to bring out an Annual
Survey for the Parliament; and
(x)               Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators for settlement of disputes among             Public             Sector Enterprises and
Government Departments except disputes relating to tax             matters.
 
1.2       The Department has five constituent Divisions, viz, the Financial Policy Division, the Management Policy Division, the
MoU Division, the Administration & Coordination Division and Permanent Machinery of Arbitration. The Financial Policy
Division comprises the Public Enterprises Survey Unit, the Policy Planning Unit and the Wage Policy Unit. The Management
Policy Division comprises the Personnel Policy Unit, Training Unit, Performance Indicator and Work Norms Unit (PIWN Unit) and
SC & ST Cell. The MoU Division comprises MoU Unit, Data Bank and Computer Cell. The Administration & Coordination
Division comprises the Administration, Library, Parliament and Coordination Wings and Hindi Cell. The Permanent Machinery of
Arbitration (PMA) provides a forum for settlement of commercial disputes between two or more PSEs as well as between a
Government Department and PSEs.
