PROFILE
National Film Development Corporation Ltd. (NFDC) is a Public Sector Enterprise set up in

1975 under the companies Act, 1956.The company was restructured during 1980 by the merger of the
erstwhile Indian Motion Picture Export Corporation (IMPEC) and Film Finance Corporation (FFC) and
the company emerged as Central Agency to promote good cinema in the country. Over the years, NFDC
has provided a wide range of services essential to the integrated growth of Indian cinema Besides
producing and financing films NFDC exports Indian films all over the world and imports commercial
films, Tele-films and serials for distribution and exhibition in the country. Other technical services
provided by NFDC include recording and dubbing, production equipment hiring, subtitling of films,
video duplication, video production, postproduction etc.

VUI. MISSION OF THE COMPANY

         The Sub-Committee IV for Ministry fo r Agro and Rural Industries at its meeting held on 14 th  
March and 41h April 2002 decided to  study the implementation of Pr ime Minister Rozgar Yojana
(PMRY in the States of Andhra Pr adesh, Karnataka and Kerala. The Sub-Committee visited the States 
of Andhra Pradesh Karnataka and Kerala from 201h to  271h June 2002 and held discussions with the 
officials of  Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, Stat e Government and Banks on issues pertaining to
PMRY. 
  
PMRY - AN OVERVIEW OF THE SCHEME 
  
1.1    The Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojana was launched on 2nd Oct ober, 1993 with a view to providing
self-employment opportunities to educated unemplo yed youth in the country. The scheme was made 
operational with effect from Is t April, 1994. Prime Minister's Rozgar Yojanawas launched on 2nd
October, 1993. The scheme was designed to provide employment to more than  a million persons by
setting up seven lakh micro enterp rises during the Eight Five Year  Plan (1993-97), through industry, 
services and business routes. The scheme was operated in urban ar eas only during 1993-94, and in both 
urban and rural areas of the country from 1994-95 onwards. From 1994-95 the erstwhile-Self-
Employment Scheme for the Educat ed Unemployed Youth (SEEUY) was merged into PMRY. During
the Eight Plan a total of 7.75 lakh cases were sancti oned and out of these, lo ans were reported to have
been disbursed in 6.52 lakh cases as reported by the Reserve Bank of In dia (REI). Until now, nearly 15
educated unemployed youth have benefited from th e scheme. The PMRY is continuing in the Tenth
Plan period. 
  
1.2    The progress, as reported by the REI for 1997-98 was against a target of 2.20 lakh beneficiaries, 
a total of 2.63 lakh cases were sa nctioned and in 2.09 lakh cases loan s were disbursed. During 1998-99, 
against a target of 2.20 lakh benefi ciaries, as many as 2.62 lakh cases  were sanctioned, and in 1.45 lakh
cases loans were disbursed as per the available reports from REI. Furt her, to enhance the coverage and
scope of the PMRY scheme, it has been modified si nce 1st April, 1999. The modified salient features o
f
the PMRY scheme are as under:-

1.3    The target envisaged for 1999-2000 was 2.20 lakh beneficiaries. Against this target, 1,14,587 cases 
have been sanctioned, and disbursement took plac e in 59,845 cases as reporte d upto the month ending
December, 1999. The Target for 2002-03 remains at the level of Rs.2.20 lakhs, as was the case on 2001-
02. 
  
1.4    The Committee observes that the target (2.20 lakh beneficiaries) set for PMRY is too low to have
any significant impact on the creati on of employment opportunities in the country. This issue weighted
on the Committee's discussion with of ficials of State Government, Mini stry of Agro & Rural Industries
during its visit to Andhra Pradesh, Kamataka, Kerala. The Committee no ted that the target fixed each
year for PMRY has remained st atic during the last three year s i.e. for 2000-01, 2001-02 and 2002-03 
only 2.20 lakh persons were to be c overed under PMRY scheme. This figure, when divided between the
states and thereafter, among districts of each state, is like a drop. Th is figure is too minuscule to have
any noticeable impact on the unemployment scenario in a country of millions. 
  
1.5    The Ministry of Small Scale Industries, with whom the matter was taken up explained that the 
fixing of target was based on two aspects: - 
(a)
    Basic Target which is fixed, and is based on th e State's population as in 1991. This target is 
given by the Planning Commissi on, and is based on the employm ent potential and the numbe r
of unemployed registered with Employment Excha nge. An annual. target of 2.2 lakhs is given
for 2002-03, on an all India basis. This is communicated in March every year, for the next year.
(b)   Additional Target: This is vari able and is fixed on the basis of recovery position during the
previous year, and the performance in the previous year. This is communicated during May. 
         The Committee was also informed that th ere is a Government of Indi a guideline that 125 per cent
of target must also be achieved. 
  
1.6    However, the Committee was of the view that  the overall target for PM RY should be increased so
that states could be given enhanc ed targets, and more and more people can be brought under the ambit
of the scheme each year.

2.1    During the course of the Committee's meeting held at Hyde rabad, Commissioner of Industries
replied that Andhra Pradesh state that the scheme with a high target of around 33,000 and the number of
sanctions have been declining since with accumulation of NPAs. 
  
2.2    The Committee was further informed that th ere are a number of reasons  for under achievement o f
tile target under PMRY which are as under:- 
  
(a)  Banks complained that there is generall y delay in communicating PMRY targets to them,
which results in delay in grounding of the unit. Also, selection of beneficiaries is done only on
specific dates. The delay in comm unicating target of the banks le ads to delay in sanctioning o f
loans and subsequent disbursal of loans to the beneficiaries. Target is communicated in two
installments, which results in delay in its implementation. 
  
(b)  It is generally seen that beneficiaries take up si milar or same lines of  activity, which makes it
unviable. Autorickshaws, photocopy shops, STD booths etc were cite d as examples. Banks
hesitate to sanction loans for activities of simi lar nature as these activities reach a saturation
point which is a major reason to the failure of the scheme. 
  
(c)  Most beneficiaries go in for trade and business activities. 
  
(d)  Percentage of overdues to total loans is 67 per cent, which is a matter of great concern. 
  
(e)  Absconding entrepreneurs who divert funds and close shop are also a matter of concern. 
  
(f)   From the entrepreneurs' side, request for change in activ ity results in delay in getting
approvals. 
  
(g)  Marketing of products is a problem area which entrepreneurs find difficult to surmount. 
  
8.      Mounting NPAs under the PMRY scheme is a problem to be addressed immediately. The
representatives of Government of  Andhra Pradesh apprised the Comm ittee that the following measures
were being taken for overcoming the problems:- 
  
(a)  A list of viable schemes is being identifie d. Project profiles on thes e lines of activities are
being prepared. 
  
(b)  List of eligible beneficiaries in each area, mandal wise, is being maintained. 
  
(c)  Technology link with instit utions is being thought of. A me ntion was made of RUDSETI o f
Karnataka and some districts of Andhra Pradesh, which provide training to beneficiaries. 
  
(d)  Deputy Tahsildars are employe d for recovery of dues. Andhra  Pradesh is the only state doing
so. 
  
(e)  Monitoring is being done by Industry Promotion Officer. 
  
(f)   Awards have been constituted for best Industry Promotion Officer. 
  
(g)  Advertisement campaign for PMRY will be undertaken.

Against the 16,782 applications sanctioned, only 13,309 cases were disbursed loan during 1999-2000,

2.5    The Committee observed that timely communication of targets s hould be made and specific dates
for selection of entrepreneurs should be communicated. As regard s large number of beneficiaries
choosing activities which become unviable, the Committee suggests th at counselling of applicants to
choose from agriculture and allied activities should be done. 
  
2.6    The Committee also observ es that coverage of SC/STs unde r the Scheme is not upto the norm
stipulated up Government of India i.e. 22.5 per cen t for SC/ST. Against the all India average of 15.9 pe r
cent, Andhra Pradesh has recorded representation for these categories as 16.9 per cent during 1998-99, 
21.3 'per cent during 1999-2000, 17.5 per cent during 2000-2001 and 15.1 per cent during 2001-02. This 
has to be brought to the stipulated norm.

2.7    The recovery scenario in A ndhra Pradesh a dismal picture. Avai lable records indicate that during
the half year ended Marc h, 1999 it was 41.1 per cent; during th e half year ended March, 2000 it was
36.8 per cent and during half year  ended March, 2001 it was 37.9 per cent. During the half-year ende d 
September, 2001 it was 38.8 per cent The representatives of State Government apprised the Committee
that Deputy Tahsildar had been specially deputed  to make recovery of loans from defaulting
entrepreneurs. 
  
2.8    The Committee, during the course of the interaction wished to know if any study on viable projects
in each district was undertaken. The Commissioner of Industries Andhra Pradesh replied that this
exercise was undertaken, and project profiles on identified lines of activities were being prepared. 
2.9    The Committee observes that in order to improve rate of gr ounding of units it was necessary to
rectify the high percen tage of NPAs as mounting NPAs were one of the reas ons for high mortality rate
of PMRY projects. The Committee obs erved that NPAs to large industr ies can not be equated with the
NPAs under the PMRY as the percenta ge. of NPAs in PMRY sector wa s but a small percent of total
NPAs in the country. Out of total NPA of Rs.18000 cr ores, small sector owed only Rs.8,000 crore. NPA
for PMRY, therefore, was only negl igible. The Committee, therefore,  suggests that bankers should be
encouraged to finance self-employment schemes as this would directly increase employment. 
  
SURVIVAL OF PMRY UNITS 
  
2.10 The Committee was informed by the Commissioner of Industries, Andhra Pradesh that the average
rate of survival in Andhra Pradesh is 60 per cent, and that mortality rate was high in business and trade
sector. This was because the beneficiary abandons his activity af ter a short period. In the absence o
f
fixed assets they are not able to pump in fresh investment, nor can they approach banks/Financial
Institutions for fresh loans. He opi ned that service oriented units s hould be encouraged, as the survival
rate in the service sector was hi gh whereas the survival rate  in business sector was onl y 30 per cent. He

2.11 The Committee observes that, looking at the high mortality rate under PMRY, Group Approach
needs to be encouraged as gr oup dynamics have more impact on any activit y. An activity can be
identified and candidates sponsored. The Central Government can take initiatives in th is regard. The
Government should concentrate on qua lity entrepreneurs, instead of th e number of entrepreneurs. As in

Government should monitor the follow up of these activities.

up of productive activities by the beneficiaries th rough training establishments of the banks and also
through institutes such as Rural Development Self  Employment Training Inst itutes (RUDSETls) and

in the identification and selection process may be considered.

REPORT
 
1.Hindustan Steel Works Construction Limited (HSCL) is an offshoot of the Construction Division of Steel Authority 
of India Ltd. ( SAIL). The company was incorporated in 1964 with the prime objective of creating in Public Sector an
organisation capable of-taking-up   the construction of  modern  Steel Plants in the country. HSCL has executed works
in Steel Plants right from inception till commissioning, viz, Bokaro Steel plant, Vizag Steel Plant, Salem Steel Plant and
was  associated  with the expansion and modernisation activities of Bhilai Steel Plant, Durgapur Steel Plant, IISCO
(Burnpur)  as  also Bhadravati Steel Plant.  With the decline  in traditional work-order , the company  diversified its
activities  in  other sectors like  power , coal, oil and  gas and also  infrastructural facilities like  roads/highways,
bridges, dams, underground-communication and transport system besides  industrial and  township  complexes
involving  high degree of planning, coordination and modern sophisticated techniques. The Company gained experience
in the areas like civil works of plant building, structural fabrication and erection in industrial plants, and erection of
Equipment in the Steel Plants. As SAIL expanded its activities, activities of HSCL also expanded.  Apart from activities
in SAIL, the company expanded its activities in other areas, like civil works for buildings, other than SAIL, Dam
Construction'. Bridge construction, coal handling plants, road construction, stadium complexes, school buildings and
industrial townships etc. The company also gained experience in planning & coordination in steel & non-steel sectors.
1.2       The authorized capital of the company has been raised from Rs.20.00 crore to Rs.150.00 crore on approval of 
Government of India through the financial restructuring-cum-financial assistance package sanctioned to the company. 
Similarly, the paid  up  capital  has also been increased from Rs.20.00 crore to rs.117.10 crore.
1.3       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub -Committee that  HSCL suffered   in 1970s primarily   due to two
reasons . The first factor was the sudden  increase in work force between 1970-79 from 4,100 to 26,537.  Of this,
Bokaro unit alone   accounted for 12,600.  This  was due to the  crisis created when a large number of public sector and
private  companies engaged by Bokaro Steel   failed and left their  work sites leaving behind  their workforce.  Due to
pressure, both from the Government and from the steel plants.  HSCL  had to take over these works along with the
workforce, in order to  complete the works within the   stipulated time.  The other major factor responsible for the
company's decline was the lack of   substantial activity in the  steel sector.   The works awarded to HSLCL by the steel
plants  after 1974 were  not adequate  to sustain the additional recurring liabilities, mainly due to increase wage bills on
account of statutory hikes including  revision of pay and increase in the number of workforce.  As a result of the above
factors,   the company began to incur continuous losses from 1978-79 onwards (except 1985-86) and  as on 31.3.1999
the accumulated loss stood at Rs.1383.28 crore.  Another  factor  which  also contributed to the downgrading of the 
company is the huge  loss suffered by HSCL on Libyan works, undertaken under  Government  of India  protocol,  due
to reasons beyond the control of the  company .
 
1.4       The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The
Committee is of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to
and sudden increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to
error of judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.

3.         FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE -CUM-RESTRUCTURING PACKAGE
3.1       With a view to bail out the company from its financial crisis, a comprehensive financial restructuring proposal
was approved by Government of India/CCEA in  9
th July, 1999.  The revival  package provided  several financial
assistance/exemptions  which, inter-alia, included :-
Conversion of plan loans  of Rs.97.10 crore as on 31.3.99 into equity
Grant of moratorium on repayment  of and interest holiday on all Government  of India    loans upto 31.3.99 for 10

6.         Reasons for  partial failure of  Financial Assistance -cum- restructuring package
6.1       The Ministry of Steel  informed the Sub-Committee that  the Restructuring package could not yield the desired
result and advocated  the under mentioned detailed reasons for the partial failure of the restructuring package: -
Delay of about eleven months by commercial bank in the sanction and disbursement of the first phase of loan for VRS
amounting to Rs.210 Crore, forcing the company to carry idle wages.   In the revival plan it was envisaged to separate
2000 employees per year beginning with 1999-2000 but the loan amount was only disbursed in June, 2000 due to late
sanction. As a result, the actual separation under VRS could be effected only thereafter.
The projections in terms of profit & loss as contained in revival package were made with regard to the prevailing market
condition at that time. Since then, the market condition have shown a down turn and even big companies like SAIL have
been incurring losses.
Most of the works undertaken by HSCL are being sub-contracted primarily because of the age profile of its employee
and also the difficulties faced in their redeployment on work sites which are scattered all over India. Most of the receipts
of HSCL are passed on as payments to Sub contractor, thereby leaving a very marginal amount for utilisation towards
meeting overheads like salaries /wages etc.
HSCL has diversified its operations in the non-steel sector as jobs from the steel sector had virtually not coming up. The
margins in the diversified areas are very low, and this  means that HSCL would continue to incur losses.
HSCL has been replacing its  obsolete equipment in order to execute the works efficiently at site. During the years
1999-2000 and 2000-2001 equipments for an amount of Rs.35 lakhs and Rs.2.38 crore respectively were purchased.
Further in 2000-01, order for one excavator cum loader for Bokaro Unit for Rs.71 lakhs have been placed during the
year.

restructuring package, is constrained to express its concern.  The Committee  is of the view that HSCL  management

7.0       HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company
7.1       Replying to the Sub-Committee's query regarding HSCL becoming a sub-contracting company from a
construction company resultant and the possibility of sustenance of company under changed circumstances, the
management stated that the company has to resort to sub-contracting to augment the order book position in the face of
stiff competition from the construction sector.  It also has to offset difficulties like severe cash crunch to deposit
EMD/SD etc. and funds for procurement of raw materials and other inputs.  Sub-contracting is also necessitated due to
the fact that shifting manpower and other resources from steel plants to short duration projects is not only expensive but
also invites social and other local resistance.  Moreover, the age profile of the employees is also a deterrent in carrying
out the works departmentally.  Low margins due to competition and inadequacy of related expertise and skill are also
strong factors compelling adoption of sub-contracting system.
7.2       The HSCL management clarified that the company has neither become, nor has any plans to become out and out
a sub-contracting company.  It has a rich team of experienced engineers, workers, technicians and a strong fleet of
construction equipments, as its backbone.  In most cases, the company executes the jobs giving maximum possible
departmental inputs combining with it the strengths of the sub-contractors.  The extent of departmental inputs varies
according to location and nature of work.  As of now, the downward trend has been witnessed and therefore, given the
difficult circumstances enveloping the Company, the process is expected to remain the way it is for some more time. 
Till then, the primary concern of the company would be the payment of salary and wages to its employees as well as
liquidation of all other liabilities.  Once out of this predicament, the company's performance is bound to increase
through better utilization of equipments, supervision, design, procurement and monitoring besides direct execution as
much as possible.  Under the changed scenario and market economy, the system of sub-contracting (with maximum
departmental inputs) cannot be altogether discarded.  The execution arrangement, as elaborated above, is practical and
sustainable, if the liabilities reduce. 
7.3       The Committee understands the  compelling  circumstances under which HSCL has to adopt the system of  sub-
contracting  business pattern but   it is also an open secret that sub-contracting   gives low margin for HSCL than if the
work done by the company itself.  The  Committee  is of the view  that VRS  offer  by HSCL  to its employees would
take care of keeping with itself the workforce consisting of  productive age profile and  willing to undertake
work/assignment from whatever concern its coming.  The Committee feels that  direct undertaking of work by HSCL
staff would give larger margin to HSCL and thus opening scope for profitability of HSCL, therefore, it would be better
that the  system of sub-Contracting  is replaced by direct involvement of HSCL employees,  sooner than later.

9.3       Since inception and over the years, majority of the resources and infrastructural facilities had been built up in
PSU Steel Plants.  However, the continuing decline in the steel sector during the last several years has cast a shadow of
uncertainty on the question of sustenance of the company.  During the earlier years, steel plant projects were being
awarded to HSCL on nomination basis.  As a time progressed, the special status of the company with SAIL Steel Plants,
for the construction which the company was framed, got eroded. With the introduction of "Internal award Procedure" by
which  HSCL are exposed to unreasonable competition.  This makes bagging jobs in steel plants further more difficult. 
Inspite of the scope of jobs of AMR, operation maintenance, waste disposal, slag processing and scrap recovery in the
steel plants, HSCL's role has been marginalized .
 
9.4       The Committee is of the view that  HSCL deserves a better deal in SAIL with Government  mediation, therefore
the Committee recommends  that  all the project as well as  AMR and operational jobs, within the execution capacity of
HSCL, should be offered on nomination on priority basis to HSCL.  This would enable the company to utilise its
infrastructure, set up over the years at SAIL plants and  meet  the expenses of the company. Award procedure  of SAIL  
should be relaxed suitably   for preferential treatment   to HSCL.  The  company may have  long term
arrangement/understanding   with SAIL on the basis of quantum of job  assured for award.   The Committee further
recommends  that a certain portion of the construction jobs in the Infrastructural sector be assigned to HSCL  on 
nomination basis,  at   least during  the initial  years of planned revival.  Purchase preference  to PSUs should be  strictly
adhered to.  Presently the PSUs/Government Department   are not  uniformly following the system.  The dismal balance
sheets of the company, for several years now, have made customers apprehensive in pre-qualifying HSCL for their

The Committee notes that the reasons as placed  by the Ministry of Steel, for the suffering of  HSCL.  The Committee is
of the  opinion  that  lack of vision for  human resource management and  lack of a concrete policy  led to and sudden
increase in work force in HSCL.  The Committee further  opines  that HSCL's present suffering is due to error of
judgment and some elements were beyond  the  control of   management   and Government due to prevailing 
circumstances, lack of managerial vision and manpower policy added to the woes  of HSCL.
 
( Para 1.4)
 
The Committee, while taking note of the current financial performance of HSCL  expresses its concern over its pathetic
conditions,  and is of the view  that  HSCL  needs  improvement for  better financial   performance.  HSCL  requires a 
new vision, new managerial  will and effective strategy for the  continuance  of  its existence.
( Para : 2.2)
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Government for approving the  financial restructuring proposal. 
Considering the  fact that resources are limited the  sanctioning    of revival  package  having financial implication is a 
considered decision of the Government.  Committee also appreciates the Ministry of Steel for its consistent    efforts in
persuading the Ministry of Finance for  giving   revival package  to  HSCL.   The  Committee notes the provisions  of
revival package for  HSCL.
 ( Para 3.2)
 
Implementation status
 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has taken action  on all provisions contained in the  revival
package.  The Committee hopes that efforts  of the Ministry of Steel in  persuading   the Department of Revenue  for
exempt  of  corporate  tax for HSCL would have a positive impact on the financial performance of HSCL.  The
Committee further  hopes that  consequent upon the  separation of  7,106  employees and reduction in the wage bill, the
financial ratio of the company  would further improve.
( Para 4.2)
 
The Committee understands that it is but natural that the accumulated loss of the company would come down once the
Government  grants waiver of interest Government loans, so far the same is a book-entry and it hardly has any reflection
on the actual financial performance  of the company.

The Committee is happy to note the  savings on the specified  overheads due to  measures undertaken by HSCL 
management to rationalise administrative expenditure.   The Committee hopes that the efforts to rationalise
administrative  expenditure would continue.

The Committee observes that financial assistance-cum-restructuring package  as proposed by the Ministry of Steel and
so approved by the Government was not as  comprehensive so as to mitigate the accumulated loss and total  liability of
HSCL.  The company continues to rein in adverse financial scenario and disadvantages in  general because
implementation of the revival package would  respond  only  if approved  measures are  taken in time for total  and

         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this Eighty-sixth Report on Performance Review of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation
Ltd. (MSTC).
2.      The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee for Ministry of Steel to examine the Performance Review
of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC). The Sub-Committee visited Kolkata on 17th to 20th July, 2001 and
interacted with the Management of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).
3.      The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 14th March, 2002 heard the Secretary, Ministry of Steel and official of
MSTC. The Report has been prepared on the basis of on the spot-study by the Sub-Committee-I for the Ministry of Steel
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry and interaction with the Secretary, Ministry of
Steel and officials of Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd. (MSTC).

REPORT
         MSTC Limited (formerly known as Metal Scrap Trade Corporation Ltd.) was incorporated as a Public Limited
Company under the Companies Act, 1956 on 9 th September, 1964. The status of the company underwent change in
February, 1974 to that of a subsidiary of Steel Authority of India Limited (SAIL). In the year 1982-83, the corporation
was converted into a Government of India Company transferring the shares of SAIL to the President of India. It was the
Canalizing Agency for import of Carbon Steel Melting’s Scrap, Sponge Iron, Hot Briquette Iron and re-rolled scrap till
February, 1992. It was also the canalizing agency for import of ships for breaking till August, 1991. Presently, the
company undertakes disposal of ferrous and non-ferrous scrap arising from integrated steel plants under SAIL/RINL
etc. and disposal of scrap, surplus stores, etc. from other public sector undertakings and Government departments and
also import of ferrous and non-ferrous scarp, coke, finished steel and petroleum products. MSTC is the only Central
PSU under the Ministry of Steel to issue bonus shares.

3.0    MAIN ACTIVITIES
3.1    The Sub-Committee was informed that MSTC has manifold activities which include (i) import (ii) export (iii)
Supply of raw material to actual users (iv) supply of materials as parallel marketer and (v) Scrap/Obsolete/Surplus
disposal on behalf of plant organizations. The company has four wings for its activities namely 
(i) International marketing (ii) Domestic Marketing (iii) Management services and (iv) Finance/HRD. Head office
located at Kolkata, the company has four regional offices at Kolkata, New Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and branch offices
located at Bangalore, Vizag, Bhopal, Vadodara, Rourkela, Bokaro, Surat and New Mangalore. The Company has two
major spheres of activities i.e. Domestic Marketing and International Marketing.
3.1.0Domestic Marketing
3.1.1While a subsidiary of SAIL, MSTC started acting as selling agent of IISCO, RSP, BSL for disposal of their scrap
arising and thus started its Domestic Marketing activity. In 1993, after being de-linked from SAIL, MSTC extended its
activities to other PSUs, Government departments etc. The objective of DM is to maximize availability of indigenous
scrap by including the principals to mobilize and sell their scrap arisings/rejected/ condemned/surplus/spares/capital
equipments etc. so that the same can be recycled. The disposal action is taken in such a manner that the maximum
possible price is realized in totally transparent manner by selling the materials through open tenders, public auctions etc.
This activity was given importance only after decanalisation. The annual volume of business that was Rs.210 crore in
1992-93 reached at Rs.600 crore in 2000-2001.

3.1.5The Sub-Committee was apprised of problems being faced by MSTC in disposal of melting scrap as a whole has
gone down due to increased production of HBI that reached around five million tonnes. Many PSUs and Government
departments have their own scrap disposal set up, therefore, they are extremely reluctant to give this job to MSTC;

3.1.6The Committee understand the compelling circumstances under which the MSTC changed its focus of activities
from acting as a selling agent of SAIL to that of maximising direct marketing (DM) when MSTC got de-linked from
SAIL in 1993. The Committee appreciates the change in strategy in post-decanalised phase of imports. The Committee
is pleased to observe the performance of MSTC in direct marketing and hopes that an all out efforts would be taken by
MSTC management to strengthen the marketing activities to improve upon financial performance to a new commanding
heights.
3.1.7The Committee understands the problems being faced by MSTC in carrying out business in a situation when
demand for melting scrap is going down due to increased production of HBI and also because of setting up of scrap
disposal unit set up by PSUs and other Government departments, MSTC management has to chalk out ‘new strategy’ to
combat the situation. The Committee feels that provided the Ministry of Steel adhere to the principle of generating an
atmosphere of inter-PSU cooperation and take concrete steps towards assisting MSTC in procuring work-order from
Government PSU, the problems of MSTC could be sorted out to a great extent. The Committee may be apprised about
the action taken by the Ministry in this direction.

10.0  PROCUREMENT OF WORKORDER FROM SAIL, RINL  AND RAILWAYS
10.1  The MSTC management stated that MSTC has been making constant efforts for getting business from SAIL and
RINL. But due to upgradation of technology, availability of scrap for disposal has been reduced. MSTC is, however,
striving to make marketing of semis and fixed products of the plants during 2001-2002. MSTC has already worked in
this direction.
10.2  Attempts have been made by MSTC on a number of occasions to get business from Railways. However, no
success could be achieved. In the latest round of efforts, a proposal was sent to Member, Engineering and Member,
Mechanical, Railway Board on 15.1.1999 and this was followed by personal visits. However, when no reply was
received, the matter was taken up through Ministry of Steel and the then Hon’ble Minister of Steel wrote to his
counterpart in Railway Ministry on 30.7.1999. This was followed by a letter to Chairman, Railway Board on 23.8.1999.
Ultimately that resulted in a meeting at the Railway Ministry on 24.5.2000 when a presentation was made. Thereafter,
as per suggestion of the Railways, MSTC officials visited various Railways and proposals were sent to Railway Board.
Since no response was coming from Railways, the matter was once again taken up through Steel Ministry and the
Minister of State for Steel has written to the Minister of Railways on 13.7.2001.
10.3  The CMD, MSTC management stated ----
“As far as business is concerned, MSTC could not make any breakthrough in the Railways scrap business in spite
of letters written by the Hon’ble Steel Minister to his counterpart in the Railways and in spite of the instructions by
the Railways and in spite of the instructions by the Railway Minister, nothing progressed. Therefore, he sought
help from the Committee to get the Railway business.”
10.4  MSTC did take part in some of the tenders floated by Railways for appointing auctioneers in the past. However, it
was seen that the rates obtained by Railways were very low, hence MSTC has stopped taking part in tenders of
Railways. MSTC has indicated a service charge of 2 per cent to the Railways and has requested Railways to try MSTC
at least on a trial basis.
10.5  Replying to the Sub-Committee’s query regarding the role of the Ministry of Steel in helping MSTC in procuring
work order the Ministry stated that MSTC has gradually been attracting more customers through periodic
advertisements, personal contact etc. most of the central PSUs, having a reasonable volume of metal scrap arising, are
already doing business with MSTC. The e-auction portal which is being introduced, is also expected to attract more
customers. The Railway Board at present gets private auctioneers to conduct their auction at very low rates, which
MSTC cannot match. MSTC believes that the rates obtained by Railways are not viable rates. It is true that RINL do not
use MSTC’s services (except for conducting a few auctions) as they manage bulk of their disposals departmentally.
Ministry of Steel has always come forward to help MSTC whenever approached for help.

13.0  PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY MSTC
13.1  Sale Tax Structure
         13.1.1Pointing out the lacuna in the Sales Tax Structure, MSTC management informed the Sub-Committee that a
provision in the recent budget allows the State Governments to impose central sales tax on declared goods at
a rate higher than 4% and also empower them to impose multi-point tax. If the States use these powers, this
will make the job of trading extremely difficult, while a uniform system of VAT will be ideal, uniformity in
the matter of sales tax i.e. one point tax whether CST of LST, shall go a long way in helping traders
particularly the trading houses carrying on trading in more than State in the country.
         13.1.2The Committee understands the problems being faced by trading organisation due to prevalence of multi-
point tax-structure. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Steel should take up the
matter with the Ministry of Finance and State Governments. The proposal of uniform system of VAT and
one-point tax may be examined and if found feasible, steps in this regard may be taken at the earliest.
13.2.0         Requirement of submission of end-use certificates for imported melting scrap
         13.2.1As regards the provision for requirement of submission of end-use certificates for imported melting scrap,
the Sub-Committee was informed that on import of melting scrap, the end use certificate is required to be
submitted by the actual users within six months. The main reason for this is to eliminate the misuse of scrap
imported for melting, being used for re-rolling. As a trader, MSTC sells such melting scrap to actual users
only but have to depend on the actual users to submit end-use certificate issues by Central Excise
Department after the melting scrap sold to them has been consumed. In the event of actual users’ failure to
obtain end-use certificate from the Central Excise, MSTC has to pay higher rate of duty on the material
imported. This requirement should, therefore, be withdrawn.
         13.2.2The Committee is of the opinion that the Government should evolve alternative effective mechanism to
check the misuse of scrap imported for melting, being used for re-rolling.

         13.2.3The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should approach the Ministry of Finance
(Department of Excise) for withdrawing the provision for requirement of submission of end-users certificate
for imported melting scrap. If the Ministry of Finance remains unmoved the provision may be made for
early submission of end-use certificate by the actual users’ and in case of default, a certain the penalty may
be imposed on the defaulter. The Committee is of the view that MSTC should not be subjected to imposition
of higher rate of duty for the default committed by the actual users.
13.3.0         Requirement of availing services of trans-chart for hiring ships for imports
         13.3.1The Sub-Committee was apprised that as per existing procedure, PSUs are to import materials on FOB basis
and shipping arrangement is to be made through Ministry of Shipping (Trans-chart). In case Trans-chart is
unable to arrange shipping, necessary waiver is to be obtained by PSUs form Trans-chart before finalising
contract on C&F basis. Import contracts by MSTC are finalised at very short notice. Since it is seldom
possible to fix a vessel through Trans-chart in the short time available, MSTC is compelled to continue
imports on C&F basis for shipload cargoes. It would be in the fitness of things, especially in the liberalized
scenario, to do away with the requirement of approaching Trans-chart.
         13.3.2The Committee understands that since MSTC finalise import contracts usually in a short span of time so it is
difficult on the part of MSTC to fix a vessel through Ministry of Shipping (Trans-chart). Therefore, the
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Steel should take the matter with the Ministry of Shipping and
help MSTC out by doing away with the requirement of approaching Trans-chart.
13.3.3The Committee notes that MSTC is one of the few Government companies which has successfully withstood
the impact of post liberalization era by changing its strategy according to the need of the situation. The
Committee hopes that the Ministry of Steel would extend a helping hand to the company in sorting out its
problems so that it can fetch a better price from the prospective buyers.
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE 
AT A GLANCE
CAPITAL  STRUCTURE
         The Committee notes that the company has an authorised Capital of Rs.5 crore and paid up capital of Rs.2.20 crore
as on 31.3.2001 of which approximately 90 per cent of the shares are held by the President of India and the balance 10
per cent by the members of Steel Furnaces Association of India and Iron & Steel Scrap Association of India and others.
The Committee recommends that MSTC management would take every step to ensure that capital restructuring of
MSTC take place in such a way that return on investment (ROI) is maximum.                                          (Para : 2.3)
MAIN ACTIVITIES
         The Committee understand the compelling circumstances under which the MSTC changed its focus of activities
from acting as a selling agent of SAIL to that of maximising direct marketing (DM) when MSTC got de-linked from
SAIL in 1993. The committee appreciates the change in strategy in post-decanalised phase of imports. The Committee is
pleased to observe the performance of MSTC in direct marketing and hopes that an all out efforts would be taken by
MSTC management to strengthen the marketing activities to improve upon financial performance to a new commanding
heights.         (Para : 3.1.6)
         The Committee understands the problems being faced by MSTC in carrying out business in a situation when
demand for melting scrap is going down due to increased production of HBI and also because of setting up of scrap
disposal unit set up by PSUs and other Government departments, MSTC management has to chalk out ‘new strategy’ to
combat the situation. The Committee feels that provided the Ministry of Steel adhere to the principle of generating an
atmosphere of inter-PSU cooperation and take concrete steps towards assisting MSTC in procuring work-order from
Government PSU, the problems of MSTC could be sorted out to a great extent. The Committee may be apprised about
the action taken by the Ministry in this
direction.                                                                                                                      
(Para : 3.1.7)
INTERNATIONAL MARKETING
         The Committee is pleased to note the performance of MSTC in international marketing and appreciates the
strategy of MSTC management for enlarging its import basket in post decanalised phase to compete with other private
parties engaged in similar business.                                                                                                            (Para : 3.2.5)
         The Committee feels that with the revival of steel industry and undergoing process of strengthening of anti-
dumping the prospect of MSTC business in international market would lead to opening of new avenues.
                                                                                                                                        (Para : 3.2.6)
         The Committee further hopes that MSTC management would chalk out strategy to ensure its survival while

production and is a trading company, however, steps taken towards modernisation and restructuring would help in
improving its operational efficiency and managerial effectiveness. The Committee is of the firm view that
modernisation in the process and system of working of the company would have a definite bearingon the physical and
financial performance of the company. The steps taken to modernise and restructure the communication and expansion
in the domestic as well as international marketing division would yield positive fruits in the functioning of the company,

enlarging import basket would add to the profitability of the

PERFORMANCE OF MSTC
         The Committee observes that the activities of MSTC has undergone noticeable change with the changing scenario
of steel industry, change in the Government policy i.e. from canalisation to the de-canalisation of imports and in
accordance with market perspective. The MSTC, which acted earlier as a selling agency for SAIL in respect of their
melting scrap arising, has started to carry the business with the other Government PSU when SAIL started selling
melting scrap directly. MSTC went, rightly, for strengthening of Direct-marketing when the Government policy stood
for de-canalisation of import. Although the performance of MSTC suffered to some extent during these phase of
tumultuous change, however, it is the managerial skill which led MSTC for changing business gear and it is the
concerted employees’ commitment which has got a bearing on the physical and financial performance of the company.
The Committee acclaims the performance of MSTC and hope that an all out effort on the part of the management and
employees would continue to improve the financial performance of the company to a new
zenith.                                                                                           (Para : 5.4)

         The Committee observes that MSTC is coming out of the woods and doing excellent performance as is reflected
from MoU rating as awarded by Department of Public Enterprises after taking into various parameters of performance
into consideration. The Committee wishes its best for MSTC for continuing its excellent performance in forthcoming
years and hopes that MoU system would always act as a catalyst to improve the physical and financial performance of
the company.         (Para : 6.3)

         The Committee is pleased to note that MSTC management is giving due consideration to diversification plans and
entering into joint ventures. The Committee is of the opinion that in the prevailing market Competitive era,
diversification of activities’ and projection of business through partnership/joint ventures has almost become a corporate
culture. MSTC is moving in the right direction by adopting the canons of modern days business practice. The
Committee hopes that MSTC, whether in existing structure i.e. as a PSU or in the post divested phase would continue its
efforts towards adopting the prevailing precepts and strategy in accordance with changing market scenario.
